title: Spatial-UMI-Dream: Scaling World Action Models with Metric Geometry for UMI Manipulation
summary: The Universal Manipulation Interface (UMI) enables scalable demonstration collection independently of a specific robot. However, its moving, close-range gripper cameras entangle camera and object motion without a stable external view, leaving the metric geometry needed for precise manipulation implicit in RGB. We introduce Spatial-UMI-Dream, a 5B spatial World Action Model (WAM) pretrained on 605 hours of RGB-D UMI data through two-stage training -- world-only adaptation followed by joint world-action learning -- to jointly predict future RGB, fisheye-aligned metric depth, and actions. Stereo-derived depth makes scene scale and spatial relationships explicit within a unified dual-gripper RGB-D representation. Furthermore, evaluating UMI policies requires testing whether UMI's robot-independent demonstration collection translates into policy generalization across robot embodiments, alongside robustness to environmental changes. We introduce RoboTwin-UMI, a twenty-task simulation benchmark built on RoboTwin with UMI wrist-mounted fisheye observations, enabling controlled, repeatable evaluation of UMI policies under environment and embodiment changes separately and jointly without additional fine-tuning. On RoboTwin-UMI, Spatial-UMI-Dream achieves 79.10% in-domain success and 72.15% under combined embodiment and environment shifts, exceeding the strongest evaluated baseline in each setting by 4.65 and 10.30 percentage points, respectively. It also exhibits the smallest success-rate drop under embodiment transfer among the evaluated policies. In a matched pretraining ablation, RGB-only pretraining leads to a 5.75-percentage-point decrease in in-domain success compared with RGB-D pretraining. Across six real-world tasks, Spatial-UMI-Dream achieves 85.0% average success, exceeding the strongest baseline by 24.2 percentage points. Project page: https://weiduoyuan.com/spatial-umi-dream/

INTRODUCTION sec:introduction The Universal Manipulation Interface (UMI)~ chi2024universalmanipulationinterfaceinthewild enables scalable collection of manipulation demonstrations without requiring a robot at the demonstration site. Its portable handheld grippers record close-range video and embodiment-agnostic end-effector trajectories during in-the-wild human manipulation. These demonstrations provide interaction data for learning policies that can execute manipulation skills across tasks, environments, and robot embodiments. Vision-Language-Action models (VLAs) and World Action Models (WAMs) offer two approaches to learning manipulation policies. VLAs~ intelligence2025pi05visionlanguageactionmodelopenworld,wei2026psi0,liu2026rdt2exploringscalinglimit,kim24openvla build on pretrained vision-language models to predict robot actions from visual observations and language instructions. WAMs~ ye2026worldactionmodelszeroshot,nvidia2026cosmos3omnimodalworld,dyna2026dyna2 instead build on pretrained video generation models to jointly predict future visual observations and actions. This joint prediction connects actions with the resulting scene changes. Future video supplies supervision across space and time, while pretrained video diffusion models provide priors over motion and scene dynamics. Although WAMs have shown promising results with RGB observations, applying them to UMI data presents two challenges. First, RGB-only models leave the metric geometry needed for manipulation implicit in appearance and image-space motion. UMI has no fixed third-person view, and its gripper-mounted fisheye cameras move with the grippers during close-range manipulation. Changes in the images therefore reflect camera motion, object motion, and scene geometry. In bimanual manipulation, both views move independently, while the model must coordinate two grippers in a shared three-dimensional workspace. The model must therefore infer scene scale and spatial relationships from RGB alone. Second, in-domain task success alone is insufficient to evaluate UMI policies. Lighting and scene appearance can vary substantially in wrist-camera observations, and demonstrations collected in a limited set of environments may not cover these variations. Moreover, because UMI decouples demonstration collection from a specific robot, cross-embodiment transfer is central to evaluating UMI policies. Evaluation must therefore test both robustness to environmental changes and the ability to transfer learned skills across robot embodiments. To address these challenges, we introduce , a spatial WAM that incorporates metric depth, and , a benchmark for evaluating UMI policies across environments and robot embodiments. is a 5B spatial WAM pretrained on hours of RGB-D UMI data to jointly predict future RGB, metric depth, and robot actions. Training proceeds in two stages: world-only adaptation to UMI RGB-D observations, followed by joint world-action learning. We recover metric depth from calibrated stereo observations and align it with the raw fisheye RGB images. Metric depth makes scene scale and the spatial layout around each gripper explicit, reducing the need to infer this information from RGB alone. We arrange both grippers' aligned RGB-D observations in a unified video canvas, incorporating geometry into world-action modeling while retaining the pretrained video tokenizer and WAM backbone. is a twenty-task benchmark built on RoboTwin~ chen2025robotwin that reproduces UMI's wrist-mounted fisheye observations. Simulation enables controlled, repeatable evaluation of the same tasks across different environments and robot embodiments. This supports testing both environmental robustness and cross-embodiment transfer, which is particularly important because UMI demonstrations are collected independently of a specific robot. The benchmark provides a common closed-loop protocol for comparing UMI policies in both in-domain and generalization settings. Environment and embodiment shifts are tested separately and jointly under a consistent UMI observation interface, with all generalization tests using the trained policies without additional fine-tuning. achieves 79.10 in-domain success on and 85.0 average success across six real-world tasks, exceeding the strongest evaluated baselines by 4.65 and 24.2 percentage points, respectively. Its advantage extends to generalization: the lead over the strongest baseline widens to 14.00 percentage points after embodiment transfer, and remains the strongest policy under environmental and joint shifts. Our contributions are twofold: Spatial world-action modeling at scale. We introduce with two-stage training on hours of RGB-D UMI data, achieving the highest in-domain and generalization success rates among evaluated policies. Ablations demonstrate the benefit of metric depth and progressive gains from the two training stages. A benchmark for UMI policy generalization. We develop the twenty-task benchmark with wrist-mounted fisheye observations and a common protocol for evaluating in-domain performance and generalization across environments and robot embodiments, including their combined shifts. RELATED WORK sec:related-work Robot Foundation Models subsec:related-foundation-models Robot foundation models seek to reuse broad visual-language knowledge for control~ kim24openvla,wu2026largerewardmodelsgeneralizable , enabling policies to interpret diverse scenes and instructions without learning each task in isolation. Representative action-centric Vision-Language-Action models~ intelligence2025pi05visionlanguageactionmodelopenworld,wei2026psi0,liu2026rdt2exploringscalinglimit,kim24openvla adapt pretrained vision-language representations to predict robot actions from visual observations and language instructions. However, predicting actions alone does not explicitly describe how the scene is expected to evolve, leaving future outcomes unavailable as a direct policy context or planning signal. More recent methods~ intelligence2026pi07steerablegeneralistrobotic,jia2026dreamplanefficientreinforcementfinetuning,zhang2026foreactsteeringvlaefficient introduce world models into this paradigm without fully coupling world and action generation. By using predicted visual futures as policy context or planning supervision, these approaches improve policy generalization and planning while retaining a separation between world prediction and action generation. World Action Models~ ye2026worldactionmodelszeroshot,nvidia2026cosmos3omnimodalworld,dyna2026dyna2,bi2025motusunifiedlatentaction instead jointly generate future observations and actions, directly connecting predicted scene evolution with control. Traditional RGB-only WAMs leave metric geometry implicit in visual appearance. In contrast, jointly predicts RGB, registered metric depth, and actions, making metric geometry an explicit component of the world state. Geometry-Aware Robot Learning subsec:related-geometry Geometric representations support spatial reasoning in robotic perception and control~ bevcalib,Ze2024DP3,3d_diffuser_actor,nguyen2026iclrincontextimitationlearning , providing explicit cues about scene layout and spatial relationships. 3D visuomotor policies explicitly encode depth or point clouds into geometric scene features, allowing action prediction to operate on metric structure rather than infer it only from visual appearance. Spatially grounded Vision-Language-Action models~ zhen20243dvla,qu2025spatialvla further incorporate explicit spatial representations into language-conditioned action prediction. Representation-aligned policies~ li2026spatialforcing,sun2026rocket instead distill geometric features from pretrained 3D models into RGB policy backbones, providing spatial supervision without requiring explicit 3D inputs at deployment. In contrast, treats metric depth as an observed and predicted component of the world state rather than only as a policy input or representation-level training target. It jointly predicts dual-gripper RGB, metric depth, and actions through a unified video canvas, without a separate 3D encoder or alignment teacher. UMI Data and Evaluation subsec:related-benchmarks Diverse robot datasets and standardized evaluation platforms~ zhao2026humanoideverydaycomprehensiverobotic,wei2026simple support systematic comparison of learned manipulation policies. UMI~ chi2024universalmanipulationinterfaceinthewild enables robot-independent demonstration collection by recording wrist-mounted fisheye observations and end-effector trajectories with a portable handheld gripper. Large-scale robot policies~ liu2026rdt2exploringscalinglimit,generalist2026gen15,zhang2026hy leverage UMI and UMI-style handheld demonstrations for generalist control and zero-shot cross-embodiment transfer. More recent UMI-oriented VLA training~ yang2026vista studies fisheye-aware visual grounding and embodiment-conditioned physical validation to reconcile handheld demonstrations with pretrained visual representations and target-robot constraints. UMI demonstrations collected across diverse scenes support learning policies beyond a single environment, motivating evaluation under environmental changes. Moreover, because UMI decouples demonstration collection from a specific robot, cross-embodiment evaluation tests whether this flexibility also carries over to the learned policies. title: Wide View Synthesis from Overlapping Perspective Cameras in Autonomous Driving
summary: Multi-perspective-camera systems are widely adopted since they provide broad visual coverage for autonomous driving, motivating the synthesis of a unified wide view from spatially separated observations. In this work, we formulate wide view synthesis (WVS), which aims to synthesize a geometrically consistent wide view at a specified virtual viewpoint from multiple perspective cameras. Unlike conventional image stitching, WVS requires reasoning about 3D geometry and visibility to handle depth-dependent parallax and occlusions arising from spatially separated camera centers. While vanilla 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) enables high-fidelity view synthesis, its reliance on per-scene optimization limits its applicability to driving scenes. Furthermore, WVS introduces additional challenges, *e.g.*, peripheral stretching under perspective projection and photometric inconsistencies across cameras. To address these challenges, we propose **Wide-View Gaussian Splatting (WV-GS)**, a feed-forward Gaussian-splatting framework that synthesizes wide views without per-scene optimization. Specifically, we introduce Piecewise Perspective Rendering (PPR) to mitigate peripheral stretching through local perspective projections sharing a common camera center, and Spatial Affine Photometric Modeling (SAPM) to account for camera-dependent photometric variations during training. We further introduce **WideDrive**, a synthetic benchmark providing dense ground-truth wide views and adapt a LiDAR-projected sparse-reference protocol to real-world datasets. Extensive experiments on multiple datasets demonstrate the effectiveness of WV-GS for WVS. Dataset and code will be publicly released.

Introduction sec:intro Multi-perspective-camera systems are widely employed in autonomous driving to provide comprehensive visual coverage through complementary and partially overlapping fields of view (FOVs) huang2021bevdet . These cameras collectively observe a wide area, but their images depict the scene from different viewpoints. Synthesizing a unified wide view at a specified virtual viewpoint would bring these complementary observations into a geometrically coherent image, combining broad visual coverage with a consistent viewing perspective. In this work, we formalize wide view synthesis (WVS), which aims to synthesize a geometrically consistent, wide-FOV image at a specified virtual viewpoint from synchronized observations captured by spatially separated, calibrated perspective cameras. Limited overlap, depth-dependent parallax, and occlusions make WVS quite challenging. Conventional image stitching methods often struggle under these conditions, producing geometric inconsistencies and visible artifacts ( ). More fundamentally, conventional image stitching methods primarily rely on image alignment and warping, rather than explicitly modeling scene geometry and visibility at the target virtual viewpoint apap, udis2 . While vanilla 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) 3dgs enables high-quality and efficient rendering, its reliance on per-scene optimization limits its applicability to unseen driving scenes. Although feed-forward Gaussian splatting variants anysplat, yonosplat, vggt, dggt provide a promising alternative by predicting scene representations without per-scene optimization at inference time, directly extending these methods to WVS introduces two additional challenges. First, even with accurate 3D geometry, rendering a wide-view image using a single perspective projection introduces pronounced stretching toward the image boundaries. Second, differences in exposure, white balance, and camera response introduce photometric inconsistencies across input views. Direct supervision with these inconsistent observations can entangle camera-dependent photometric variations with the underlying scene appearance, potentially introducing brightness and color discontinuities in the synthesized wide view ( ). To address these challenges, we propose , a feed-forward Gaussian splatting framework for WVS ( ). To mitigate peripheral stretching, we introduce Piecewise Perspective Rendering (PPR) that renders the predicted Gaussian representation through multiple local perspective projections sharing a common optical center, thereby reducing peripheral stretching while maintaining a consistent virtual viewpoint ( ). To address cross-camera photometric inconsistencies, we introduce Spatial Affine Photometric Modeling (SAPM), which predicts per-pixel affine color transformations conditioned on spatial and camera features to accommodate cross-camera photometric variations during training. By modeling camera-dependent photometric variations during training, SAPM encourages the learning of consistent scene appearance across views ( ). Two modules operate at complementary stages: PPR modifies the rendering process, while SAPM adapts photometric supervision during training. However, evaluating WVS in real-world driving scenes poses an additional challenge as existing datasets such as nuScenes nuscenes and Lyft lyft lack ground-truth wide-FoV images. To enable quantitative evaluation, we adapt the LiDAR-Projected Sparse-Reference (LPSR) protocol lan2026geo, arbiviewgen to construct sparse target-view references from synchronized camera images and LiDAR measurements. We further incorporate histogram matching (HM) to mitigate photometric discrepancies during evaluation. To complement sparse evaluation with dense ground truth, we introduce , a synthetic benchmark built on CARLA carla with dense, pixel-aligned ground-truth wide views for comprehensive quantitative evaluation (see ). Our are summarized as follows. First, we formalize WVS as a novel task that aims to synthesize a geometrically consistent wide view from partially overlapping perspective images captured by spatially separated cameras. Second, we propose WV-GS, a feed-forward Gaussian splatting framework that combines PPR and SAPM to address peripheral stretching and cross-camera photometric inconsistencies, respectively. Third, we establish an evaluation framework for WVS by adapting an LPSR protocol for real-world datasets and introducing WideDrive, a synthetic benchmark with dense ground-truth wide views. Related Work sec:related_work Image stitching. Traditional image stitching aligns and blends overlapping images using 2D transformations, ranging from global homographies to spatially varying warps designed to accommodate parallax and preserve scene structure autostitch, udis2, chang2014shape . Learning-based approaches further improve alignment and parallax handling through unsupervised learning and adaptive warping nie2021unsupervised, udis2, rewarp, ropstitch, unistitch , while video stitching methods additionally address temporal consistency stabstitch++ . Despite these advances, most stitching methods remain centered on 2D image alignment and warping, rather than explicitly synthesizing a geometrically consistent view by reasoning about 3D scene geometry and visibility at a specified virtual viewpoint. Neural rendering Neural radiance fields (NeRFs) nerf and 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) 3dgs have advanced novel view synthesis (NVS) through learned 3D scene representations. Recent feed-forward methods enable generalizable Gaussian reconstruction charatan2024pixelsplat, chen2024mvsplat, anysplat, yonosplat and geometric prediction vggt, omnivggt without per-scene optimization. Beyond conventional NVS, MVSplat360 chen2024mvsplat360 combines Gaussian reconstruction with generative priors for 360-degree synthesis, while panoramic methods choi2023egonerf, li2025omnigs, huang2025scomnigs, chen2025splatter360 support omnidirectional rendering. Other methods accommodate wide-angle and distorted cameras through lens calibration or generalized Gaussian projection deng2025self, wu20253dgut . While these methods advance scene reconstruction and flexible-view rendering, our work focuses on synthesizing geometrically consistent wide-view images from spatially separated perspective cameras, with PPR specifically designed to mitigate projection-induced peripheral stretching. Cross-view photometric consistency Photometric variations across images have been addressed through appearance embeddings martinbrualla2021nerfw, chen2022hallucinated , exposure and camera-response modeling huang2022hdrnerf , and appearance modeling in Gaussian splatting kulhanek2024wildgaussians, shimomura2026p2gs . Related color correction techniques have also been explored in image stitching bellavia2018dissecting . Unlike methods that primarily model image-dependent appearance during scene optimization, our SAPM incorporates spatially varying, camera-conditioned affine transformations into feed-forward training supervision to account for cross-camera photometric discrepancies. title: CRISP: Constraint-Resolved Interactions between Subsystems for Predictive Whole-Body Cooperation
summary: This paper presents a layered control framework that recasts high-dimensional system dynamics as a composition of dynamically interconnected subsystems, with dynamic dual-arm manipulation on the humanoid serving as a representative application. The humanoid is decomposed into a single rigid body (SRB) representing the torso and floating-base dynamic models representing the articulated arms and lower-body. The rigid connections between arm and torso and the closed kinematic chain formed between the end-effectors during cooperative manipulation are represented as holonomic constraints. The corresponding Lagrange multipliers parametrize the interaction wrenches transmitted at the shoulders and between the end-effectors. The high-level nonlinear model predictive control (NMPC) jointly optimizes the subsystem state trajectories, arm torques, ground reaction forces (GRFs), and interaction wrenches, enabling online wrench design and optimization while preserving the dynamic coupling among the independently modeled subsystems. The optimized arm torques are applied directly for cooperative dual-arm manipulation, whereas the prescribed GRFs are mapped to lower-body joint torque for whole-body coordination. We validate the proposed framework through numerical simulations and hardware experiments on a G1 humanoid robot. The results demonstrate optimal interaction wrenches consistent with simulated contact measurement, cooperative dual-arm trajectory tracking, and stable whole-body coordination while executing the NMPC in online manner.

Introduction Recent advances in whole-body force control have enabled humanoid robots to exploit highly articulated arms together with coordinated whole-body motion for manipulation and multi-contact interaction nori2015icub, garcia2019integration, rouxel2024multi . Extending such capabilities to dynamic dual-arm manipulation of a commonly grasped object, however, remains challenging. In a floating-base system, the manipulation wrenches applied at the end-effectors are coupled with the generalized dynamics and must be reconciled with the support wrenches required to maintain balance garcia2019integration, abi2019torque . Consequently, inaccurate or incomplete treatment of these wrenches can degrade both manipulation tracking and whole-body balance feasibility. Related Works Accounting for the interaction forces by explicitly regulating end-effector forces through hybrid position/force or impedance control bonitz1996internal, caccavale2008six, heck2013internal , or by incorporating measured or estimated contact wrenches into a whole-body controller nori2015icub, rouxel2024multi has been studied. Although force feedback provides direct information about contact conditions and load transmission, these methods often rely on wrist-mounted force/torque sensors, distributed force or tactile sensing, or an auxiliary model-based wrench estimator. Sensorless approaches alleviate the sensing requirement by analytically predicting or optimizing contact forces, but introduce additional dependence on the object model, contact model, and force-estimation procedure shahbazi2017inverse, ren2017adaptive, lin2018projected . Accounting for the interaction forces becomes particularly important when both hands rigidly grasp a common object. The two arms and the object then form a closed kinematic chain (see Fig. fig:hero ), and the end-effector wrenches contain not only a resultant component that drives the object motion, but also an internal component that does not produce net object wrench williams1993virtual, erhart2015internal, erhart2016model . Such internal wrenches cannot, in general, be characterized independently for each arm because they depend on the coupled kinematic constraints and the load distribution across the closed-chain system. Moreover, the load distribution is not uniquely determined by the grasp matrix alone erhart2015internal , and even small inconsistencies in the closed-chain kinematics can lead to excessive internal loading and degraded control performance ren2017adaptive . Constrained dynamics formulations provide a systematic representation of reaction forces through the Lagrange multipliers associated with holonomic constraints in various different system setups de2005operational, aghili2005unified, kim2023layered, sambhus2026nonlinear . Similarly, optimization-based inverse dynamics controllers for floating-base robots treat contact wrenches as optimization variables so that they remain consistent with the full-body dynamics and contact constraints righetti2013optimal . For fixed-base dual-arm systems, internal and contact forces have also been parametrized through constraint directions or recovered using orthogonal and projected inverse dynamics, reducing the need for direct force measurements ren2017adaptive, shahbazi2017inverse, lin2018projected . Nevertheless, existing formulations primarily address either fixed-base cooperative manipulation, contact forces between robot and environment, or closed chains embedded in the mechanical structure of the robot sovukluk2023whole . Although dual-arm interaction wrenches have been incorporated into humanoid whole-body controllers garcia2019integration, teng2026passive , jointly recovering the internal interaction wrench induced by the dual-arm and object within the floating-base whole-body optimization remains comparatively less explored. Contributions This work addresses the challenge of accounting for interaction wrenches induced by closed-chain couplings during dynamic dual-arm manipulation and rigid connections between subsystems while maintaining dynamically consistent whole-body cooperation (see Fig. fig:hero ). To this end, we propose an optimization based whole-body cooperation framework with nonlinear model predictive control (NMPC) that represents both the object mediated coupling between the arms and the interfaces between the arms and torso as holonomic constraints. This formulation recasts the complex humanoid system as a composition of dynamically coupled subsystems, while the Lagrange multipliers associated with their interconnection constraints parametrize the transmitted interaction wrenches. These wrenches are then jointly optimized with the whole-body motion and control inputs. Moreover, the unified constraint representation preserves dynamically consistent interactions across subsystem boundaries, providing a scalable basis for composing and extending whole-body models. We further validate the framework through dynamic dual-arm manipulation experiments on a humanoid robot where an upper-body is tracking the optimal control inputs from the proposed control framework while the low-level controller on the lower-body further enables the prescribed optimal ground reaction forces (GRFs) on torso. The main contributions of this work are as follows: A modular holonomic-constraint formulation that represents both the object-mediated closed-chain coupling between the arms and the structural coupling between the arms and torso, enabling the high Degrees of Freedom (DOFs) system, like humanoid, to be modeled as a composition of dynamically interconnected subsystems. An optimization-based layered whole-body cooperation architecture that jointly computes the whole-body motion, control inputs, and interaction wrenches across the subsystem interfaces, thereby enabling online wrench optimization and dynamically consistent control. Experimental validation on dynamic dual-arm manipulation tasks, demonstrating the effectiveness of the proposed constraint-resolved formulation for online interaction-wrench optimization and whole-body cooperation under structural couplings with closed-chain interactions. Holonomically Constrained Subsystems The dynamics of a humanoid are represented as a collection of subsystems connected through holonomic constraints. This modular representation illustrated in Fig. fig:overview allows the dynamics of each subsystem to be formulated independently while preserving the motion compatibility and interaction forces arising from their connections. Specifically, each subsystem retains its own coordinates and dynamics, while the holonomic constraints enforce kinematic compatibility at the arm-torso interfaces and along the closed kinematic chain formed through dual-arm manipulation. This representation provides a modular and scalable description of the high-DOF system while preserving the interaction forces transmitted among its subsystems. title: VREgo: Consumer VR Headsets for Learning Robot Manipulation from Egocentric Demonstrations
summary: VREgo trains manipulation policies from demonstrations recorded on consumer VR headsets; we instantiate it with EgoKit on one such headset, the PICO 4 Ultra. On-device head and hand tracking and stereo object localisation allow the operator to begin a demonstration at the table. We adapt HumanEgo's preprocessing to estimate grasp thresholds per recording, update object positions after release, and propagate segmentation masks between keyframes. We evaluate policies in simulation on two tabletop tasks recorded by one operator. For cube placement, we compare PICO and Project Aria recordings of the same 41 layouts. With 40 training demonstrations, the PICO policies placed the cube on the tray in 67, 74, and 60 of 100 evaluation layouts across three training seeds. The corresponding Aria results were 73, 78, and 0. For a two-stage stacking task recorded with the PICO alone, the baseline placed the block on the tray in 94 of 100 layouts and met the end-of-episode criterion for both placements in two. In one diagnostic episode, repeated replanning deferred release beyond the eight executed steps. Demonstration replays also showed that the open gripper could displace the cube before grasping it. After adapting the training trajectories and adding task-specific execution rules that use simulator object positions, the system met both placement criteria in 93.8% of episodes across four evaluation noise seeds. The same 100 layouts informed rule development and evaluation. VREgo is available at https://vrego.chuange.org/.

Introduction Head-mounted cameras can record manipulation demonstrations without requiring an operator to teleoperate a robot. EgoMimic~ kareer2025egomimic co-trains on human and robot demonstrations, whereas EgoZero~ liu2025egozero , Phantom~ lepert2025phantom and HumanEgo~ humanego2026 train manipulation policies from human demonstrations alone. We use HumanEgo as our reference. It represents a demonstration through hand trajectories, object keypoints and images in which a virtual gripper replaces the human arm. HumanEgo~ humanego2026 reports training with approximately 30 minutes of human video per task. EgoMimic~ kareer2025egomimic , EgoZero~ liu2025egozero and HumanEgo~ humanego2026 use Project Aria glasses~ engel2023project . In our Aria workflow, Meta's Machine Perception Services (MPS) process uploaded recordings to estimate head and hand poses. HumanEgo~ humanego2026 triangulates object keypoints from successive RGB views during an initial scene sweep, which can be a lateral head movement or a forward approach. We used a forward approach (the walk-up) for the matched-device comparison. Consumer VR headsets offer a different profile: they track the head and both hands on the device, and several give applications access to their see-through cameras. The PICO 4 Ultra, which we use, has two such cameras 64\,mm apart, and EgoKit~ yu2026egokit records both cameras' images together with the head pose and 26-joint hand tracking. We present VREgo, an approach that learns robot manipulation policies from such recordings. It represents a demonstration as HumanEgo does, by the hand's trajectory, the objects' keypoints and an image without the arm, and learns the same kind of policy, so HumanEgo serves as the reference throughout. VREgo differs from it in four ways: Capture device. A consumer VR headset, the PICO 4 Ultra, records the demonstrations and tracks the head and hands itself, and a stereo step locates the objects from its two cameras. Data collection. Because stereo, not head motion, supplies the parallax, the wearer stands at the table from the first frame; there is no walk-up. Pipeline. We adapted grasp labelling, object tracking and segmentation to a new operator and to recordings with two sequential moves. Execution. For a two-move task, the training records are rewritten for a gripper, and rules for executing the policy's output guide release timing, grasp position and placement. We evaluate in simulation, using a MuJoCo arm, on two tasks recorded by one operator. Task~1, a cube onto a tray, was recorded on the same 41 layouts with the PICO and with Aria glasses, the reference's device. Section~ sec:task1 summarizes the device comparison also reported in the unpublished revision of the EgoKit manuscript~ egokitrevision . Task~2, a block onto the tray and then the cube onto the block's studs, was recorded with the PICO alone and without a walk-up. We examine two failure modes of the baseline and evaluate trajectory and execution changes designed to address them. Our contributions are: A capture path from a consumer VR headset, the PICO 4 Ultra, that reproduces all 864 training images in a format-conversion test on one Aria recording and which locates objects by stereo, so that a take needs neither a cloud service nor a walk-up; A pipeline tuned to recordings from another device and operator, including two-move tasks, with each change measured on pilot takes, and fixes for defects in the reference implementation; A simulated evaluation of closed-loop policy execution and replays every demonstration's own hand path before any training, as a check on the data; A collection of 123 demonstrations on two tasks and the policies trained on them, an analysis of why the two-move task fails, and changes to the training records and to the execution of the policy's output that increase the proportion of episodes meeting both placement criteria from 2 to 93.8\, on the development layouts. Related Work EgoMimic~ kareer2025egomimic co-trains on Aria recordings of people and on robot data. EgoZero~ liu2025egozero learns from Aria recordings alone, with the hand and the objects reduced to 3D points. Phantom~ lepert2025phantom inpaints the human arm and overlays a rendered robot. HumanEgo~ humanego2026 combines an inpainted image with tokens for the hand and the objects. EgoDex~ egodex collected 829 hours with Apple Vision Pro, using the headset's own hand tracking, and EgoVLA~ yang2025egovla and EgoVerse~ punamiya2026egoverse pretrain on or pool such data at scale. Our reference is HumanEgo, whose representation of a demonstration VREgo shares; VREgo differs in how demonstrations are captured, processed and executed. Project Aria~ engel2023project records egocentric video that MPS processes; HOT3D~ banerjee2024hot3d includes recordings from Aria glasses and Quest~3 headsets, with motion-capture ground truth. UMI~ chi2024umi records with a handheld gripper and DexCap~ wang2024dexcap with motion-capture gloves. XR headsets are widely used to teleoperate robots, for example in Open-TeleVision~ cheng2024opentelevision and in XRoboToolkit~ zhao2026xrobotoolkit , which supports PICO headsets. EgoKit~ yu2026egokit exposes one recording workflow on six host devices, including the PICO 4 Ultra used here. VREgo sec:method Representation and Policy VREgo starts from the released implementation of HumanEgo~ humanego2026 , our reference, and keeps its representation of a demonstration and its policy; Section~ sec:improvements lists where the pipeline departs from it. Preprocessing turns a recording into per-frame images, camera poses and hand landmarks. In our processing configuration, motion-based phase labels separate the approach and stop from manipulation. The final second supplies training examples for the terminal-state output. A grasp label comes from the distance between the thumb and index fingertips; the configuration we evaluated counts the hand as closed while they are less than 10.5\,cm apart. Grounding DINO~ liu2024groundingdino and SAM~2~ ravi2024sam2 detect and segment each object and the arm. Twenty keypoints are picked on each object's outline, tracked with CoTracker3~ karaev2024cotracker3 , and triangulated during an object window, which in the reference is the end of the approach. The arm is removed by inpainting~ suvorov2022lama , a virtual gripper is drawn at the hand, and the objects' keypoints are drawn on them. A carried object is attached to the hand while the grasp label is closed. A flow-matching policy~ lipman2023flow takes the image together with tokens for each hand (its pose and current grasp state) and each object, and predicts the hand's pose and grasp state over the next 50 frames. A robot gripper follows the prediction in a closed loop. Hardware sec:hardware Table~ tab:devices compares the two devices. The Aria glasses recorded with HumanEgo's settings, and each take went through MPS for SLAM and hand tracking. On the PICO 4 Ultra, EgoKit recorded both see-through cameras side by side (2560\, \,960 at 30\,fps, 76 \, \,61 per eye), together with the head pose, both hands' 26 OpenXR joints, and both cameras' intrinsics and extrinsics. The hand skeleton that EgoKit can paint into the video was switched off. A take is ready for processing when the recording stops. A device-specific import stage converts the recording into images, camera poses and hand landmarks. Both devices then use the same representation, with device-specific settings for object localisation. For the PICO, this stage reads an EgoKit episode. The left eye is resized to 640\, \,480 (focal length 407\,px). The head pose is composed with the camera's extrinsic and converted from OpenXR's y-up frame to the pipeline's z-up frame. The 26 OpenXR joints are mapped to the 21 landmarks of MPS, and the wrist and palm normals, which MPS provides and OpenXR does not, are reconstructed from the knuckles. To test agreement between the two import paths, we rewrote a recording from HumanEgo's release as an EgoKit episode and processed it through VREgo's PICO path. The camera poses, the hand frames that serve as training targets, the grasp labels, the phases and the object poses match those from the Aria path to the reported precision of 0.00\,mm and 0.00 , and all 864 training frames are identical. Only the reconstructed palm orientation differs (median 0.61 ), and it feeds no training target. Stereo Localisation of Object Keypoints sec:stereo With one camera, a keypoint can be triangulated only from views taken at different places, so the reference needs the head to move during the object window; on the Aria, the walk-up provides that. VREgo adds the other eye's view of the same instant to every view the triangulator receives. The pair is rectified, so each keypoint is matched by normalized cross-correlation of the object's pixels along the same image row, at the native resolution. The triangulator itself is unchanged. On static background points 0.5--0.6\,m away, triangulated twice from two halves of a 60-frame window while the wearer stood still, the two results disagreed by 1.1--4.3\,mm with the second eye and by 9--925\,mm from the head's motion alone. For locally uniform edges parallel to an epipolar line, multiple candidate patches can yield similar correlation scores. The matcher rejects these ambiguous correspondences. On the tray this is every keypoint on its two long edges, 12 of 20.

title: Kinematic Hypothesis Context: Embodiment-Conditioned Learned Video Coding for Bandwidth-Limited Robot Policy Uplinks
comment: 15 pages, 12 figures. Preprint; supplementary material and code to be released upon formal publication
summary: Robots increasingly run large vision-language-action policies on remote servers, making the camera uplink the bottleneck. Existing video codecs spend bits on content the receiver could predict: the robot's own motion. We introduce the kinematic hypothesis context, a zero-rate conditioning signal that both ends build from joint states, the robot model and the camera calibration. Ego-motion homographies, per-link robot reprojections, an end-effector plane and a background memory warp the previous reconstruction into hypotheses that condition a learned video codec. We prove that history-only and global-pose conditioning with a limited receptive field cannot access this information under large motion, and that coding gains become task gains at the policy's success cliff. On LIBERO, the context saves 23.9% bit rate over a capacity-matched history-conditioned codec and 40-56% over x264, x265 and SVT-AV1, and needs 23.2% fewer bits than DCVC-RT at equal policy action deviation; trained to lower rates, it matches DCVC-RT in PSNR. In closed loop at equal rate, OpenVLA-OFT success nearly doubles from 22.8% to 43.1% at 6 kbps (72.6% with lower-rate training, 23.6 points above DCVC-RT), pi_0.5 success rises from 55.5% to 77.4%, and the gain grows under packet loss. The context transfers across three codec hosts and to real robot data.
full_text: Kinematic Hypothesis Context: Embodiment-Conditioned Learned Video Coding for Bandwidth-Limited Robot Policy Uplinks Lu: Kinematic Hypothesis Context for Robot Policy Uplinks Robots increasingly run large vision--language--action policies on remote servers, making the camera uplink the bottleneck. Existing video codecs spend bits on content the receiver could predict: the robot's own motion. We introduce the kinematic hypothesis context, a zero-rate conditioning signal that both ends build from joint states, the robot model and the camera calibration. Ego-motion homographies, per-link robot reprojections, an end-effector plane and a background memory warp the previous reconstruction into hypotheses that condition a learned video codec. We prove that history-only and global-pose conditioning with a limited receptive field cannot access this information under large motion, and that coding gains become task gains at the policy's success cliff. On LIBERO, the context saves 23.9 bit rate over a capacity-matched history-conditioned codec and 40--56 over x264, x265 and SVT-AV1, and needs 23.2 fewer bits than DCVC-RT at equal policy action deviation ; trained to lower rates, it matches DCVC-RT in PSNR. In closed loop at equal rate, OpenVLA-OFT success nearly doubles from 22.8 to 43.1 at 6\,kbps (72.6 with lower-rate training, 23.6 points above DCVC-RT), success rises from 55.5 to 77.4 , and the gain grows under packet loss. The context transfers across three codec hosts and to real robot data. Learned video compression, conditional coding, robot policy, task-oriented communication. Introduction sec:intro eneralist robot policies have moved to the server. Vision--language--action (VLA) models such as RT-2~ brohan2023rt2 , OpenVLA~ kim2024openvla , OpenVLA-OFT~ kim2025oft and / ~ black2024pi0,pi05 carry billions of parameters and are routinely executed on remote GPUs, while the robot streams camera observations and proprioception to the policy and receives action chunks in return~ kehoe2015cloud,ichnowski2023fogros2 . Field robots on cellular or satellite links, fleets sharing one access point and underwater platforms have uplinks of a few kilobits per second per robot. At such rates, task success is decided by what the uplink delivers. Video coding has a long record of exploiting what the decoder already knows. Motion-compensated prediction reuses the past frame~ wiegand2003h264,sullivan2012hevc,bross2021vvc , and learned codecs condition on temporal contexts mined from decoded history~ lu2019dvc,agustsson2020ssf,li2021dcvc,sheng2022tcm,li2023dcvcdc,li2024dcvcfm,jia2025dcvcrt . A robot camera stream differs from generic video because much of its temporal change is caused by the robot itself. The wrist camera moves because the arm moves; in the third-person view the arm and the grasped object sweep across the scene along trajectories fixed by the joint angles. The receiver of a remote-policy uplink knows these joint angles, which are part of the policy input, as well as the robot model and the camera calibration. Source coding with side information~ slepian1973,wyner1976,girod2005dvc shows that knowledge available at the decoder need not be transmitted again. No existing codec turns robot kinematics into a coding context : history-conditioned codecs must rediscover the robot's motion from pixels and pay bits whenever that rediscovery fails, and conditioning on a global pose vector cannot move pixel content to where it needs to be (Section~ sec:theory ). This paper introduces the kinematic hypothesis context ( ), a zero-rate conditioning signal that both ends of the link derive from shared embodiment knowledge. Given the decoded previous frame and the joint states at the previous and current transmission, builds a volume of warped references: plane-sweep homographies that explain the ego-motion of a moving camera with a one-dimensional inverse-depth search~ collins1996planesweep , a robot layer that moves every robot pixel with its own link, a plane attached to the end effector that carries grasped objects, and a decoder-side background memory that fills regions uncovered by the arm. A learned fusion network turns the volume into multi-scale contexts that condition the analysis transform, the entropy model and the synthesis transform of a conditional codec. The construction uses no bits, adds no learned parameters relative to a capacity-matched history-only counterpart, and is host-agnostic : it plugs into an implicit conditional codec, a flow-based codec and an entropy-only codec whose reconstruction stays bit-identical. Because the same hypotheses predict a whole frame without any residual, also enables kinematic SKIP: under extreme budgets the sender may transmit only a slot index, and the receiver displays the robot at its current pose instead of a stale frame. We evaluate from bits to task success (Fig.~ fig:teaser ). On the LIBERO benchmark~ liu2023libero with real bitstreams and a fully pre-registered protocol, saves 23.9 of the bit rate of a capacity-matched history-conditioned codec at equal PSNR and 49--56 relative to low-delay x264 and x265 . At equal deviation of the predicted actions, needs 23.2 fewer bits than the state-of-the-art DCVC-RT~ jia2025dcvcrt , and in the low-rate range where the closed loop operates it is on par with the offline VVC reference encoder VTM-23 in perceptual and action-level distortion, and the kinematic context lifts a 7\,M-parameter host from 37.2 behind DCVC-RT in PSNR to within 7.5 (difference not significant). In 20 , 800 paired closed-loop episodes with OpenVLA-OFT, nearly doubles task success at 6\,kbps (43.1 vs.\ 22.8 ) and adds 14.8 percentage points at 8.3\,kbps; inside the same uplink it outperforms DCVC-RT by 19.5 points at 10.7\,kbps, keeps its advantage under 10 packet loss (46.4 vs.\ 22.9 ), and raises the success of a second policy, , from 55.5 to 77.4 . Trained to lower rates with a recipe identical for both arms, -LR reaches 72.6 at 6\,kbps, 23.6 points above DCVC-RT and the equally trained history codec, and matches DCVC-RT in PSNR with 30.1 fewer bits at equal action deviation. The main contributions are: Embodiment as zero-rate side information. We formalize the embodiment information of a robot camera stream, prove that history-only and global-vector conditioning with a limited receptive field cannot exploit it under large motion, show that kinematics reduce static-scene motion to a one-dimensional family, and derive when coding gains become task-success gains (Section~ sec:theory ). The kinematic hypothesis context. We design a zero-rate hypothesis volume of plane-sweep, articulated robot-layer, end-effector-plane and background-memory hypotheses, together with its fusion into conditional, flow-based and entropy-only hosts and a kinematic SKIP mode (Section~ sec:method ). A deployable uplink. We provide a bit-exact packet protocol with lossless state coding, a leaky-bucket rate controller that tracks kilobit budgets with SKIP (x265 overshoots the same budgets by 47--64 ), offline hand--eye self-calibration from recorded data, a batched implementation, and an end-to-end latency model showing that shortens delivery time on the narrow links it targets. Causal and closed-loop evidence. With capacity-matched, shuffled-kinematics, two-reference and global-vector controls, ablations, robustness tests, real DROID data~ khazatsky2024droid , perceptual and action-level distortion measures, and 38 , 400 paired closed-loop episodes with two policies, neural and budget-compliant baselines, packet loss and a lower-rate extension, analyzed with exact tests and multiplicity control, we establish that improves both compression and task success, and we decompose the closed-loop gain into a coding part and a kinematic-synthesis part. Related Work sec:related Remote execution of robot policies. Generalist manipulation policies have grown from task-specific visuomotor networks with action chunking~ zhao2023act to vision--language--action models with billions of parameters~ brohan2023rt2,kim2024openvla,black2024pi0,pi05 . OpenVLA-OFT~ kim2025oft predicts chunks of continuous actions in parallel, and real-time chunking~ black2025rtc hides inference delay by overlapping execution and inference. Cloud and fog robotics~ kehoe2015cloud,ichnowski2023fogros2 provide the systems substrate for running such models off-board, and recent measurement and system studies of offloaded manipulation~ pohland2026offload,nguyen2026speculative identify network bandwidth and latency as the limiting resources. These works treat the observation stream as a fixed payload. Our work makes the uplink itself embodiment-aware and measures its effect on task success. Learned video compression. End-to-end video codecs replaced the hand-designed tools of H.264/AVC, HEVC, VVC and AV1~ wiegand2003h264,sullivan2012hevc,bross2021vvc,han2021av1 by learned motion estimation and residual coding~ lu2019dvc , scale-space flow~ agustsson2020ssf , feature-space alignment~ hu2021fvc , flexible-rate low-delay designs~ rippel2021elfvc and transformer entropy models~ mentzer2022vct . Conditional coding~ li2021dcvc replaced residual coding by temporal contexts; subsequent work mined multi-scale contexts~ sheng2022tcm , diversified them~ li2023dcvcdc , modulated features over long sequences~ li2024dcvcfm , and recently reached real-time operation by dropping explicit motion estimation altogether~ jia2025dcvcrt . In all of these codecs the context is a function of the decoded history only. adds a context that is a function of the embodiment, enters the same conditioning paths, and is orthogonal to architectural progress in the host. Side information and geometry-aided coding. Slepian--Wolf and Wyner--Ziv theory~ slepian1973,wyner1976 quantifies the value of side information, and distributed video coding~ girod2005dvc and learned decoder-side-information codecs~ ayzik2020dsi exploit it when only the decoder has it. Geometry enters standard coding as depth-based view synthesis prediction in the multiview and 3D extensions of HEVC~ tech2016mvhevc , which require transmitted depth maps, as global-motion initialization from inertial and positioning metadata for aerial video~ mi2019uav , and as background models for moving cameras built from estimated camera motion~ wang2018bgmoving or camera pose~ fang2024posebg . These methods describe a single rigid camera motion. Plane sweeping~ collins1996planesweep is a standard tool for multi-view matching. differs in three respects: its side information is available at both ends at zero rate, it describes an articulated body rather than one rigid motion, and it turns the unknown scene depth into a discrete hypothesis set that the network selects from per pixel. Coding for machines and task-oriented communication. Video coding for machines~ duan2020vcm and task-oriented communication~ shao2022taskoriented,gunduz2023beyond optimize transmission for a downstream model instead of a human viewer, typically measuring accuracy of an open-loop inference task. A remote robot policy closes the loop: decoded frames change actions, actions change future frames, and errors compound over hundreds of steps. We therefore evaluate in closed loop with paired episodes, connect the rate--distortion gain to the success gain analytically (Proposition~ prop:cliff ), and keep the codec task-agnostic so that the same bitstream serves any policy. title: LMGN: A Unified Policy Learning Model for Last-Mile Grasp-Navigation
summary: Legged robots equipped with manipulators have shown significant potential in the fields of daily life and industry in complex environments. However, existing methods mainly focus on global navigation or manipulation independently, while overlooking the last-mile navigation problem, where the robot must jointly determine the base placement, approach direction, and grasp execution to achieve reliable object grasping, and different manipulation stages require distinct control behaviors. To address these challenges, we propose Last-Mile Grasp-Navigation (LMGN), a unified policy learning model for Quadruped robot loco-manipulation. An Explicit Distance and Directional Reachability (ED-DR) representation is first introduced to explicitly represent the features of grasp-compatible base placement and approach direction. We then develop a semantically aligned Hierarchical Mixture-of-Experts (HMoE) policy that models stage-aware behaviors across the stages of base adjustment, pre-grasp alignment and grasp execution, and object lift. Finally, a new optimization method that jointly aligns navigation and manipulation, stage-dependent expert routing, and action-level consistency is proposed to optimize the HMoE policy. Extensive experiments on the Habitat and Isaac Gym simulators demonstrate that LMGN consistently outperforms state-of-the-art methods, denoting that integrating grasp-aware reachability with stage-aware policy learning significantly improves the success rates of last-mile navigation and target grasp for robots.
full_text: Legged robots equipped with manipulators have shown significant potential in the fields of daily life and industry in complex environments. However, existing methods mainly focus on global navigation or manipulation independently, while overlooking the last-mile navigation problem, where the robot must jointly determine the base placement, approach direction, and grasp execution to achieve reliable object grasping, and different manipulation stages require distinct control behaviors. To address these challenges, we propose Last-Mile Grasp-Navigation (LMGN), a unified policy learning model for Quadruped robot loco-manipulation. An Explicit Distance and Directional Reachability (ED-DR) representation is first introduced to explicitly represent the features of grasp-compatible base placement and approach direction. We then develop a semantically aligned Hierarchical Mixture-of-Experts (HMoE) policy that models stage-aware behaviors across the stages of base adjustment, pre-grasp alignment and grasp execution, and object lift. Finally, a new optimization method that jointly aligns navigation and manipulation, stage-dependent expert routing, and action-level consistency is proposed to optimize the HMoE policy. Extensive experiments on the Habitat and Isaac Gym simulators demonstrate that LMGN consistently outperforms state-of-the-art methods, denoting that integrating grasp-aware reachability with stage-aware policy learning significantly improves the success rates of last-mile navigation and target grasp for robots. Introduction Mobile robots that can perceive, move and manipulate are increasingly important for industrial applications, emergency response, space operations, and life services in complex environments~ bellicoso2018advances . Quadruped robots equipped with manipulators are especially promising because they combine terrain mobility with fine local interaction. They can operate on stairs, slopes, rubble, and narrow passages where conventional wheeled and humanoid robot manipulators are limited, making legged loco-manipulation an active direction in robotics~ bellicoso2019alma, liu2024visual, wang2026odyssey . Recent studies on quadruped robots equipped with manipulators have made substantial progress in navigation, obstacle traversal, and whole-body control~ wang2025quadwbg . However, in practical mobile manipulation, task success is not determined only by entering the target neighborhood. The last few steps before grasping are often decisive, which is not only a terminal correction to a path, but also a coupled local decision problem in which the robot must choose an approach direction, assess whether the current stance supports the grasp, decide whether to move the base or the arm first, and recover after a failed grasp. This is the issue of ``last-mile navigation", whose key question is how local motion should be planned to support the final grasp. Most previous studies related to last-mile navigation focus on local approach~ jauhri2024active , base placement~ makhal2018reuleaux, shao2026momapos , pre-grasp positioning~ jauhri2022robot , and final approach~ zhang2024gamma . These methods improve local correction near the target, but several limitations remain for legged robots with manipulators. Firstly, navigation and manipulation are often modeled and optimized separately. In this case, a robot may reach the target, but does not stop in a stance that supports the subsequent grasp. Secondly, existing policies often lack explicit models of distance and directional reachability in the last mile. These methods can recognize object shape and pose, but still lack a direct cue for where the robot should stand or which direction should be used for grasping. Thirdly, the loco-manipulation process is strongly stage-dependent, where approach, pre-grasp, grasp, and lift require different policy distributions. Existing loco-manipulation methods often use a single shared network, which may confuse these distributions, leading to the decrease in grasping and navigation success rates. To address these challenges, we propose Last-Mile Grasp-Navigation (LMGN), a unified policy learning model for robot loco-manipulation. Instead of treating target navigation and grasp execution as separate problems, LMGN integrates an explicit representation for grasp reachability into the last-mile navigation policy and expresses the policy distributions in different manipulation stages with Hierarchical Mixture of Experts (HMoE), so as to make the robot learn to jointly choose poses and approach directions, thus improving the loco-manipulation performance. In conclusion, this paper offers the following three contributions: 1) We propose a unified policy learning model that integrates grasp reachability into the last-mile navigation to improve the loco-manipulation performance. 2) A semantically aligned hierarchical mixture-of-experts policy and a joint optimization method are developed to express the policy distributions in different manipulation stages, improving policy expression. 3) Extensive experiments on the Habitat and Isaac Gym simulators show that LMGN consistently outperforms state-of-the-art methods in terms of gaze and grasp success rates, denoting more reliable and accurate last-mile navigation and object grasp. Related Work Legged Loco-Manipulation Legged loco-manipulation that combines the terrain mobility of quadrupeds with the local manipulation capability of robotic arms demonstrates considerable potential in industry. Modular methods that decompose the legged loco-manipulation process into separate components including locomotion, perception, planning, and manipulation~ bellicoso2019alma, yokoyama2023asc, wang2025quadwbg can leverage well-established task-specific controllers and simplify system development, but they suffer from limited coordination between modules and error accumulation. Unified methods study integrated control and long-horizon quadruped manipulation and achieved good coordination of whole-body control by optimizing the policies of leg, torso, and robotic arm~ fu2023deep, yang2023visualforce, liu2024visual . Compared to modular methods, unified methods effectively improve mobility and coordination, but control policies of different parts of the robots, such as body motion and arm manipulation, are independently optimized with different objectives, leading to the result that the robot can reach the target neighborhood but cannot reach a pose that supports the subsequent grasp. The closest baseline to our method is Visual Whole-Body Control (VBC)~ liu2024visual , which adopts a hierarchical framework, where a high-level policy predicts the robot base velocity and end-effector pose commands from visual observations, while a low-level whole-body controller tracks these commands for object grasp. However, unlike VBC, our method focuses on last-mile navigation for target grasp, where robot base placement, approach direction, and grasp execution are coupled through reachability-aware features and structured multi-stage policies. Last-Mile Navigation for Robotics Last-mile navigation refers to local decision-making after the robot has reached the target neighborhood. Geometry and planning-based methods use reachability maps~ makhal2018reuleaux , object constraints~ shao2026momapos , or active perception~ jauhri2024active to select feasible manipulation poses. These methods are interpretable, but their reliance on explicit scene models, online planning, or task-specific heuristics makes high-frequency closed-loop control difficult in dynamic local scenes. Learning-based methods introduce behavior priors, skill coordination~ jauhri2022robot,hu2023learning,Chen2024Mixed , or grasp-aware rewards into local navigation~ zhang2024gamma . Recent manipulation policies further improve robustness through primitive skills~ gu2026diffusion , flow policies~ zhang2025flowpolicy,Hu2026Enhancing , one-step learning~ sheng2026mp1 , and self-correction~ pan2025selfcorrecting . However, most of these methods focus on wheeled or indoor mobile manipulators, fixed-base manipulation, or search for an observable base pose, but do not directly model the coupled choice of quadruped base placement, approach direction, and end-effector pre-grasp motion, resulting in low grasp success rates. We address this gap by converting candidate grasps into navigation-oriented reachability features and proposing a joint optimization framework for navigation and grasp policies combined with a hierarchical MoE to align last-mile navigation with grasp execution. Problem Formulation The last-mile grasp-navigation is a local navigation for the target grasp after the robot enters the target neighborhood. The objective is not the global path search, but the joint choices of base placement, approach direction, and end-effector action within a limited local workspace. These choices should move the robot toward configurations with high grasp reachability. Therefore, we formulate the last-mile grasp-navigation as a cooperative navigation and manipulation problem rather than a local position-correction problem. Our method is based on reinforcement learning (RL) hu2026Long . The last-mile navigation policy aims to select an action to optimize a comprehensive loss that contains three components: the basic RL loss , the navigation loss , and the grasp loss , as shown by Eq. eq:last_mile_objective . where , and are the weights for the three losses, respectively. Method As shown in Fig.~ fig:gglmn_overview , the proposed LMGN takes local observations, target pose, and robot proprioceptions as inputs. GSNet~ wang2021graspness is first used to generate candidate 6D grasp poses from the object point cloud, and then the proposed ED-DR representation converts them into a grasp-guided representation that includes the grasp height, the approach direction, and the recommended relative base placement. Meanwhile, a pretrained PointNet~ qi2017pointnet is used to extract the surrounding features of the environmental point cloud. Because a feasible grasp also depends on the surrounding geometry and the current robot configuration, the policy backbone that consists of a three-layer multilayer perceptron (MLP) fuses these features with the target pose and robot proprioception. In addition, since the stages of approach, pre-grasp alignment and grasp execution, and the lift or retry require different behaviors, we develop a hierarchical MoE to express policy distributions in different manipulation stages, where semantically aligned Top-1 routing selects a stage-specific expert route and generates the base velocity, end-effector pose increment, and gripper command. In LMGN, navigation--manipulation cooperative optimization integrates stance selection, approach direction adjustment, and end effector grasping in a unified decision objective, so that the policy learns to establish executable grasp rather than merely approach the target. Grasp-Guided Navigation Feature Representation In the last-mile grasp-navigation of robots, the policy needs to infer where the robot should stand, which direction it should approach from, and whether the current base placement allows the grasp to be executed. This representation can express how the end effector should grasp, but cannot represent the relation between base placement and grasp direction, leading to the result that the robot approaches the target without reaching a favorable stance for grasp. title: Concertina: Embodying Manipulation and Cognition in One Diffusion Vision-Language Model
summary:
Most vision-language-action (VLA) policies decouple manipulation from cognition by bolting an external action mechanism onto a vision-language model (VLM)--either quantizing actions into discrete tokens whose errors bear no stable correspondence to physical displacements, or delegating continuous trajectory generation to a separate action expert whose gradients compete with or are blocked from updating the VLM backbone. We argue that manipulation and cognition should instead be embodied in the same model, shifting from a decoupled VLA to an Embodied Vision-Language Model (eVLM). We introduce Concertina, an eVLM that places continuous trajectory representation, blockwise generation, and physical-coordinate supervision directly on the computation and parameter path of a shared diffusion VLM backbone. Each control timestep is encoded as one continuous latent action token in the backbone hidden space, and the shared Transformer reconstructs temporally ordered action blocks via the same corrupt-and-reconstruct operator used for multimodal pretraining. Active action projections account for only 0.21% of parameters in the 4.46B model with zero separate action-generator layers, compared with 16.5%-35.1% dedicated action-expert capacity in representative continuous VLAs. Using our proposed Action Interface Audit, we confirm that cross-time trajectory coupling emerges in the middle and late layers of the shared backbone rather than at the action interfaces. On standard benchmarks, Concertina achieves 98.15% average success on regular LIBERO, 85.9% on the 10,030-task LIBERO-Plus benchmark, and 4.142 average completed chain length on CALVIN ABC-D.

Introduction sec:introduction The premise of vision-language-action (VLA) policies is to transfer the visual perception, semantic grounding, and generalization of pretrained vision-language models (VLMs) to physical manipulation. Beneath specific design choices lies a foundational question: how can we enable a pretrained VLM to natively output precise continuous actions while preserving its visual-language generalization, its model architecture, and its native training paradigm? Existing VLAs largely compromise on at least one of these requirements by treating action as an external attachment to a VLM---dividing manipulation and cognition across separate representations, modules, or training objectives, where the VLM handles scene and instruction understanding while another mechanism handles action representation, trajectory generation, or coordinate supervision. Our thesis is that manipulation and cognition should not be decoupled across a bolted-on VLA pipeline; they should be embodied in a single Embodied Vision-Language Model ( ). Concretely, in an , actions are represented directly in the backbone's continuous hidden space, generated across time by the same parameters and native generative operator that process vision and language, and supervised in physical coordinates end-to-end without degrading the shared VLM. Three principles motivate this shift from decoupled VLAs to a unified . First, cognition should participate in manipulation at every layer. Grasping, placement, and obstacle avoidance rely on the same spatial and physical cues as scene understanding; when trajectory generation happens outside the VLM, cognition is reduced to a one-time conditioning handoff and cannot interact with evolving action states across depth. Second, manipulation should shape cognition in return. Robot trajectories are the primary source of physical and spatial grounding for a VLM; only when continuous action gradients directly update the vision-language parameters can manipulation experience consolidate into the backbone's spatial cognition rather than remaining confined to an external head. Third, preserving the backbone's architecture, training paradigm, and representation stability enables end-to-end scaling. When cognitive and motor modules rely on incompatible paradigms or objectives, their gradients compete and degrade pretrained representations, often forcing practitioners to insulate or freeze the backbone~ knowledgeinsulation,ddvla and permanently fixing the separation between perception and control. From this perspective, conventional VLAs fail to form a unified in two primary ways (Table~ tab:arch-properties ). The first is representational decoupling. Methods such as RT-2~ rt2 and OpenVLA~ openvla quantize each action dimension into discrete bins and reuse the language vocabulary under cross-entropy loss, while FAST~ pi0fast compresses action chunks via a discrete cosine transform and byte-pair encoding. Although these methods preserve the VLM architecture and training paradigm, control is moved from physical space into symbol space: token-level cross-entropy penalizes adjacent-bin and far-bin errors equally, and compressed tokens entangle multiple timesteps and dimensions so that a single token error can corrupt an entire trajectory. The second is computational and parameter decoupling. Continuous policies such as ~ pi0 , ~ pi05 , SmolVLA~ smolvla , GR00T N1~ gr00tn1 , and X-VLA~ xvla preserve physical coordinates via flow matching or diffusion, but alter the model architecture and training paradigm by delegating trajectory generation to a dedicated action expert or 24-layer action Transformer outside the VLM. Because action supervision primarily updates the external expert and its competing gradients can degrade pretrained VLM features, Knowledge Insulation~ knowledgeinsulation blocks expert gradients from entering the backbone---resolving training instability by hard-wiring architectural decoupling. Recent hybrids partially restore coupling along individual axes---sharing a backbone over discrete diffusion tokens~ ddvla,mmadavla,blockvla,tbdvla , combining discrete and continuous branches~ hybridvla , training a separate trajectory codec~ cat , or switching from discrete pretraining to downstream flow matching~ dreamvla ---yet none realizes a true that natively generates continuous physical trajectories while preserving its model architecture, its native pretraining paradigm, and its visual-language generalization. We instantiate this paradigm in through an end-to-end continuous latent action representation inside a diffusion VLM. Prior latent-action works (LAPA, IGOR, UniVLA, Moto, villa-X, CAT~ lapa,igor,univla_latent,moto,villax,cat ) show that mapping diverse robot controls into a shared latent space decouples embodiment-specific kinematics from sequence modeling, but they rely on separately pretrained VQ codebooks or trajectory codecs. We place this latent space directly inside the hidden space of a diffusion VLM (BARD-VL~ bard ): at each control timestep, a lightweight position-wise action encoder maps the complete -dimensional action vector into a single continuous latent action token in , so a horizon- trajectory occupies tokens rather than scalar symbols. Vision, language, and latent action tokens are jointly contextualized across every layer of the shared Transformer, and a lightweight position-wise action decoder maps output hidden states back to physical coordinates under direct coordinate reconstruction loss. Building on this principle, partitions the -step horizon into temporally ordered action blocks that are causal across blocks and bidirectional within each block, allowing contiguous action segments to be generated and refined jointly. During training, the multimodal conditioning prefix, corrupted action tokens, and teacher-forced clean action tokens are packed into a single sequence, supervising all block-conditional distributions in one forward pass and providing a compute-efficient, scalable end-to-end training path. Because the VLM backbone is already pretrained with masked block reconstruction~ bard , reuses the exact same corrupt-and-reconstruct generative operator for continuous control without introducing a second training paradigm or external diffusion network. To rigorously test whether a policy acts as a decoupled VLA or a true ---and to localize where action representation and trajectory computation reside---we introduce the Action Interface Audit, a checkpoint-level methodology comprising three metrics aligned with the three decoupling axes: (i) Error-Geometry Consistency ( ), measuring whether unit training errors map stably to physical action errors; (ii) Trajectory Coupling Attribution (TCA) via the non-local response ratio ( ), using deterministic finite differences to localize where cross-time dependencies emerge; and (iii) Action-Specific Capacity Ratio ( ), quantifying parameters dedicated solely to action generation. The audit reveals that uniform discrete bins induce a physical-error span per single-token error and FAST-style compressed tokens suffer -- structural decoding failures under single-token edits; and derive all cross-time coupling from external action experts ( and , rising to in SmolVLA and in X-VLA); whereas 's active action interfaces occupy only of the 4.46B model, exhibit zero cross-time response on their own ( ), and delegate all temporal trajectory coupling to the middle and late layers of the shared VLM backbone ( in pretraining, on CALVIN, and on LIBERO). Furthermore, a matched counterfactual intervention shows that attaching a second coordinate objective to the shared hidden space induces opposing gradients (cosine ) and collapses CALVIN chain length from to , confirming that enabling native action generation in an without degrading the shared VLM requires co-designing the action representation and its supervision objective as a unified whole. On standard closed-loop benchmarks, reaches average success on regular LIBERO, on the 10 , 030-task LIBERO-Plus benchmark, and average completed chain length on CALVIN ABC--D (Table~ tab:main-libero ). Our contributions are threefold: Embodied Vision-Language Model ( ) Paradigm. We formulate the paradigm, embodying manipulation and cognition within a single VLM across representation, supervision, and generation so that a pretrained VLM natively generates continuous action trajectories while preserving its model architecture, native training paradigm, and visual-language generalization. Continuous Blockwise Architecture ( ). We introduce , representing a horizon- trajectory as continuous latent action tokens with blockwise causal-bidirectional visibility and packed teacher forcing, requiring only active interface parameters and no external action expert, tokenizer, or codec. Action Interface Audit and Empirical Validation. We introduce EGC, TCA ( ), and ASCR to audit representative discrete VLAs, action-expert VLAs, and our , provide counterfactual evidence on shared-space objective design, and demonstrate state-of-the-art closed-loop performance on LIBERO and LIBERO-Plus alongside strong zero-shot transfer on CALVIN ABC--D. Related Work sec:related_work Latent action representations. Several recent works learn compact latent action variables from video or robot demonstrations before policy learning. LAPA and IGOR extract discrete latent actions from action-free videos and image-goal pairs before grounding them into physical controls in a subsequent stage~ lapa,igor , while UniVLA~ univla_latent , Moto~ moto , villa-X~ villax , and CAT~ cat introduce task-centric codebooks, motion tokens, proprioceptive latent dynamics, or frozen trajectory codecs. Because these methods freeze the tokenizer or codec prior to policy optimization, the latent space is never shaped directly by closed-loop physical control gradients. title: Real-Time Event-Based LED Tracking and Pose Estimation with PWM-Encoded Markers
comment: This work has been submitted to the IEEE for possible publication
summary: Event cameras are neuromorphic vision sensors with pixels that independently and asynchronously respond to brightness changes at microsecond resolution, supporting state estimation under rapid motion, motion blur, and high dynamic range (HDR) illumination. This also enables capture of high-frequency blinking patterns from light-emitting diodes (LEDs). Based on this, we propose a real-time event-based framework for LED tracking and six-degree-of-freedom (6-DoF) relative pose estimation using pulse-width modulation (PWM)-encoded LED markers. Multiple LEDs share a common blinking frequency and encode identities through distinct PWM duty cycles, reducing frequency-resource requirements and computational cost. Our dual-rate asynchronous tracking framework combines low-rate LED detection with high-rate raw-event updates, maintaining robust LED identity association and accurate pixel-level tracking under rapid motion. LED identities and positions establish reliable 2D-3D correspondences for real-time metric 6-DoF relative pose estimation. Extensive evaluations on a self-collected dataset demonstrate robustness under large motion flow and transient image-plane LED overlap. Furthermore, we develop a coordinated robotic platform comprising a quadrotor and a Mecanum-wheeled mobile robot, demonstrating the proposed framework's potential for closed-loop drone guidance through hovering and target-following experiments under time-varying HDR illumination, with onboard deployment on an NVIDIA Jetson Orin NX. The dataset and implementation will be released to facilitate further research.
