Multimedia Material Video: \\ Introduction obust and low-latency estimation of the 6-DoF relative pose between rigid bodies is important for robotic manipulation, multi-robot coordination, autonomous landing, and augmented reality~ Gallego2022Survey, Jiao2023LCECalib, Li2026IEICalib, Liu2026AEVINS . Conventional solutions often rely on radio-frequency links, motion-capture infrastructure, or frame-based fiducial markers such as AprilTag~ Wang2016AprilTag2 and ArUco~ Garrido2014Aruco , whose performance can degrade when communication or external infrastructure is unavailable, or when rapid motion and challenging illumination cause motion blur and intermittent observations. Active LED markers provide a compact and controllable alternative~ Muller2011LED,Censi2013LED . Given a known geometric configuration of LEDs, their position measurements can be used to recover the metric relative pose of the marker~ Ebmer2024ALM . Marker identity can be encoded either spatially, through the geometric arrangement of multiple LEDs, or temporally, through their blinking patterns. Compared with spatial coding, temporal coding allows individual LEDs to carry identification information independently, thereby reducing the dependence on complex spatial layouts. Reliable decoding of such temporal patterns requires accurate sensing of rapid ON-OFF transitions. Event cameras are particularly well suited to this task, as they asynchronously capture pixel-wise intensity changes with microsecond-scale temporal resolution, high dynamic range, and low latency~ Lichtsteiner2008DVS,Brandli2014DAVIS,Liu2026AEVINS , enabling robust perception under high-speed motion and challenging illumination~ Mueggler2014Pose,Wang2024AEB,Niu2025ESVO2,Lyu2026RadarEventFusion . For active LEDs, the precise timestamps and polarities of the resulting events directly capture the temporal structure of their blinking signals, supporting event-based LED detection and identification. Despite these advantages, existing event-based LED identification methods face limitations in achieving robust multi-marker association under asynchronous event streams. Existing active-marker systems commonly associate LEDs through event counts, inter-event intervals, or distinct blinking frequencies~ Censi2013LED,Ebmer2024ALM,Wang2022Beacons . Assigning a separate frequency to each marker, however, becomes increasingly restrictive as the marker count grows: within a fixed frequency range, increasing the number of markers reduces the spacing between assigned frequencies and can require longer observation intervals for reliable identification~ Bauersfeld2025Mocap . Pulse-interval encodes avoid allocating a distinct frequency to each marker by encoding identities through sequences of unequal transition intervals~ Shiba25cvprw . This motivates a coding scheme that distinguishes multiple LEDs while retaining a common fixed blinking period for detection. Moreover, many pipelines accumulate events into fixed-duration windows or pseudo-frames. When tracking updates rely on these accumulated detections, the detection interval limits the update rate of position measurements. These limitations reveal two key challenges: developing a coding scheme that reduces the required frequency resources for reliable multi-marker identification, and designing an asynchronous tracking strategy that combines detection robustness with event-level temporal precision. We address these challenges with an event-based relative-pose framework based on PWM-encoded LED markers. As demonstrated in Fig.~ fig:eyecatcher , all markers share a common blinking frequency while encoding their identities through duty cycles, thereby reducing the frequency range that needs to be covered by the detector. Inspired by event-wise blob tracking~ Wang2024AEB , we adopt a dual-rate asynchronous tracking framework fram that combines periodic detection corrections with high-rate updates from associated raw events. Finally, the recovered marker identities establish 2D-3D correspondences for accurate perspective- -point (PnP) pose estimation. The primary contributions of this paper are summarized as follows: A PWM marker encoding and identification method for event cameras, where multiple LEDs can share the same blinking frequency and be distinguished by their PWM duty cycles, reducing the required frequency resources and consequently lowering the computational cost of marker identification (Sec.~ sec:detection ). A dual-rate asynchronous tracking framework that combines low-rate LED detections with high-rate updates from associated raw event data for robust marker tracking. By integrating both measurements into a unified state estimation framework, the proposed method achieves accurate and responsive tracking under scenarios with large optical flow (Sec.~ sec:tracking ). A real-time 6-DoF relative pose estimation framework based on the identification and tracking of PWM-encoded LED markers, which can be used for drone guidance in time-variant HDR environments. Extensive experiments on a self-collected dataset and drone flight experiments demonstrate its effectiveness and practical performance, and the dataset and implementation will be released to facilitate further research (Sec.~ sec:pose ). Outline: The remainder of the paper is organized as follows. Sec.~ sec:related work reviews active LED coding and identification, as well as event-based marker tracking and pose estimation. Sec.~ sec:method introduces the proposed PWM detection, asynchronous tracking, and pose-estimation pipeline. Sec.~ sec:evaluation presents the experimental evaluation, followed by the conclusion in Sec.~ sec:conclusion . Related Work sec:related work Event-based optical markers have been studied for tracking, localization, and communication~ Tofighi2026Survey . For active-marker pose estimation, LED identification and image-plane tracking are two important components. The former establishes marker identities for 2D-3D correspondence, while the latter provides temporally consistent visual measurements for geometric pose recovery. Active LED Encoding and Identification. Existing active-marker systems commonly distinguish LEDs by their blinking frequencies or by encoded blinking patterns. Early systems demonstrate LED tracking and low-latency localization using temporally modulated light sources~ Muller2011LED,Censi2013LED . Chen ~ Chen2020VLP extend this direction to visible-light positioning by identifying multiple flickering LEDs, while Salah ~ Salah2022Localization combine active-landmark measurements with inertial sensing for relative localization. More recently, Ebmer ~ Ebmer2024ALM exploit distinct LED frequencies and a known marker geometry to estimate the 6-DoF relative pose. Bauersfeld and Scaramuzza~ Bauersfeld2025Mocap adopt a similar identification principle for individually mounted point-source LEDs, whose measured frequencies determine the correspondences used in PnP pose estimation. In these frequency-encoded systems, periodic blinking provides a detection cue and an identity cue. When distinct blinking frequencies are assigned to individual LEDs, increasing the number of LEDs within a fixed frequency range reduces the frequency spacing between them, potentially requiring longer observation windows for reliable frequency discrimination. An alternative manner is to encode information through temporal sequences. Wang ~ Wang2022Beacons develop smart visual beacons with LED modulation and event-based demodulation for optical communication. Howard and Hirakawa~ Howard2025Timing address sensor-induced timing mismatch through dynamic timing correction for LED signal decoding. For marker identification, Shiba ~ Shiba25cvprw introduce the E-VLC dataset with an interval-based protocol, where sequences of unequal transition intervals encode identities for camera localization. This avoids assigning a distinct frequency to each LED, but requires resolving the intervals within the transmitted sequence. Kitade ~ Kitade2024Bicode propose Bicode, which combines a blinking LED for long-range identification with a spatial 2D marker for short-range pose estimation. Su ~ Su2025Motion instead use screen-displayed dynamic visual markers together with event-based tracking to support localization and optical communication under camera motion. These approaches suggest an alternative design space in which LED identity is encoded independently of the carrier frequency, while a common periodic signal can still be retained for robust detection. Event-Based Marker Tracking. The asynchronous output of event cameras has motivated methods that associate and track features directly in the event stream. Representative methods in this area are summarized in Tab.~ tab:tracking_comparison . Zhu ~ Zhu2017Association formulate event-to-feature matching through probabilistic data association. Other approaches track corner events~ Alzugaray2018Corner,Alzugaray2018ACE or maintain patch trajectories through asynchronous hypothesis updates~ Alzugaray2019Hypothesis,Alzugaray2020HASTE . Hybrid methods use intensity frames to initialize features and events to track them, including the photometric formulation of EKLT~ Gehrig2020EKLT and the learned tracker of Messikommer ~ Messikommer2023Tracking . title: Not Losing Your Way: Mitigating Visual-Inertial Odometry Drift through On-Demand Visual Feature Creation
comment: 8 pages, 4 figures. Submitted to the 2027 IEEE International Conference on Robotics and Automation (ICRA 2027)
summary: Visual-inertial odometry (VIO) can degrade during aerial inspection in repetitive or poorly textured environments. We propose an active environment-modification framework for unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs) relying on cameras and an inertial measurement unit only, without prior maps or additional localization sensors. Inspired by the fairy tale of Tom Thumb, the UAV creates visual features on demand by releasing ground markers or marking walls through physical contact. An information-based indicator triggers interventions using temporal confirmation and hysteresis. Evaluation includes three simulated environments and a 900-run factorial campaign. Lower cruise speed and active marking are associated with reduced divergence, while accuracy among non-divergent runs depends on speed-strategy interactions. Corridor experiments, with five runs per configuration, use OptiTrack for flight control while VIO-based marking decisions remain active online. The combined framework reduces the reported position root mean square error by approximately 35% relative to baseline VIO, supporting active feature creation for drift mitigation.

title: AffectiveVLA: Safe and Intent-Aware VLA Control for Human-Humanoid Social Interaction
summary: Social touch interactions, such as handshakes, fist bumps, and hugs, require humanoid robots to infer human intent, generate contact-rich motions, and maintain safe physical contact. We present AffectiveVLA, an intent-gated Vision-Language-Action (VLA) pipeline deployed on a Unitree G1 humanoid with dexterous hands. A lightweight RGB-based model recognizes interaction intent from two onboard cameras and converts it into a language prompt for the VLA policy. Low-confidence predictions suppress motion execution, reducing unintended activations. During physical contact, interaction-specific compliance profiles adjust arm impedance, while an independent voice-triggered mechanism initiates a latched safe-stop procedure. Using VR teleoperation, we collected approximately 1,300 multimodal interaction episodes and fine-tuned four VLA models: GR00T, RLDX-1, Being-H0.5, and UnifoLM-VLA-0. On-robot evaluation identifies GR00T as the best-performing standalone model. Integrating intent recognition increases its macro-F1 score from 0.75 to 0.90, while the intent model achieves a p95 inference latency of 6.27 ms. These results demonstrate that explicit intent gating improves the reliability of VLA-based social interaction without compromising real-time operation.
full_text: AffectiveVLA: Safe and Intent-Aware VLA Control for Human–Humanoid Social Interaction Nikita Kuzmin Georgii Demianchuk Mariya Lezina Yara Mahmoud Iana Zhura Miguel Altamirano Cabrera Dzmitry Tsetserukou Kuzmin et al. Social touch interactions, such as handshakes, fist bumps, and hugs, require humanoid robots to infer human intent, generate contact-rich motions, and maintain safe physical contact. We present AffectiveVLA, an intent-gated Vision-Language-Action (VLA) pipeline deployed on a Unitree G1 humanoid with dexterous hands. Using VR teleoperation, we collected approximately 1,300 multimodal interaction episodes and fine-tuned four VLA models: GR00T, RLDX-1, Being-H0.5, and UnifoLM-VLA-0. On-robot evaluation identifies GR00T as the best-performing standalone model. These results demonstrate that explicit intent gating improves the reliability of VLA-based social interaction without compromising real-time operation. AffectiveVLA enables intent-aware and contact-safe execution of three social interactions: (a) handshake, (b) fist bump, and (c) hug. Arrows indicate the direction of interaction motion, and red regions highlight physical contact. fig:teaser Introduction As humanoid robots enter human environments, they must participate in social rituals like handshakes, hugs, and fist bumps (Fig.~ fig:teaser ). Unlike object manipulation, these interactions involve an active human partner whose intent must be inferred, requiring the robot to meet a moving target while ensuring safe, comfortable contact~ block2021six,block2023arms . Existing approaches address this only partially: learned whole-body policies rely on explicit operator commands~ huang2026beyond , compliance controllers typically use fixed settings~ lu2025gentlehumanoid , and vision-language pipelines infer intent with high latency, lacking physical execution~ bao2025hierarchical . While end-to-end Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models can generate contact-rich motions, they risk unsafe false activations when human intent is uncertain. To address this, we propose a four-component pipeline: (1) RGB-based intent recognition to gate and prompt the VLA, (2) VLA-based whole-body motion generation, (3) task-specific compliance adaptation, and (4) an independent voice-triggered safe stop. This work investigates the following research questions: RQ1: Which VLA model best performs contact-rich HRI actions after fine-tuning on the same dataset? RQ2: Does the preferred arm compliance depend on the type of social interaction? RQ3: Does intent gating improve the selection of the correct interaction, and can ongoing contact be safely interrupted? Our main contributions are: A comparative evaluation of four fine-tuned VLA models (Being-H0.5, GR00T, RLDX-1, UnifoLM-VLA-0) on social touch tasks . An intent-gated VLA pipeline with task-conditioned compliance and voice-triggered safe stopping, validated via ablation and user studies. Related Work Social touch and learning-based interaction. Social touch in HRI has focused on single, pre-selected interactions: HuggieBot established design guidelines for hugging robots~ block2021six,block2023arms , and tactile sensing has been used to time handshake phases~ pequeno2024tactile . Reinforcement learning now scales to general-purpose whole-body controllers~ luo2025sonic , with systems like ECHO~ mascaro2024robot , RHINO~ chen2025rhino , and D-STAR~ huang2026beyond learning hug and handshake policies. However, these systems rely on fixed skill sets and operator-selected interaction types rather than inferring intent from the partner. For safe contact, impedance control allows the robot to yield~ lu2025gentlehumanoid , but most systems use fixed compliance settings. For intent inference, foundation models can reason about social cues~ kim2024understanding , but VLM-based approaches like HIAER~ bao2025hierarchical suffer from multi-second latency and cannot execute contact-rich gestures. Vision-language-action models. VLA models map images and language to robot actions~ gr00tn1_2025 , extending to humanoid control~ xue2025leverb , cross-embodiment learning~ beingbeyond2026beingh05 , and dexterous manipulation~ rldx2026,unifolm-vla-0 . These models target manipulation rather than social contact, though GIVE~ liu2026give shows that textual gesture descriptions improve intent grounding. We use GR00T~N1.6~ gr00tn1_2025 , RLDX-1~ rldx2026 , Being-H0.5~ beingbeyond2026beingh05 , and UnifoLM-VLA-0~ unifolm-vla-0 as interchangeable action backbones. Positioning. Unlike skill-specific policies~ huang2026beyond , we infer interaction from dual RGB views and verbalize it as a VLA prompt, enabling new gestures through data rather than reward design. Unlike HIAER~ bao2025hierarchical , intent is recognized in 6\,ms by a lightweight video model, and the robot performs physical contact. Unlike fixed-compliance controllers~ lu2025gentlehumanoid , impedance adapts to each interaction. To our knowledge, this is the first system combining RGB-based intent recognition with VLA execution and interaction-specific impedance for social touch on a humanoid. System and Dataset Robot and Teleoperation Setup sec:setup The platform used is a Unitree G1 humanoid with BrainCo dexterous hands, controlled by the SONIC whole-body controller, which retargets operator motion into joint commands with per-joint impe-dance gains ( , ) for 17 upper-body motors. Teleoperation uses a PICO~4 Ultra headset running XRoboToolkit~ zhao2026xrobotoolkit , streaming head/controller poses and 26-joint hand tracking at 90\,Hz with stereoscopic passthrough feedback. Upper-body commands are forwarded to SONIC and finger trajectories to the BrainCo hands at 50\,Hz, with grip presses serving as the episode-control interface. Each episode records three synchronized RGB views --- ego-centric ( ) and head-mounted ( ) on the robot at 15\,FPS, plus an external scene view ( ) on the host --- and upper-body telemetry (joint states, velocities, torques, commands) at 50\,Hz. Dataset Collection and Cleaning sec:dataset Demonstrations were collected by teleoperating the robot with a human partner in four interaction classes: handshake, fist bump, hug, and no interaction. Each episode stores participant profile, multimodal observations, robot states, action commands, and interaction labels in LeRobot format. Retained episodes were annotated with four temporal markers --- approach start, contact start, release start, and idle start --- used to train the interaction-intent model (Sec.~ sec:human_intent_recognition ). Episodes with tracking loss, safety stops, unintended contacts, or anomalous duration were discarded. The final dataset contains 1,270 episodes from 19 participants (13 male, 6 female; age years; height cm), with no participant overlap between the extended set (982 episodes, 15 participants) and test set (288 episodes, 4 unseen participants). VLA Models sec:vla We evaluate four VLA models: Being-H0.5~ beingbeyond2026beingh05 , GR00T~N1.6~ gr00tn1_2025 , RLDX-1~ rldx2026 , and UnifoLM-VLA-0~ unifolm-vla-0 . All follow the same architecture --- a ViT-based VLM backbone, a projector aligning visual and language features, and an action expert predicting chunked actions --- operating in a unified 76-dimensional action space: 64-dimensional SONIC motion tokens for the upper body plus 6-DoF finger commands for each BrainCo hand, chunked over 40 steps. All models are fine-tuned using model-specific recipes. For Being-H0.5, RLDX-1, and UnifoLM-VLA-0, the language backbone is frozen while the ViT encoder, projector, and action expert are trained. For GR00T~N1.6, only the action expert and projector are updated. Fine-tuning runs on a single A100 80GB GPU for 30k steps; UnifoLM additionally requires converting the dataset to HDF5/RLDS format. Human-Aware VLA Pipeline Figure~ fig:pipeline presents the proposed pipeline. Camera observations are used to recognize interaction intent. A confirmed intent is converted into a task prompt for the VLA model, while task-specific compliance and an independent voice-triggered safe-stop mechanism supervise physical execution. Human Intent Recognition sec:human_intent_recognition The human-intent module recognizes the interaction initiated by the human from two synchronized onboard RGB views: one for full-body motion and one for the hand-contact area. At each inference step, it processes the 16 most recent frame pairs sampled at 15 Hz, corresponding to about one second of motion history. Frames are resized to using letterboxing. A shared TinyViT encoder extracts frame-level features from both views. Separate causal VideoLightFormer modules aggregate temporal information, and attention-based fusion combines the two representations. The model classifies each observation window as handshake, hug, fist bump, or no interaction. The recognized interaction is converted into the task prompt for the VLA policy. An intent is committed only when its probability exceeds 0.6 for three consecutive inference steps. Until then, motion execution remains disabled, reducing unintended activations from uncertain predictions. VLA Whole-Body Execution Once an intent is accepted, it is mapped to a task prompt such as hug, handshake, or fist bump. The corresponding compliance profile is activated, and the prompt is passed to the VLA together with two camera views, the robot state, and measured BrainCo hand states. The VLA runs at \(5\, \) and outputs action chunks with 64-dimensional motion tokens and normalized commands for the six actuators of each BrainCo hand. Actions are executed at \(50\, \). Motion tokens are passed to GEAR-SONIC for whole-body joint targets and balance control, while finger commands are sent directly to the BrainCo controllers. Per-actuator rate limiting prevents abrupt changes between chunks. Contact is detected from the difference between commanded and measured finger positions; after contact, further closing is blocked while opening remains enabled. If the prompt changes, queued actions are discarded and execution is held until a matching chunk is received. The compliance profile is maintained by a \(10\, \) heartbeat; if it stops, the last gains are held. Task-Conditioned Compliance The compliance layer scales the impedance gains of the 14 arm joints, leaving torso and leg gains unchanged: with . The recognized intent selects the profile; see Table tab:compliance_profiles . Profiles change along minimum-jerk ramps (0.3\,s softening, 1.0\,s stiffening) that keep damping high during each transition. Voice-Triggered Safe Stop An offline Vosk recognizer~ vosk with a restricted vocabulary (``stop'', ``hold on'') triggers a deterministic, latched stop: operator and VLA commands are ignored, locomotion is set to idle, the arms soften to and are then lowered to the rest pose (first outward if a hug is detected), and the BrainCo fingers open. Only a manual release resumes control. Experiments sec:experiments Offline VLA Comparison sec:exp_offline Each model (30k fine-tuning steps) predicts 40-step action chunks along the 288 held-out test episodes, and the predictions are compared with the teleoperated ground truth (Table~ tab:vla_offline ). Being-H0.5, GR00T, and RLDX-1 are within 2 of each other in overall RMSE, while UnifoLM-VLA-0 is worse on all metrics. GR00T is the most accurate at the first and last chunk steps. title: Don't Prompt Your Agents. Equip Them: Skillware as a Modular Standard for Sovereign, Auditable, and Deterministic Capability Execution for Logical Systems
comment: 51 pages, 26 figures. Code repository and benchmarks available at https://github.com/arpahls/skillware
summary:
Current autonomous logical systems rely on a fragile assumption: that language models should dynamically write code, guess API payloads, and memorize operational constraints through prompt engineering. In practice, this burns massive context windows, inflates API bills, and produces brittle agents that fail unpredictably in production.
  In this work, we present Skillware, an open architectural framework and capability registry that formally separates what an agent wants to do from how that task is executed. Instead of prompting models with loose text instructions or markdown files baptized as 'skills', Skillware equips them with modular, versioned software capability bundles. Much like skill hotkeys in video games that execute deterministically under fixed world rules, each bundle combines a typed JSON input contract, deterministic Python code, task directives, bundled datasets, and automated unit tests. In-process adapters translate these capabilities into native tool declarations for any model, from frontier cloud APIs to local open-weight runtimes with zero network latency.
  Evaluating 23 frontier and open-weight models across 368 benchmark conditions, we show that small local models (3B to 8B parameters) equipped with Skillware consistently outperform unequipped frontier models on complex multi-step workflows. They cut token usage by up to 84.8%, slash inference costs by up to 97.3%, and eliminate parameter errors entirely. True agent reliability does not come from larger models or longer prompts, but from equipping logical systems with verified, deterministic software.
  Finally, we articulate the trajectory of capability bundles across an invariant continuum of information processing systems: from digital logical systems today, to IoT, drones, and embodied robotics tomorrow, establishing a foundation for auditable, real-time capability execution.
full_text: Current autonomous logical systems rely on a fragile assumption: that language models should dynamically write code, guess API payloads, and memorize operational constraints through prompt engineering. In practice, this burns massive context windows, inflates API bills, and produces fragile agents that fail unpredictably in production. In this work, we present Skillware, an open architectural framework and capability registry that formally separates what an agent wants to do from how that task is executed. Instead of prompting models with loose text instructions or markdown files baptized as ``skills'', Skillware equips them with modular, versioned software capability bundles. Much like skill hotkeys in video games, which execute deterministically under fixed world rules rather than conversational negotiation, each bundle combines a typed JSON input contract, deterministic Python code, task directives, bundled datasets, and automated unit tests. In-process adapters translate these capabilities into native tool declarations for any model, from frontier cloud APIs to open-weight, local, and edge runtimes with zero network latency. Evaluating 23 frontier and open-weight models across 368 benchmark conditions, we show that small local models, even 3B to 8B parameters, equipped with Skillware consistently outperform unequipped frontier models on complex multi-step workflows. They cut token usage by up to , slash inference costs by up to , and eliminate parameter errors entirely. True agent reliability does not come from larger models or longer prompts, but from equipping logical systems with verified, deterministic software. Finally, we articulate the trajectory of capability bundles across an invariant continuum of information processing systems. Today, Skillware serves as a modular, installable capability library for digital logical systems. Tomorrow, the exact same framework powers robust capabilities for IoT devices, smart appliances, vehicles, drones, and embodied robotics. Down the line, as brain-computer interfaces advance, this modular architecture provides the foundation to install verified capabilities directly into organic information processors (brains), turning the instant skill acquisition of science fiction into a concrete, auditable engineering discipline. : Autonomous Agents Capability Engineering Tool-Augmented Language Models Small Language Models (SLMs) Deterministic Execution Token Economics Agent Software Architecture Skillware Introduction: The Stochastic Impedance Mismatch sec:introduction Computer systems research has historically progressed by establishing formal boundaries between distinct abstraction layers: the separation of physical memory from virtual addressing, the isolation of user space from kernel execution, and the decoupling of declarative query specification from relational execution engines~ saltzer1975protection, lampson1974protection, parnas1972criteria, hoare1969axiomatic . Each transition replaced stochastic, ad-hoc programming conventions with deterministic, verifiable contracts. The contemporary paradigm of autonomous artificial intelligence agents represents a sharp departure from this historical trajectory. As foundation models have scaled, practitioners have attempted to bridge the gap between linguistic reasoning and real-world execution by coercing auto-regressive language models into serving simultaneously as planners, compilers, runtime engines, and policy arbiters~ wang2024survey, xi2023rise, yao2023react, schick2023toolformer . In this prevailing architectural approach---which we term the prompt-driven execution paradigm---an agent is provided with unstructured natural-language descriptions of external APIs, instructed to synthesize execution code or structured payloads on the fly, and expected to self-regulate its operational boundaries through in-context prompting. This approach suffers from a foundational stochastic impedance mismatch. Deep transformer architectures compute conditional probability distributions over discrete token sequences: While auto-regressive token generation is exceptionally well-suited for semantic interpretation, open-domain summarization, and human-machine dialogue, it possesses no formal mechanisms for enforcing computational invariants. When task complexity scales compositionally, transformer architectures experience severe combinatorial degradation, non-deterministic branching, and state hallucination~ dziri2023faith, valmeekam2023planning, ji2023survey, huang2023survey . The Crisis of Prompt-Driven Capability subsec:five_flaws Treating auto-regressive language models as direct computation runtimes introduces five critical systemic bottlenecks: [leftmargin=*] Stochastic Non-Determinism: An identical operational intent executed across multiple turns yields variable argument casing, hallucinated parameters, and dropped structural invariants. Quadratic Context Dilution: Injecting thousands of tokens of API manuals and directives into system prompts permanently taxes transformer attention ( ), causing models to ignore critical safety predicates~ liu2024lost . Egress Insecurity and the Confused Deputy: Natural-language prompts cannot enforce security perimeters; untrusted inbound text easily repurposes ambient model authority into unauthorized side-effects~ greshake2023not, liu2023promptinjection . Schema Balkanization: Fragile, incompatible tool formats across major cloud providers (e.g., Protobuf, XML, JSON) force developers to maintain brittle prompt shims that break across model releases. Cyber-Physical Incompatibility: Multi-second cloud latency and stochastic parameter drift are fundamentally incompatible with real-time physical control and millisecond reflex envelopes~ ahn2022can, brohan2023rt2, willett2023speech . These failure modes are not cosmetic developer inconveniences; they form a systemic crisis where critical software workflows become trapped inside a centralized, rented loop. Section~ sec:problem_layers provides a comprehensive technical deconstruction of these failures across enterprise, developer, macroeconomic, and cyber-physical layers. The Core Principle: Don't Prompt. Equip. subsec:thesis In 1975, Saltzer and Schroeder articulated the foundational tenets of secure and reliable systems: Economy of Mechanism, Fail-Safe Defaults, Least Privilege, and Complete Mediation~ saltzer1975protection . In classical computing, operating systems do not generate utility binaries at runtime; they package pre-compiled, verifiable, and isolated software libraries behind typed system calls. A compelling systems analogy emerges from role-playing video games (RPGs), where players and non-player companions personalize and customize characters through modular skill systems. In a game engine, activating an ability is never an ambiguous negotiation, a conversational plea, or a probabilistic discussion with the character model. It is a hotkey bound to deterministic engine logic: provided environmental preconditions and background policies hold true---the entity is in combat outside a sanctuary town, targeting a hostile creature rather than an immune town guard, and possessing sufficient resource reserves---the skill executes with a single trigger and produces the exact same state transition every time. The character never invents the physics of the ability at runtime, nor does it negotiate its operational boundaries; it is strictly in the position to trigger the action. Skillware introduces this exact computational discipline to autonomous agents: the language model evaluates semantic context and decides when to trigger a capability, but has zero authority over how the capability executes, how its parameters are validated, or how its constitutional policies are enforced. [doctrinebox, title= THE PRINCIPLE OF SEPARATION OF COGNITION AND CAPABILITY ] Formal Boundary Invariant:\\[0.2em] Let an autonomous system be partitioned into a Cognitive Planner and a set of Executable Capabilities . The planner is restricted strictly to semantic routing and parameter instantiation. The capability must be a self-contained, pre-compiled, deterministic software bundle enforcing an immutable contract, local dependency isolation, and offline verification. The model decides when to act; the capability bundle governs how the action is executed. The assistant is a guest; the function does the work. In this paper, we present Skillware, an open architectural framework and registry that formalizes this separation. While the term skillware has historical currency in corporate compliance software and speculative fiction, its coinage and introduction into artificial intelligence and autonomous systems was originated by ARPA Hellenic Logical Systems~ skillware2026framework . Recent academic literature, notably Fan and Lan~ fan2026skillware , has acknowledged this origin while exploring theoretical software ontologies for persistent agent behaviors. In this work, we present the production-validated execution standard: self-contained, versioned capability bundles. Each bundle unifies a typed contract (manifest.yaml), a deterministic execution class (skill.py), a cognitive directive (instructions.md), offline assurance verifiers (test skill.py), and metadata presentation (card.json). Through in-process dynamic adapters, Skillware translates declared capabilities into native host formats across all major frontier and local models without IPC or network overhead. We demonstrate that this architecture not only restores determinism to the execution layer of autonomous systems, but enables Small Language Models (SLMs) to achieve superior operational reliability at a fraction of the token and financial cost of unequipped frontier models. [contribbox] [leftmargin=2.2em, itemsep=2.5pt, labelsep=0.5em] The Separation Invariant ( subsec:thesis ): We formalize the separation of cognitive planning from deterministic execution and show why runtime code generation and prompt-only tools fail production safety and economics. The 5-Role Capability Bundle ( sec:architecture ): We specify the anatomy of an Agent Skill (Contract, Effect, Directive, Assurance, Presentation), supported by static lookup corpora, enabling offline verification and type safety. Universal In-Process Adapters ( subsec:interface_morphism ): We provide zero-IPC interface morphisms across Gemini, Claude, OpenAI, DeepSeek, Bedrock, and Ollama, eliminating vendor lock-in and client-server daemon overhead. Deterministic Chaining Engine ( sec:runtime_operations ): We introduce declarative DAG execution with dot-notation state bindings and zero-token conditional skip gates, accompanied by segregated local operator stores. The SLM Parameter Paradox ( sec:slm_token_economy ): We show that 3B--8B parameter models equipped with Skillware outpace unequipped frontier models in execution reliability, latency, cost ( reduction), and air-gapped sovereignty. Generalization Across Physical Scales ( sec:embodied_bmi_horizon ): We formulate the scaling of capability bundles from digital software runtimes to industrial control, embodied robotics, and neural interfaces. The remainder of the paper is organized as follows. Section~ sec:problem_layers dissects the capability crisis across technical layers and constituencies. Section~ sec:architecture formalizes the Skillware bundle and its interface morphism; Section~ sec:runtime_operations describes runtime discovery, chaining, and operator stores. Section~ sec:slm_token_economy analyzes complexity, empirical scaling, and token economics, and Section~ sec:comparative_analysis positions Skillware against adjacent ecosystems alongside multi-model empirical evaluation under . Sections~ sec:tripartite_ecosystem and~ sec:security_privacy cover ecosystem integration and adversarial security verification, Section~ sec:embodied_bmi_horizon extends the abstraction to cyber-physical scales, and Section~ sec:conclusion concludes. title: A Sequential Framework for Urban Drone Delivery: Network Design, Vehicle Sizing, and Energy and Cost Assessment
summary: A sequential engineering framework is presented for urban drone delivery, linking hub location, route planning, mission-specific vehicle sizing, and energy and operating cost assessment. Aggregate origin-destination demand is assumed known a priori. For each hub configuration, the maximum required link distance is minimized, and feasible routes that return to their departure hubs are generated. Route frequencies are determined using mixed-integer linear programming to satisfy delivery demand. The resulting range requirement guides motor-propeller selection and battery sizing to minimize vehicle takeoff mass. Flight distances and frequencies, cruise performance, and vehicle dimensions are combined to estimate monthly energy consumption, fleet size, hub area, staffing, and operating cost. The framework is applied to district-level Seoul delivery data. Increasing the number of hubs from one to four reduces the required range from 30.6 to 21.9 km and vehicle takeoff mass from 8.12 to 6.12 kg. Despite a 21.5% increase in total flight distance, monthly flight energy consumption decreases by 13.1%, from 15.2 to 13.2 MWh. Battery replacement is the largest vehicle-related operating expense, while operating cost per delivery increases from USD 1.18 to USD 2.20 because of higher rent and labor costs at the hubs. Among the designs evaluated, range-matched vehicles achieve the lowest operating cost in the two- and four-hub networks; a longer-range vehicle is least costly in the three-hub network. Sensitivity analyses further examine the effects of delivery demand and operating assumptions. The results demonstrate that reductions in vehicle mass and energy consumption do not necessarily lead to lower system operating cost.

Introduction sec:intro E-commerce and on-demand delivery have increased interest in fast and flexible last-mile transportation. Drones can operate independently of the road network and have been studied in terms of efficiency, accessibility, and sustainability moshref2021,jazairy2025,garg2023 . However, the feasibility and cost of urban drone delivery depend on numerous technical and operational factors. These include vehicle range and energy consumption, hub locations, fleet size, and facility and staffing costs. Furthermore, these factors are not independent, and changes in one may affect several others. Quadrotor drones are considered in this study because their vertical takeoff and landing capabilities and ability to hover are advantageous for urban delivery. However, their relatively low cruise efficiency compared with fixed-wing aircraft limits their flight range. Consequently, the distances between delivery hubs and service locations become important factors in vehicle design, as longer required ranges generally lead to larger batteries and heavier vehicles. For example, increasing the number of hubs may reduce the required flight range and allow lighter vehicles, but it may also increase facility and staffing costs while changing fleet requirements. Such competing effects motivate an integrated assessment of network design, vehicle sizing, energy consumption, and operating costs. Drone routing research addresses cooperation between transportation modes and vehicle energy constraints. Murray and Chu murray2015 formulated a drone-assisted delivery routing problem, and Agatz et al. agatz2018 investigated optimization approaches for the traveling salesman problem with a drone. Dorling et al. dorling2017 incorporated energy consumption dependent on battery and payload mass, together with drone reuse, into route planning. Other studies have addressed cost minimization in truck--drone cooperation ha2018 and extensions of operating range using public transportation networks choudhury2021,moadab2022,huang2020 . These studies demonstrate the importance of linking feasible routes and energy use when evaluating delivery plans. Facility and network studies relate flight range and base locations to service coverage and routing. Hong et al. hong2018 considered the coverage of recharging facilities under range restrictions, whereas Pinto and Lagorio pinto2022 addressed point-to-point drone delivery networks with intermediate charging stations. Liu liu2023 evaluated a battery-constrained depot network through optimization and simulation. Studies of facility coverage and capacity chauhan2019 and delivery routing with parcel lockers zhu2024 also connect transportation infrastructure with route planning. These contributions provide a basis for evaluating networks in which facility location and vehicle range constraints interact. Research on urban-scale operations has expanded to corridor and route-network design he2022,he2024,he2025 , risk-aware unmanned aerial vehicle traffic networks nicholson2025 , urban airspace availability assessment cho2018,cho2021 and very-low-level traffic-density estimation doole2020 . Online demand planning paul2025 , consumer delivery preferences kim2020 , third-party ground-risk assessment choi2025 , and barriers to urban air mobility adoption sadrani2025 further highlight the role of demand, safety, and institutional conditions. Doole et al. doole2020 estimated drone-based food-delivery costs of 0.40--2.51 EUR per meal order across scenarios that included annualized investment and operating costs. Bao et al. bao2026 estimated 4.17 EUR per parcel in a 200-customer-node scenario using a five-year total-cost-of-ownership model that included vehicle and battery acquisition, labor, and infrastructure costs. Differences in service units, operating assumptions, and cost coverage limit direct comparisons of these estimates. Moreover, the effects of network-dependent range requirements on component level vehicle design, and their subsequent implications for energy consumption, fleet requirements, and hub operating costs, have received comparatively limited attention. Vehicle sizing and performance evaluation are based on the approaches of Jeong jeong2021 , Pollet et al. pollet2021 , and Nam et al. nam2024 . The main contributions of this study are summarized as follows: A closely linked framework is established to integrate network design, flight-route optimization, component-based vehicle sizing, and energy consumption and operating cost assessment. The sequential procedure explicitly accounts for the interdependencies among these stages. The framework is applied to Seoul using actual ground delivery data. Increasing the number of hubs from one to four reduces vehicle mass and total flight energy consumption despite an increase in total flight distance, but increases operating cost per delivery from USD 1.18 to USD 2.20. Comparisons across vehicle designs show that minimum-mass designs do not necessarily minimize operating cost because vehicle range also affects flight frequency and staffing requirements. The effects of delivery demand, operating hours, component lifetimes, hub area, and staffing are examined to assess the robustness of operating cost comparisons. The one-hub configuration remains the least costly across the evaluated parameter ranges, although the relative cost rankings of multiple-hub configurations can change. Section~ sec:framework introduces the delivery system and the framework. Section~ sec:network presents hub location and flight-route planning, and Section~ sec:vehicle describes vehicle sizing and performance evaluation. Section~ sec:cost uses their outputs to calculate energy consumption, fleet size, hub space, staffing, and operating costs. Section~ sec:results presents the Seoul baseline, comparisons across vehicle designs, propulsion selection, and sensitivity results. Section~ sec:conclusions concludes the paper. Delivery System and Analysis Framework sec:framework The proposed framework connects delivery network design, flight-route planning, vehicle sizing, and operating cost assessment. Hub locations determine the required flight range, which affects both flight routes and vehicle design. The flight plan and vehicle performance determine the number of drones needed to meet delivery demand. Delivery System and Demand sec:definition A hub-based delivery system using electric quadrotor drones is considered. Each delivery area is represented by a demand node and assigned to one hub. Hubs provide space for cargo handling, drone deployment, battery charging and replacement, and maintenance. Drones serve demand nodes within their assigned zones. Shipments between different zones are transported through inter-hub connections. A drone may visit several demand nodes during a flight but must return to its departure hub. Each closed-loop route is counted as one flight. A shipment may require multiple flights to reach its final destination. Therefore, the number of deliveries is distinguished from the number of flights. Each delivery is counted once, regardless of the number of flights needed to complete it. Delivery demand is represented by origin–destination (OD) shipment counts between demand nodes. The original ground-delivery data are scaled to obtain the planned drone delivery demand. The aggregate OD demand for the monthly planning period is assumed to be known a priori. Demand forecasting and real-time dispatching are not considered. Framework Overview sec:framework_flow The overall framework is shown in Fig.~ fig:framework . For a specified number of hubs, the locations of delivery demand nodes and candidate hub sites are used to select hub locations and assign demand nodes to service zones. The resulting network determines the required flight range, . The required range is used for both route planning and vehicle sizing. In route planning, candidate flight routes are generated, and their frequencies are optimized to meet the planned OD demand with the minimum number of flights. In vehicle sizing, the motor–propeller combination and battery mass are selected to minimize take-off mass while satisfying the required range and other mission requirements. The selected vehicle design is used at all hubs within each scenario. However, the number of drones at each hub depends on its flight activity. Flight distances and frequencies are combined with the vehicle's cruise speed and power to calculate flight hours and energy consumption. These results are used to estimate fleet size and battery and motor replacement requirements. Rent, wages, battery charging, and component replacement costs are then combined to calculate monthly operating cost and operating cost per delivery. Table~ tab:stages summarizes the objectives and conditions of each stage. The design stages are optimized separately, and their outputs are used in subsequent calculations. The framework therefore provides an integrated cost assessment without jointly optimizing the network, flight routes, and vehicle design. title: Learning Robotic World Models with Semantic and Visual Feedback
comment: 27 pages, including supplementary material. Project and code: https://github.com/Alexander-wu/RoboImagine . Data and weights: https://huggingface.co/easylearning/RoboImagine
summary: Robot world models predict action-conditioned future visual states to support robotic planning and decision making. However, visual reconstruction does not fully capture task progress, semantic evaluation alone provides limited constraints on fine-grained visual errors, and homogeneous predictions limit comparative feedback. We present RoboImagine, a framework for post-training autoregressive robotic world models through candidate-future comparisons with semantic and visual feedback. Diverse search promotes diversity among candidate trajectories under shared visual observations, action sequences, and task instructions. A frozen multimodal evaluator provides task-relevant semantic preferences through pairwise video comparisons in both presentation orders, complemented by pixel- and perceptual-level visual consistency feedback that constrains local structural and appearance errors. These signals drive policy optimization through group-relative advantages. Fixed initial context and branch-specific rolling histories support long-sequence generation with bounded context and consistent conditioning between candidate generation and policy optimization. Experiments with separately trained models on RT-1, BridgeV2, and RoboCasa cover real-world and simulated manipulation. On RT-1, under matched initialization, update counts, and evaluation protocols, RoboImagine improves PSNR by 1.26 dB and reduces LPIPS by 11.93% relative to continued supervised fine-tuning. Ablations show that diverse search improves prediction quality and that combined semantic and visual feedback yields higher external multimodal evaluation scores than visual feedback alone while maintaining comparable visual fidelity. Rolling histories further improve long-horizon prediction. These results support improving visual fidelity, task relevance, and long-horizon prediction through candidate comparison and complementary feedback.
full_text: Robot world models predict how scenes evolve under actions, enabling robots to assess potential outcomes before execution~ ha2018world,ni2025maskgwm,brooks2024video,hou2026worldmodel . As learnable internal simulators, they support planning, policy evaluation, and long-horizon reasoning~ tan2026towards,hansen2023td,li2024evaluating,zhang2026thinkingvideo . Unlike generic video generation, which primarily emphasizes visual quality, robot world models must capture action-induced state changes, object contacts, and interactions to provide reliable guidance for manipulation decisions~ li2025worldmodelbench,wu2025rlvr . Visual observations describe the current scene, action sequences specify the execution process, and natural-language instructions provide task goals; together, they form the multimodal context for understanding and predicting robot interactions. Prediction quality therefore depends not only on visual fidelity, but also on how accurately the model captures physical evolution under the given actions and its relationship to the task goal~ barcellona2024dream,pang2025learning . However, evaluating predicted futures remains a central challenge in training robot world models. Existing methods typically use maximum-likelihood, reconstruction, or perceptual objectives~ wu2025rlvr,huang2025vid2world,mao2025robot,ding2025understanding . These objectives provide effective visual supervision, but visual similarity alone does not fully capture task-relevant changes. For example, a prediction that preserves scene appearance may still miss action-induced object displacement or changes in contact. Conversely, multimodal semantic evaluation assesses visible task progress using instructions and scene context, yet may be insufficiently sensitive to local structural distortions and fine-grained appearance errors. As Figure~ fig:motivation_feedback illustrates, visual fidelity and task semantics provide complementary perspectives on prediction quality. Aligning robot world models therefore calls for both forms of feedback: constraining visual detail while assessing whether predicted state transitions are plausible under the given actions and task conditions. Prior work explores reward-based post-training for robotic world models~ wu2026futureworlds . RLVR-World rewards action-conditioned forecasts using visual prediction metrics~ wu2025rlvr . RoboAlign-R1~ wu2026roboalignr1 distills a vision--language judge into a lightweight reward model that scores individual generated videos. Such semantic feedback motivates a broader question: how should alternative futures be constructed and evaluated to provide informative learning signals? Absolute video scores require calibration across scenes and tasks, whereas futures generated under shared observations, actions, and instructions can be compared directly for visible task progress. However, nearly identical candidates provide little basis for comparison, and semantic preferences alone may overlook local visual errors. Effective comparative learning must therefore address both candidate construction and feedback design. We propose , a framework for learning autoregressive robotic world models by comparing candidate futures with semantic and visual feedback. Conditioned on visual observations, actions, and task instructions, grouped diverse beam search (GDBS)~ vijayakumar2016diverse constructs alternative trajectories under shared inputs. A frozen multimodal evaluator, mJev (hereafter Jev)~ somark2026mjev , compares candidate videos for visible task progress using the instruction and initial observation; evaluating both presentation orders mitigates position bias. Pixel- and perceptual-level visual consistency feedback~ zhang2018unreasonable complements these preferences by constraining fine-grained prediction errors. The two signals are standardized across candidates and combined into group-relative advantages for policy optimization~ shao2024deepseekmath . Each branch retains fixed initial context and a dynamic anchor together with its own rolling state--action history. This bounded history supports continued generation, while replaying the recorded history keeps policy scoring consistent with the conditions under which each candidate is generated. We evaluate separately trained models on RT-1, BridgeV2, and RoboCasa, and conduct controlled studies of post-training, candidate search, feedback composition, and memory. On RT-1, comparative post-training improves PSNR by 1.26~dB and reduces LPIPS by 11.93 relative to continued supervised fine-tuning from the same initialization for the same number of updates, at a higher computational cost. Visual-only feedback achieves the strongest visual metrics in the reward ablation, whereas combined feedback yields a higher external multimodal evaluation mean while retaining comparable visual fidelity. Long-horizon evaluations further assess the benefits of rolling history and the associated inference costs. Our main contributions are summarized as follows: Learning robot world models by comparing imagined futures. We introduce , which couples GDBS with comparative post-training under shared observations, actions, and instructions. Bounded branch-specific histories support autoregressive rollouts and are replayed during policy scoring to preserve conditioning consistency. Complementary semantic preference and visual consistency feedback. A frozen multimodal judge evaluates pairwise task progress among candidates with bidirectional comparisons to mitigate order bias, while pixel- and perceptual-level consistency feedback constrains fine-grained visual errors. Group-wise standardization and relative advantages translate both signals into policy updates without backpropagating through the evaluator or the video decoder. Evaluation of prediction quality and learning mechanisms. Experiments on three manipulation datasets assess visual prediction and task-level consistency. Controlled RT-1 comparisons isolate the effects of additional supervised training, feedback composition, and candidate search, while long-horizon and window-size studies characterize the quality and inference cost of bounded memory. Related Work World models learn environment dynamics for planning and policy learning~ ha2018world,hafner2019planet,hafner2025dreamerv3,hansen2023td . Visual prediction represents anticipated interaction outcomes as videos: iVideoGPT models videos with discrete tokens~ wu2024ivideogpt , while RoboDreamer, IRASim, and Vid2World condition future generation on task descriptions or robot actions~ zhou2024robodreamer,zhu2024irasim,huang2025vid2world . title: TactileLab: Sim-to-Real Dexterous Robot Manipulation with Efficient Shear-Sensitive Tactile Simulation
summary: Robotic simulators that represent shear within tactile sensing are becoming increasingly important for contact-rich manipulation. However, simulating contact shear with high-fidelity deformable or soft-body simulation is computationally demanding, limiting scalability to large-scale reinforcement learning. Here we introduce \textit{TactileLab}, a scalable multimodal tactile simulation framework built on IsaacLab, with a particular focus on a new optical-flow-based tactile representation termed \textit{simulated tactile flow}. Instead of relying on soft-body physics to model shear deformation, TactileLab uses rigid-body simulation to efficiently estimate dense tangential motion at the contact interface, producing tactile flow fields that encode shear-relevant contact dynamics. This flow field complements geometric features from a contact depth field. We further introduce a novel policy architecture for jointly processing long-horizon proprioceptive signals and rich tactile observations. Across multiple contact-rich tasks, policies trained using simulated tactile flow learn efficiently at scale and exhibit emergent contact-aware behaviours. To facilitate sim-to-real policy deployment, we then propose a novel real-to-sim tactile translation method that maps real tactile image streams to simulated tactile flow and depth fields, together with a new tactile data collection method, and validate it across diverse tactile sensor designs. Using this pipeline, we demonstrate real-world deployment on tasks encompassing dual-arm and dexterous in-hand manipulation. Overall, TactileLab provides an end-to-end sim-to-real framework for scalable tactile policy learning, enabling diverse shear-sensitive manipulation across heterogeneous tactile robotic systems.
full_text: & TactileLab is an end-to-end framework for efficient, shear-sensitive tactile robot learning. Built on IsaacLab, it integrates GPU-accelerated tactile simulation with a novel sensing modality, simulated tactile flow, for diverse contact-rich tasks and heterogeneous robotic systems. The framework includes modules for tactile policy and representation learning, a real-to-sim transfer pipeline supporting several real tactile sensors, and sim-to-real deployment of tactile reinforcement learning policies for various robots. This unified design enables scalable policy training, efficient collection of simulated tactile data, and effective transfer from simulation to real-world contact-rich manipulation. fig:overview ] YL and NFL were supported by ARIA Robot Dexterity award SMRB-PR01-P19. YL conducted this work at the University of Bristol. OpenDIM Lab, School of Aerospace Engineering, Beijing Institute of Technology, Beijing, China. Department of Engineering Mathematics and Bristol Robotics Laboratory, University of Bristol, Bristol BS8 1UB, U.K. Xi'an Jiaotong-Liverpool University, Suzhou, China. Robotic simulators that represent shear within tactile sensing are becoming increasingly important for contact-rich manipulation. However, simulating contact shear with high-fidelity deformable or soft-body simulation is computationally demanding, limiting scalability to large-scale reinforcement learning. Here we introduce TactileLab, a scalable multimodal tactile simulation framework built on IsaacLab, with a particular focus on a new optical-flow-based tactile representation termed simulated tactile flow. Instead of relying on soft-body physics to model shear deformation, TactileLab uses rigid-body simulation to efficiently estimate dense tangential motion at the contact interface, producing tactile flow fields that encode shear-relevant contact dynamics. This flow field complements geometric features from a contact depth field. We further introduce a novel policy architecture for jointly processing long-horizon proprioceptive signals and rich tactile observations. Across multiple contact-rich tasks, policies trained using simulated tactile flow learn efficiently at scale and exhibit emergent contact-aware behaviours. To facilitate sim-to-real policy deployment, we then propose a novel real-to-sim tactile translation method that maps real tactile image streams to simulated tactile flow and depth fields, together with a new tactile data collection method, and validate it across diverse tactile sensor designs. Using this pipeline, we demonstrate real-world deployment on tasks encompassing dual-arm and dexterous in-hand manipulation. Overall, TactileLab provides an end-to-end sim-to-real framework for scalable tactile policy learning, enabling diverse shear-sensitive manipulation across heterogeneous tactile robotic systems.\\ Project webpage: INTRODUCTION sec:Intro Tactile sensing provides local, contact-grounded feedback that is essential for fine manipulation tasks. This is the case when a robot must finely regulate interaction forces such as to maintain contact or respond to small changes at the contact interface. For such tasks, vision-based tactile sensors are attractive because they provide high-resolution and highly-sensitive spatial observations. However, scalable simulation methods still struggle to represent tangential interaction efficiently, which is needed for tasks that depend on shear forces. Most existing tactile simulators fall into two categories: 1)~ soft-body simulators can model compliant contact with high fidelity~ si2024difftactile, zhang2026simtac, li2026taccel , but can be too slow for large-scale reinforcement learning; 2) rigid-body simulators are fast and scalable, but usually provide only depth-like signals~ church2022tactile,lin2022tactilegym2,gomes2021generation, wang2022tacto, luu2023simulation . As a result, they are well suited for normal-contact reasoning but less effective for tasks in which shear, slip, or tangential motion matters. This limitation is important for manipulation problems such as in-contact trajectory following, insertion, and in-hand object manipulation in the presence of external perturbations. Depth-only observations cannot fully capture contact dynamics over time: similar depth signals may correspond to different contact states and future outcomes, making the task partially observable and harder for policies to learn. Because of this, recent tactile simulators have modelled distributed normal and shear feedback by relying on geometry-dependent contact formulations and object-specific preprocessing~ akinola2025tacsl,dang2026hydroshear . Here we introduce a new way to instead calculate dense shear cues directly from rigid-body simulation without those assumptions, using a novel optical-flow-based tactile representation that we term simulated tactile flow. This new flow representation allows us to address the gap of efficient shear-sensitive tactile simulation and robot learning, by introducing TactileLab: a complete sim-to-real framework that augments rigid-body tactile sensing with a dense tangential displacement field. Rather than explicitly simulating elastomer deformation, the framework represents contact using two complementary components: normal-contact depth and a tangential-displacement vector field. This combination gives a compact and sim-to-real transferable tactile observation that is efficient to compute, maps onto various tactile sensor designs, and is suitable for large-scale reinforcement learning. Our main contributions are as follows: 1. A scalable multimodal tactile simulation framework for contact-rich manipulation: TactileLab is built on top of IsaacLab~ mittal2025isaaclab and supports GPU-parallel simulation for efficient reinforcement learning. It provides multiple tactile sensing modalities, including contact forces, contact positions, contact depth images, and simulated tactile flow, allowing researchers to study both low-dimensional and high-dimensional tactile feedback within a unified framework. 2. A novel simulated tactile modality for shear-relevant contact interaction: We introduce simulated tactile flow, an optical-flow-inspired tactile modality that represents dense tangential motion at the contact interface. Together with contact depth, simulated tactile flow provides complementary high-dimensional tactile observations of normal contact geometry and tangential contact motion, enabling policies to exploit shear-relevant cues without explicit soft-body simulation. 3. A diverse suite of tactile robotic manipulation environments: TactileLab provides a set of contact-rich robotic environments for single-arm, dual-arm, and dexterous in-hand manipulation. These show the scalability and generality of TactileLab for policy learning with high-dimensional contact-depth and tactile flow observations. We conduct detailed simulation studies on two representative tasks: dual-arm object following and dexterous in-hand object manipulation. 4. A new sample-efficient policy architecture for fusing proprioceptive history and tactile observations: We propose PETS-Net (Positional-Encoding Temporal-Spatial Network) for encoding long-horizon low-dimensional proprioceptive histories and fusing them with high-dimensional tactile observations. Experimental results show that PETS-Net learns more efficiently than baseline policy architectures, demonstrating the benefit of jointly encoding temporal robot-state histories and spatial tactile features for contact-rich manipulation. 5. A new real-to-sim tactile transfer method for multimodal tactile observations: Building on a previous static transfer method for single tactile images, we propose separate real-to-sim translators for contact depth and tactile flow. Specifically, the tactile-flow translator takes real tactile image streams as input and predicts simulated tactile flow, extending real-to-sim transfer from static contact-depth reconstruction to dynamic tangential-motion representations. We further validate the real-to-sim pipeline across diverse tactile sensor designs, demonstrating its applicability beyond a single sensor configuration. 6. Real-world deployment of TactileLab-trained policies: Using the proposed multimodal tactile simulation and real-to-sim transfer pipeline, we demonstrate successful real-world deployment of policies trained in TactileLab on two representative contact-rich manipulation tasks: dual-arm object following and dexterous in-hand object manipulation. These results demonstrate the applicability of the TactileLab framework across distinct robotic embodiments and manipulation settings. TactileLab will be released as an open-source framework to lower the barrier to entry to tactile robot learning, enable reproducible research, and accelerate progress in tactile robotics. RELATED WORK sec:related Tactile Simulation subsec:simulation Existing tactile simulators broadly separate into rigid-body and deformable-body approaches. Rigid-body methods, including Tactile Gym~ church2022tactile,lin2022tactilegym2 , TACTO~ wang2022tacto , and other large-scale frameworks~ gomes2021generation,luu2023simulation , generate tactile signals from contact geometry, penetration depth, or contact forces available in conventional physics engines. They support efficient contact simulation but generally represent instantaneous normal contact without explicitly modelling shear deformation. In contrast, soft-body simulators model marker or elastomer deformation using analytical or calibrated approximations, FEM, or material-point methods~ si2022taxim, chen2023tacchi, si2024difftactile, du2024tacipc, zhao2024fots, li2026taccel, xu2026etac, chen2026univtac, zhang2026simtac . Although they capture richer contact information, they require sensor-specific deformation models and calibrated material parameters. Full soft-body solvers are also computationally intensive and generally offer lower throughput than rigid-body simulation~ chen2026univtac, zhang2026simtac , limiting large-scale parallel data generation for data-hungry methods such as RL. Recent geometry-aware approaches additionally model shear-sensitive signals. TacSL~ akinola2025tacsl computes dense normal and shear force fields, while HydroShear~ dang2026hydroshear models path-dependent hydroelastic shear. However, both require prior access to the contacting object shape through a signed-distance-function (SDF) representation and produce modelled force or marker-displacement fields. TactileLab instead derives tactile flow directly from rigid-body contact kinematics without object-specific SDF preprocessing, retaining scalable simulation while providing dense tangential-motion observations for shear-sensitive tasks. A central design goal of TactileLab is to support both traditional low-dimensional tactile signals and rich high-dimensional tactile observations. Low-dimensional signals, such as contact positions, contact forces, and shear vectors, provide compact information about contact events and interaction dynamics~ xu2022efficient, yang2023sim2real, chen2023tacchi, yang2024anyrotate, si2024difftactile, freud2025simshear . In contrast, high-dimensional tactile observations, such as contact-depth images~ gomes2021generation, church2022tactile, wang2022tacto, lin2022tactilegym2, akinola2025tacsl and optical-flow-based tactile flow~ du2021otf2, zhang2022otf3densecolor, funk2024evetac , provide dense spatial information over the tactile sensing surface. This allows researchers to study how different levels of tactile feedback affect policy learning, from compact contact-state representations to image-like tactile observations suitable for end-to-end learning. title: Symmetry-Aware Surrogate-Assisted Testing of UAVs
summary: We investigate a symmetry-aware surrogate-assisted testing approach for UAV autopilots. The proposed approach exploits geometric symmetries between flight missions by trans- forming obstacle configurations into a shared canonical coordi- nate frame. This enables a neural-network surrogate trained on a single reference mission to be reused across arbitrary missions, reducing the amount of high-fidelity simulation data required for training. The surrogate model is trained to predict the minimum clearance distance between a UAV and surrounding obstacles and is used to guide test generation towards safety-critical scenarios. We evaluate this approach using the Aerialist UAV test bench and benchmark its performance against techniques from the 2024 to 2026 UAV Testing Competitions. Results show that the approach achieves an average critical-test-case hit rate of 42% across the evaluated missions, compared with approximately 10% for the constrained-random baseline used to generate the training data. This approach also achieves high input diversity and competitive benchmark performance. However, our findings reveal limitations in transferring surrogate predictions across missions with differing flight-path characteristics, highlighting the boundaries of geometric canonicalization. To support reproducibility and future research, we provide the trained surrogate model and a dataset comprising more than 2,500 high-fidelity simulations.
