Introduction Unmanned Aerial Vehicles (UAVs) are increasingly employed in applications that require autonomous navigation in complex environments, such as indoor facilities~ lam2025minav , urban areas~ lin2021urban , and disaster sites~ oh2021disaster . In such environments, failures in obstacle avoidance can lead to collisions, making the safety and reliability of autonomous navigation systems a critical concern. To address these concerns, verification and validation methods, such as simulation-based testing, play an important role in establishing confidence in the trustworthiness of these systems. Simulation-based testing uses high-fidelity simulators to evaluate autonomous UAVs under a diverse range of environmental conditions while reducing the time, cost, and safety risks associated with physical flight testing. However, the input space makes exhaustive testing impractical. Search-based testing offers a systematic approach to this challenge by guiding test generation towards scenarios that are more likely to reveal system failures~ nejati2023reflections . This process, however, requires evaluating numerous candidate scenarios, making the computational cost of high-fidelity simulations a significant bottleneck. Surrogate-assisted testing offers an approach to mitigating this bottleneck by using computationally inexpensive surrogate models to estimate test outcomes without executing the high-fidelity simulator~ beglerovic2017testing . These models learn an approximation of the relationship between test inputs and simulation outcomes using data from previously executed high-fidelity simulations. Since evaluating a surrogate model is generally much less expensive than executing a high-fidelity simulation, a large number of candidate test scenarios can be assessed before selecting a smaller subset for simulation. In UAV obstacle-avoidance testing, test scenarios can be constructed by placing obstacles along a flight mission, with the objective of identifying configurations that cause the UAV to approach obstacles closely or exhibit unsafe behaviour. A flight mission may consist of multiple segments with different positions and orientations, each requiring its own obstacle configurations. Developing an accurate surrogate model for such scenarios requires training data representative of the configurations encountered across these segments. However, obtaining sufficient training data through high-fidelity simulations can be prohibitively expensive, especially when separate training data must be collected for different flight segments or missions. An opportunity to address this challenge arises from the geometric symmetries between flight segments. Obstacle configurations associated with different flight segments may have identical relative geometries despite differing in their global positions and orientations. Such geometrically equivalent configurations can be represented relative to a reference flight segment in a canonical coordinate frame, which we refer to as the canonical flight frame. In this work, we investigate a surrogate-assisted test-generation approach that exploits these geometric symmetries to reuse a neural-network surrogate across different flight missions. During training, the surrogate is trained to predict the minimum clearance distance between a UAV and surrounding obstacles for a reference flight mission. This reference flight mission defines the canonical flight frame. During test generation, candidate obstacle configurations for a target flight mission are transformed into the canonical flight frame and evaluated using the trained surrogate. Promising configurations are then transformed back into the target mission's coordinate system and evaluated using the high-fidelity simulator. Geometric equivalence does not necessarily imply equivalent UAV behaviour. The response of an autonomous UAV may also depend on factors such as its incoming velocity, heading, controller state, preceding flight segments, and the surrounding environment. Consequently, the extent to which a surrogate trained in a canonical frame can provide accurate predictions for different missions must be established empirically. This work investigates the efficiency and effectiveness of canonical surrogate reuse for simulation-based UAV testing, as well as its limitations. Specifically, we address the following research questions: RQ1: How does surrogate prediction accuracy vary across different flight missions? RQ2: To what extent does an NN-based surrogate improve the efficiency of test generation? RQ3: How does filtering based on a canonical surrogate affect test-suite diversity? To answer these questions and evaluate our approach, we apply it to efficiently create effective test cases for PX4-Avoidance, a vision-based autonomous obstacle avoidance system developed on top of PX4-Autopilot~ px4avoidance . We benchmark our approach against the test case generators that participated in the UAV Testing Competition 2024, 2025 and 2026 versions khatiri2024sbftuav,khatiri2025sbftuav,khatiri2025icstuav,uysal2026sbftuav,uysal2026icstuav . By addressing these research questions, this work makes the following main contributions: A neural network surrogate model that approximates the PX-4 obstacle avoidance system and estimates the minimum clearance distance between a UAV and an obstacle. An extensive empirical evaluation comparing the efficiency and effectiveness of the surrogate-guided test-case generator with those of state-of-the-art test-case generators. The limitations of canonical surrogate reuse for simulation-based UAV testing. A dataset of simulation results for over 2500 different obstacle configurations for a flight mission, which can be used to develop other types of surrogate models. The remainder of this paper is organized as follows. Section~ sec:related-work reviews related work and Section~ sec:casestudy introduces the UAV case study. Section~ sec:approach describes the symmetry-aware testing approach, while Section~ sec:evaluation reports the empirical evaluation. Section~ sec:discussion discusses the findings, assumptions, and limitations. Finally, Section~ sec:conclusion concludes the paper and outlines future work. Related Work sec:related-work The UAV testing competition has motivated several strategies for exploring the test-input space. In particular, DeepHyperion-UAV~ zohdinasab2024deephyperion uses illumination search, CAMBA~ deliso2024camba employs cost-aware mutation, and TUMB~ tang2024tumb uses Monte Carlo Tree Search to generate obstacle configurations. These approaches employ different search strategies to identify critical test cases, but evaluating candidate configurations through high-fidelity simulation remains computationally expensive. To address the cost of simulation-based testing, researchers have explored alternative approaches to test evaluation and generation. Shrinah and Eder~ shrinah2025pseudorandom employed a manually constructed low-fidelity path simulator to approximate UAV behaviour at a lower computational cost. Other approaches have investigated learning-based techniques. Zhu et al.~ zhu2024saflite proposed SaFliTe, which uses a large language model to predict test interestingness from textual safety objectives and the current system state. Peltom\"aki and Porres~ peltomaki2024learning proposed WOGAN, which iteratively trains a Wasserstein generative adversarial network to learn a distribution over counterexamples from which failure-inducing inputs can be sampled. The use of surrogate models to reduce the cost of search-based testing is well established. Nejati et al.~ nejati2023reflections provide a taxonomy of surrogate-assisted search-based testing. Beglerovic et al.~ beglerovic2017testing combined surrogate modelling with stochastic optimisation to search for fault-revealing regions when testing autonomous vehicles. Similarly, Haq et al.~ haq2022efficient employed surrogate-assisted many-objective optimisation to improve the efficiency of online testing of DNN-enabled systems. These approaches establish that learned approximations can reduce the cost of evaluating candidate tests during search. In contrast, our work is concerned with the representation used to train such an approximation: rather than learning separately over mission-dependent spatial coordinates, geometrically equivalent local flight configurations are mapped to a common reference frame. Menghi et al.~ menghi2019approximation proposed ARIsTEO for testing compute-intensive cyber-physical models. ARIsTEO constructs a cheaper surrogate of the model under test, searches this approximation for failure-revealing inputs, validates candidate failures on the original model, and refines the approximation when a candidate is spurious. This approximation--refinement strategy addresses errors in the surrogate dynamically. Neural-network-based guidance has also been investigated in evolutionary testing. Zhong et al.~ zhong2021autofuzz proposed AutoFuzz, which combines neural-network guidance with evolutionary fuzzing to identify traffic-violation scenarios for autonomous vehicles. Similarly, Zohdinasab et al.~ zohdinasab2024focused proposed DeepAtash-LR, which integrates a surrogate model into an evolutionary focused-testing process for autonomous driving, directing test generation towards specified combinations of structural and behavioural features. While these approaches demonstrate different ways of using learned models to guide test generation, they do not investigate the reuse of a single surrogate across geometrically related test scenarios through canonical representation. Geometric symmetry has been widely investigated as a means of reducing redundant variation in machine learning. Cohen and Welling~ cohen2016group introduced group-equivariant convolutional networks, which incorporate transformations such as rotations and translations into the network architecture. Bietti et al.~ bietti2021sample studied the sample-complexity benefits of learning under invariance. These works motivate the exploitation of geometric symmetry, but do not address surrogate reuse in simulation-based testing. title: GuidedWAM: Training-Free Energy Guidance for World Action Models in Autonomous Driving
summary: World action models (WAMs) for autonomous driving couple the driving policy and the visual world model in a single generative network whose objectives are fixed post-training. Conditioning on a new driving objective requires retraining. We study energy guidance as a general mechanism and present GuidedWAM, a model-agnostic framework for injecting driving objectives into frozen WAMs at sampling time. Our framework constructs each objective as differentiable energies on the sampler's intermediate clean-action estimate, which needs only forward access to the frozen model, and is stabilized by sampling-time guidance scheduling, per-energy normalization, and velocity-bounded correction. On the NAVSIM v2 hard-split, guidance improves all three frozen, publicly released WAMs by 1.8 to 3.6 EPDMS, averaged over three sampler seeds, and adds less than 10% to the sampling time per step. These results position energy guidance as a practical post-training control channel for WAMs.

Conditioning on a new driving objective requires retraining. We study energy guidance as a general mechanism and present GuidedWAM, a model-agnostic framework for injecting driving objectives into frozen WAMs at sampling time. Our framework constructs each objective as differentiable energies on the sampler's intermediate clean-action estimate, which needs only forward access to the frozen model, and is stabilized by sampling-time guidance scheduling, per-energy normalization, and velocity-bounded correction. On the NAVSIM v2 hard-split, guidance improves all three frozen, publicly released WAMs by to EPDMS, averaged over three sampler seeds, and adds less than to the sampling time per step. These results position energy guidance as a practical post-training control channel for WAMs. Introduction sec:intro World action models (WAMs) are an emerging family of end-to-end driving models. The generative model learns the driving policy simultaneously with a visual world model, where the policy inherits the physical and visual knowledge of a large video prior, and the model can imagine the future driving scene drivewam2026,simwam2026,universe2026,xia2026drivelaw . Recent WAMs reach planning scores above 90 PDMS on NAVSIM v1 dauner2024navsim,drivewam2026,simwam2026 . Despite these advantages, WAMs come with their own drawbacks. By training as a whole, the driving objectives freeze once the training is finished and cannot be extended at will. In practice, a driving policy has to serve objectives that change with the operating context during deployment: a wider margin to the road edge on a narrow street, a larger clearance around vulnerable road users, a temporal speed limit, or a passenger's comfort preference. A WAM learns its driving behavior mainly from driving data. Sampling-time condition is only possible if such driving objectives are available in the data during training. Adding one means collecting supervision for it and retraining a billion-parameter model, which has to be repeated for every new objective. What is missing is a control channel that acts on the frozen model at sampling time. Therefore, we present GuidedWAM, a training-free energy-guidance framework for world action models for autonomous driving. Each driving objective is constructed as a differentiable energy on the sampler's one-step clean estimate of the action stream, whose gradient is added to the frozen model's velocity field during sampling. We investigate whether the driving policy of a frozen WAM can be guided at sampling time toward an objective it was never trained on. Our contributions are two-fold: We derive energy guidance on the one-step clean estimate of the flow-matching sampler that current WAMs share, in a Jacobian-free form that needs only forward passes through the frozen model, and show that it steers three public WAMs on NAVSIM v2. We show that the guidance is stabilized by sampling-time guidance scheduling, per-energy normalization, and velocity bounded correction. Related Works sec:related World action models as driving planners A video world model learns how an environment evolves under the agent's actions, so that a policy can be trained or evaluated on imagined rollouts ha2018worldmodels,hafner2020dreamer . In autonomous driving, this idea first produced action-conditioned video world models, which render the future camera view from past frames and actions wang2023drivedreamer,hu2023gaia,gao2024vista . World action models close the gap by also generating the action stream, so that the driving knowledge learned from a large video prior can transfer to planning. DriveWAM and UNIVERSE train video and ego action tokens in one shared attention sequence under a single flow-matching objective drivewam2026,universe2026 , SimWAM co-trains a video expert with a light action expert and drops the video branch at inference for run-time simwam2026 , and DriveLaW plans from the latent of its video generator xia2026drivelaw . They reach planning scores above 90 PDMS on NAVSIM v1 dauner2024navsim . For this paper, the three public models we guide share one property: the plan is produced by a flow-matching sampler conditioned on a fixed set of context channels, past frames, ego status, and a navigation command.\\ Control channels for flow-matching planners Most current WAMs are built on diffusion or flow-matching backbones lipman2023flow,liu2023rectified,peebles2023dit . Conditional flow matching trains the velocity field on a context. Classifier guidance adds the gradient of a noise-aware classifier to the score at sampling time dhariwal2021classifier , and classifier-free guidance replaces the classifier with the model's own unconditional prediction ho2022cfg . Independent of training, energy guidance instead descends an external differentiable objective on the sampler's clean estimate. Diffusion posterior sampling evaluates the objective on the denoiser’s clean estimate chung2023dps , manifold-preserving guided diffusion drops the network Jacobian he2024mpgd , and feng2025flowguidance carry the construction to flow matching. In the driving domain, CTG and CTG++ guide traffic simulation with signal-temporal-logic and language-derived costs zhong2023ctg,zhong2023ctgpp . Diffusion Planner applies classifier guidance to a vectorized-state planner zheng2025diffusionplanner . GuideFlow corrects constraint violations inside the sampling loop with a constraint vocabulary fixed at training guideflow2025 . A second family steers a frozen planner from outside the sampler by search rather than by gradients. Diffusion-ES applies evolutionary search to a trajectory diffusion model yang2024diffusiones . TOAD runs cross-entropy-method search over the proposals of six frozen NAVSIM planners against a learned trajectory scorer xu2026toad . We adopt the Jacobian-free clean-estimate gradient. We apply the analytic energies directly on the diffusion policy instead of searching or scoring sampled trajectories.\\ Safety filters and constrained flow matching Another way to enforce a driving constraint on a learned planner is a safety filter applied after the plan is produced, a control barrier function certificate that defines a safe set and a minimal correction that keeps the plan inside it ames2019cbf,shalevshwartz2017rss . SafeFlow enforces control barrier functions across the sampler dai2025safeflow , SafeFlowMatcher alternates prediction with barrier-based correction yang2025safeflowmatcher , UniConFlow shapes a prescribed-time guidance field for equality and inequality constraints yang2025uniconflow , HardFlow solves a receding-horizon optimization on the clean estimate at every step li2025hardflow . Safety-guided flow shows that negative guidance must act within a critical time window kim2026sgf , which is the closest precedent for our noise-level scheduling. These methods target hard satisfaction of known constraint sets on planners. We construct soft and composable energies for frozen models and compare the in-sampling channel with the post-hoc member of this family on the same constraint. title: Reinforcing End-to-End Autonomous Driving Safety via Negative-Aware Planning in a Unified World-Action Model
summary: World-action models (WAMs) jointly model future traffic states and driving actions for end-to-end autonomous driving in intelligent transportation systems. However, their action learning remains dominated by expert-trajectory imitation, leaving unsafe alternatives close to expert trajectories insufficiently constrained. To improve WAM robustness in safety-critical scenarios, we propose NegWAM, a safety post-training framework for unified WAMs that learns explicit safety boundaries from near-expert failure trajectories. NegWAM constructs negative trajectories that are geometrically close to the expert trajectory yet carry safety risks, uses them as repulsive anchors to steer predictions away from dangerous behavior, and encodes them as scene-conditioned rider tokens to learn scene--trajectory compatibility. During training, NegWAM jointly optimizes the flow-matching and near-expert negative objectives, while the auxiliary rider branch is discarded at inference, incurring no additional overhead. On NAVSIM v2, NegWAM achieves 40.4 EPDMS on navhard, a 4.1% relative improvement over the strongest compared scorer-free WAM baseline, and achieves 93.3 EPDMS on navtest. These results demonstrate that NegWAM achieves strong performance in safety-critical scenarios while preserving routine-driving performance. Zero-shot closed-loop evaluation on HUGSIM further demonstrates cross-benchmark generalization. The code is available at https://github.com/Zizizi-hao/NegWAM.
full_text: Methods sec:method NegWAM post-trains a unified world--action model using scene-specific failures close to expert trajectories. Each retained failure supplies two related learning signals: a motion to avoid during action generation and a scene--trajectory pair to distinguish from the expert. Figure~ fig:fig2_methods illustrates how repulsive anchors and scene-conditioned rider tokens introduce these signals into the same backbone while retaining its flow-matching objective. A training sample comprises a current camera image , future visual targets , an expert trajectory , and navigation and ego-state conditions including four historical ego poses. A frozen causal video VAE encodes the observed and future frames into the clean visual stream . The action tokenizer forms by normalizing the expert's eight future -pose steps and prepending a zero conditioning chunk. Rider groups and the compatibility head are used only during post-training. Training Objective sec:training_objective Our training procedure consists of two consecutive stages. In the first stage, we initialize the model from the pretrained video generative model Wan2.2-TI2V-5B~ wan2025wan and adapt it to autonomous driving by following the unified world--action flow-matching paradigm of DriveWAM~ shi2026drivewam . This stage optimizes only the flow-matching objective defined in Section~ sec:preliminaries , enabling the model to jointly learn future visual dynamics and expert trajectory prediction. The resulting model serves as the base WAM checkpoint shared by all subsequent experiments. In the second stage, we initialize from this shared checkpoint and perform hard-negative safety post-training. We retain the original flow-matching objective as supervision for visual dynamics and expert actions, while introducing repulsive trajectory supervision and scene-conditioned compatibility learning. At inference, we discard the rider groups and compatibility head and use the original world--action generation pathway with the updated backbone. The model encodes the available observations, generates future visual latents with three Euler updates, and then generates the eight-step action chunk with ten Euler updates. These are integration-step counts rather than total backbone forward-call counts. The action decoder converts the generated tokens to the final trajectory; no hard-negative candidates or evaluator are used at this stage.

title: FlyingDrones: A Dataset and Benchmark for Optical Flow Estimation from UAV motion
summary: Optical flow is an important cue for drone analysis in aerial surveillance, airspace monitoring, and long-range target tracking, where motion remains informative when appearance is weak. Estimating the motion of small Unmanned Aerial Vehicles, however, is difficult because distant targets occupy few pixels, have low contrast, and move against complex dynamic backgrounds. Standard optical-flow benchmarks emphasize large, object-centric motions and therefore do not characterize distant aerial targets well. We introduce FlyingDrones, a generated benchmark with dense ground-truth optical flow and segmentation masks derived from physically based rendering, and define resolution-normalized metrics (EPE Norm) that normalize flow by image dimensions. We evaluate 16 state-of-the-art model families on a motion- and size-stratified subset of 999 flow pairs at three resolutions. Every family recovers drone motion better than the zero-flow reference, but the gap between families widens with resolution: at 1920x1080, global-matching, recurrent, transformer, and short-window temporal models separate clearly from pyramid, classical, self-supervised, lightweight, and diffusion models. Within-family checkpoint spread is comparable to or larger than between-family spread, so the training curriculum is as important as the architecture. Two complementary studies test the benchmark beyond synthetic accuracy: a ground-truth-free motion-alignment evaluation on 21 cameras of real UAV footage shows that the synthetic ranking carries a moderate, significant signal about real-world performance (Spearman \r{ho} = 0.63 over 41 checkpoints) while the exact top ranks differ, and a fine-tuning study shows that 800 FlyingDrones pairs reduce held-out drone-region error by up to 37% and improve drone localization on the real footage for all four architectures tested.
full_text: Optical flow is an important cue for drone analysis in aerial surveillance, airspace monitoring, and long-range target tracking, where motion remains informative when appearance is weak. Estimating the motion of small Unmanned Aerial Vehicles (UAVs), however, is difficult because distant targets occupy few pixels, have low contrast, and move against complex dynamic backgrounds. Standard optical-flow benchmarks emphasize large, object-centric motions and therefore do not characterize distant aerial targets well. We introduce FlyingDrones, a generated benchmark with dense ground-truth optical flow and segmentation masks derived from physically based rendering, and define resolution-normalized metrics (EPE Norm) that normalize flow by image dimensions. We evaluate 16 state-of-the-art model families (88 public checkpoints) on a motion- and size-stratified subset of 999 flow pairs at three resolutions, with bootstrap confidence intervals and a zero-flow reference. Every family recovers drone motion better than the zero-flow reference, but the gap between families widens with resolution: at , global-matching, recurrent, transformer, and short-window temporal models separate clearly from pyramid, classical, self-supervised, lightweight, and diffusion models. Within-family checkpoint spread is comparable to or larger than between-family spread, so the training curriculum is as important as the architecture. Two complementary studies test the benchmark beyond synthetic accuracy: a ground-truth-free motion-alignment evaluation on 21 cameras of real UAV footage shows that the synthetic ranking carries a moderate, significant signal about real-world performance (Spearman over 41 checkpoints) while the exact top ranks differ, and a fine-tuning study shows that 800 FlyingDrones pairs reduce held-out drone-region error by up to and improve drone localization on the real footage for all four architectures tested. Introduction Apparent motion is an important visual cue in drone analysis and aerial surveillance~ srigrarom2020, mahalanobis2025 . At long ranges, drones often occupy only a few pixels and lack stable features due to simple appearance textures and complex backgrounds. This means that the relevant signal is weak, localized, and additionally often superimposed by camera-induced background motion, making motion computation challenging. This work therefore evaluates and compares a broad range of optical flow methods under the tiny motion regime: classical and early deep baselines such as PyFlow~ pathak_learning_2017 , FlowNet2~ ilg2017 , PWC-Net~ sun2018 , LiteFlowNet3~ hui_liteflownet3_2020 , and VCN~ yang_volumetric_2019 ; recurrent correlation-based models such as RAFT~ teed2020 and SEA-RAFT~ wang2025a ; lightweight or self-/unsupervised variants such as FastFlowNet~ kong_fastflownet_2021 and ARFlow~ liu_learning_2020 ; transformer-style correspondence models such as GMFlow~ xu_gmflow_2022 , UniMatch~ xu_unifying_2023 , FlowFormer++~ shi_flowformer_2023 , and WAFT~ wang2025 ; temporally extended models such as VideoFlow~ shi_videoflow_2023 and MemFlow~ dong_memflow_2024 ; and the generative FlowDiffusion~ saxena_surprising_2023, dong_open-ddvm_2023 . State of the art (SOTA) datasets and metrics account to the uncertainty in the behavior of optical flow methods with tiny motions: FlyingChairs~ dosovitskiy2015 and FlyingThings3D~ mayer_large_2016 provide large-scale synthetic supervision, Sintel~ Butler:ECCV:2012 emphasizes cinematic effects and non-rigid motion, KITTI~ Menze2015CVPR focuses on outdoor driving scenes, and TartanAir~ tartanair2020iros broadens camera trajectories and environments. None of the existing datasets target drones, tiny aerial objects or in general tiny motion regions. Standard measures such as end-point error (EPE), 1px, 3px, 5px, and Fl-all are informative for moderate or large motion regions but become hard to interpret when the target occupies only a few pixels. To address these issues, we introduce FlyingDrones, a synthetically generated benchmark for optical flow assessment of drone motion, with dense optical-flow and segmentation ground truth across controlled image resolution regimes. The paper also proposes drone-pixel-only metrics and a new resolution-normalized EPE, which makes flow components independent of image width and height, and use them to study SOTA optical flow methods and training curricula independently of image resolution. To the best of our knowledge, this work is the first systematic assessment of optical flow methods applied to tiny motion regions like those created by drones. To summarize, this papers makes the following contributions: We introduce FlyingDrones, a synthetically generated dataset with dense optical-flow and segmentation ground truth for evaluating drone motion across target sizes and image resolutions. We define resolution-normalized evaluation measures, especially EPE Norm, to make cross-resolution performance more interpretable. We compare 16 optical-flow methods (88 public checkpoints) on a motion- and size-stratified subset of the benchmark with confidence intervals and a zero-flow reference, and show that the families separate increasingly with resolution, that within-family checkpoint spread rivals between-family spread, and that Sintel-style fine-tuning increasingly outperforms KITTI-style fine-tuning as resolution grows. We validate the benchmark beyond synthetic accuracy: a ground-truth-free motion-alignment study on 21 cameras of real UAV footage~ li_reconstruction_2020 measures how far the synthetic ranking transfers to real data, and a fine-tuning study on a held-out FlyingDrones split shows that the dataset improves both held-out synthetic accuracy and real-footage drone localization. Related Work Classical optical flow methods such as Horn--Schunck~ horn1981 and Lucas--Kanade~ lucas1981 formulate motion estimation as a variational problem with brightness-constancy and smoothness assumptions, but struggle with large displacements, strong appearance changes, and complex non-rigid motion. Early deep optical-flow models replaced handcrafted optimization with supervised end-to-end learning. FlowNet and FlowNet2~ dosovitskiy2015, ilg2017 established the Chairs/Things pre-training pipeline used by many later methods, while coarse-to-fine architectures such as PWC-Net~ sun2018 , LiteFlowNet/LiteFlowNet3~ hui18liteflownet, hui_liteflownet3_2020 , and FastFlowNet~ kong_fastflownet_2021 combined feature pyramids, warping, and compact cost volumes for efficient inference. These models perform well on conventional benchmarks, but repeated downsampling can suppress very small motion cues. A related family emphasizes richer matching representations. VCN~ yang_volumetric_2019 uses volumetric correspondence reasoning; RAFT~ teed2020 replaces coarse-to-fine refinement with a dense all-pairs correlation volume and iterative updates at fixed feature resolution; SEA-RAFT~ wang2025a simplifies RAFT and models uncertainty more explicitly; and WAFT~ wang2025 uses warping-based alignment with a transformer-style update module. These methods are especially relevant here because they preserve finer spatial information than traditional pyramid approaches. ARFlow~ liu_learning_2020 learns optical flow with self-supervised consistency constraints, and PyFlow remains a useful non-deep variational baseline. Such methods are attractive when labels are scarce or speed matters, but often trade accuracy for robustness or efficiency. GMFlow~ xu_gmflow_2022 , UniMatch~ xu_unifying_2023 , and FlowFormer++~ shi_flowformer_2023 model long-range interactions more explicitly than local convolutional pipelines. VideoFlow~ shi_videoflow_2023 uses multi-frame inputs, MemFlow~ dong_memflow_2024 adds an explicit memory mechanism, and FlowDiffusion~ saxena_surprising_2023, dong_open-ddvm_2023 formulates prediction with a diffusion-style process. Across these categories, models differ in supervision, matching representation, temporal context, and computational budget, but most were developed on datasets dominated by moderate or large motions. Our benchmark studies their behavior when the relevant signal is the weak motion of a tiny aerial target. Small aerial-target analysis is usually framed as object detection. Appearance-based detectors such as YOLO~ redmon2016a and Faster R-CNN~ ren2017 are widely used, but their performance degrades when targets shrink to a few pixels because discriminative features are attenuated or lost during pooling and strided convolutions~ lin_feature_2017, tong_recent_2020, liu_survey_2021, cheng_towards_2023 . Motion estimation can therefore provide complementary information~ sun_enhancing_2023, alkentar_utilize_2024 . Early motion-based strategies relied on background subtraction, which assumes a static viewpoint and fails under the ego-motion typical of aerial surveillance. Deep optical flow instead models dense pixel-wise displacements and can separate object motion from camera-induced parallax, but objects occupying only a fraction of a percent of the image generate weak, localized signals that are easily overwhelmed by background flow or smoothed out by spatial regularization and coarse-to-fine downsampling~ sun2018 . Despite the importance of optical flow for small-target analysis, empirical validation remains limited by the lack of suitable data. title: AffineGS: Unlocking Accurate Geometry in 3DGS via Spatially Varying Affine Rectification
comment: Accpeted to NeurIPS 2026. Project page: https://eldentse.github.io/AffineGS/
summary: 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) has become the leading approach for photorealistic novel view synthesis, yet its geometric accuracy lags behind its visual quality. Existing depth-guided methods attempt to resolve this by regularizing the optimization with monocular depth priors, typically using a single global scale-and-shift alignment. Crucially, we discover a fundamental flaw in this assumption: modern monocular depth networks systematically exhibit region-dependent, piecewise-linear distortions. This discovery invalidates standard global alignment strategies, which warp scene geometry by enforcing a single transform. To address this, we introduce a spatially varying affine rectification model that corrects monocular disparity into consistent metric depth using regionally smooth, edge-aware fields. We further derive a normal-aware regularizer that uses spatial gradients to couple the rectified disparity with 3DGS depth and normals. Across diverse experimental settings, our sensor-free method shows strong photometric quality of Gaussian Splatting while substantially improving geometric accuracy and outperforming state-of-the art geometry-focused methods.
full_text: Experiments sec:experiments details. We train 3DGS using the following loss objective, which is a weighted combination of our proposed geometric regularization: We empirically set , , and is the original photometric loss~ kerbl20233d . On the MuSHRoom scenes kokko and sauna, these default weights produce floaters, so we scale all three weights by 0.5 and 0.25, respectively. On ScanNet++, we use the 0.25 scaling and train at half resolution ( ). Appendix Sec.~ sec:hyperparams_appendix lists all per-scene settings. We train all models for 30k iterations. For densification, we use the unmodified adaptive density control of Splatfacto~ tancik2023nerfstudio (gradient-based cloning and splitting, opacity-based pruning, and periodic opacity reset) with its default settings, identical for our method and all Gaussian-based baselines. We change no densification logic, so all reported gains come from our supervision signal alone. To obtain disparity maps, we propagate RGB images through the pre-trained Depth-Anything-V2-Large model~ yang2024depth . Crucially, the spatially varying affine parameters ( the scale factor ) used to rectify these monocular priors are iteratively updated alongside the 3DGS scene parameters during optimization. By following~ turkulainen2025dn , we initialize the Gaussian scene using 1M back-projected points from training dataset sensor depths. The Algorithm column of Tables~ tab:main-table-mesh-mushroom and~ tab:main-table-mesh-scannetpp lists the meshing algorithm of each method. We mesh our method, and DN-Splatter (Monodepth) on MuSHRoom, by fusing the depth maps rendered at the training views with Open3D TSDF fusion (voxel size 0.01 and truncation 0.03, in scene units). Methods meshed with Poisson reconstruction extract a total of 2M points from back-projected depth/normal maps and use a depth level of 9; Neusfacto and MonoSDF use marching cubes, and 2DGS uses TSDF fusion. Appendix Sec.~ sec:meshing_appendix compares Poisson and TSDF meshes of the same trained models. We refer readers to turkulainen2025dn for more details. . We evaluate across implicit, explicit, and classical representations. Implicit baselines include Nerfacto, Depth-Nerfacto~ tancik2023nerfstudio , Neusfacto~ yu2022sdfstudio , and MonoSDF~ yu2022monosdf . Explicit baselines feature standard Splatfacto~ tancik2023nerfstudio , geometry-focused SuGaR~ guedon2024sugar and 2DGS~ huang20242d , alongside depth-regularized DRGS~ chung2024depth and DN-Splatter~ turkulainen2025dn . For a fair sensor-free comparison, we introduce DN-Splatter (Monodepth), which replaces its physical sensor data with dynamically aligned monocular priors (Depth-Anything-V2~ yang2024depth ). Finally, we include classical Poisson surface reconstruction from back-projected sensor depth to contextualize upper-bound mesh performance~ turkulainen2025dn . . We validate our proposed method across a diverse set of challenging indoor environments. For standard forward-facing captures, we utilize the NeRF-LLFF dataset~ mildenhall2019local , which comprises distinct real-world scenes. To assess generalization to complex camera movements, we evaluate on the MuSHRoom dataset~ ren2024mushroom , a real-world indoor benchmark specifically designed with disjoint camera trajectories for training and testing. Finally, to evaluate geometric accuracy, we benchmark on ScanNet++~ yeshwanth2023scannet++ , a large-scale real-world dataset providing dense RGB sequences paired with high-fidelity 3D ground-truth geometry. metrics. We follow standard practice and report PSNR, SSIM and LPIPS metrics for color images and common depth metrics to analyze depth quality for datasets containing ground truth sensor data. For assessing mesh quality, we follow turkulainen2025dn and report accuracy, completion, Chamfer distance, normal consistency and F-scores with a threshold of 5cm. . Following the evaluation protocol of DRGS~ chung2024depth , we partition each scene into distinct training and testing sets. For our sparse-view experiments, we optimize the scenes using randomly sampled training images ( ) and evaluate novel-view synthesis on the fixed test set. To ensure statistical reliability, all reported metrics are averaged over ten random seed selections. Additionally, we reference the Oracle performance established by DRGS. This oracle serves as an upper bound to demonstrate the theoretical impact of perfect depth geometry; it is generated by optimizing a model on the entire dense image collection (both train and test) to create pseudo-ground-truth depth maps, which are then used in place of standard depth estimates. . title: La-JEPA: Compact Robot Policies with Latent World Modeling
summary: World-action models adapt pretrained video generators, and vision-language-action models build on pretrained vision-language backbones; both tie policy architecture and inference cost to large transformers designed for generation rather than control. It remains unclear how much these generation-oriented choices affect control. In this work, we introduce Latent Action JEPA (La-JEPA), a compact world-action model whose policy transformer is trained from scratch in the feature space of a pretrained V-JEPA 2.1 encoder. Following Fast-WAM, La-JEPA learns to predict future features jointly with actions during training and generates only actions at inference. Among policies without embodied pretraining, La-JEPA achieves state-of-the-art performance in clean and randomized RoboTwin 2.0 scenes and on LIBERO-Plus with correct instructions, while using far fewer parameters than the strongest competing policies. It runs substantially faster than Fast-WAM at comparable performance and outperforms the closest JEPA-based methods, LeapBot-WA and JEPA-WAM, on LIBERO-Plus and RoboTwin 2.0 without their pretrained policy backbones. On four real-robot tasks, its average success is comparable to pi0.5 and above non-embodied-pretrained baselines. Through a design study of the choices behind La-JEPA, we show that JEPA features outperform video VAE latents, most clearly out of distribution, and that training-time future prediction choices significantly impact the policy even when future prediction is skipped at inference. We correct the LIBERO-Plus instructions, as the officially released evaluator corrupts them for most variants, and re-evaluate several strong open baselines. Without a generative pretrained policy backbone, La-JEPA is better and faster than far larger policies, suggesting that robot foundation models may benefit from architectures designed for control rather than inherited from generation.
full_text: Code: World-action models commonly adapt pretrained video generators, and vision-language-action models build on pretrained vision-language backbones; both tie policy architecture and inference cost to large transformers designed for generation rather than control. While the knowledge accumulated through large-scale pretraining is certainly useful, it remains unclear how much generation-oriented architectural choices affect control performance, and whether the trade-off required to access this pretraining is worth it. In this work, we introduce Latent Action JEPA (La-JEPA), a compact world-action model whose policy transformer is trained from scratch in the feature space of a pretrained V-JEPA~2.1 encoder, so that its architecture and capacity can be chosen for control. Following Fast-WAM, La-JEPA learns to predict future features jointly with actions during training and generates only actions at inference. Among policies without embodied pretraining, La-JEPA achieves state-of-the-art performance in clean and randomized RoboTwin~2.0 scenes and on LIBERO-Plus with correct instructions, while using far fewer parameters than the strongest competing policies. It runs substantially faster than Fast-WAM at comparable performance and outperforms the closest JEPA-based methods, LeapBot-WA and JEPA-WAM, on LIBERO-Plus and RoboTwin~2.0 without their pretrained policy backbones. On four real-robot tasks, including contact-heavy pushing and long-horizon multistep manipulation, its average success is comparable to , outperforming non-embodied-pretrained baselines. Through a design study of the choices behind La-JEPA, we show that JEPA features outperform video VAE latents, most clearly out of distribution, and that training-time future prediction choices significantly impact the policy even when future prediction is skipped at inference. We also correct the LIBERO-Plus instructions, as the officially released evaluator corrupts them for most variants, and re-evaluate several strong open baselines. These results establish a compact, efficient foundation for JEPA-based world-action modeling: without a generative pretrained policy backbone, La-JEPA is better and faster than far larger policies built on video and language generation models, suggesting that robot foundation models may benefit from architectures designed specifically for control rather than inherited from generation. Introduction sec:introduction World-action models increasingly adapt pretrained video-generation transformers to robot control, inheriting useful visual and temporal priors along with the representation space, tokenization, and architecture of a model built for video synthesis~ fastwam,fasterwam,cosmos_policy . Vision-language-action policies take a similar route using language-generation transformers aligned with visual inputs~ openvla,pi0,pi05 . The success of these two types of architectures raises two practical questions: must robot policies necessarily inherit the architecture of a generative backbone to be competitive, and can a compact world-action transformer trained from scratch actually reach the performance of these policies? Most world-action models (WAMs) are VAE-based because they build on pretrained video generators, yet better-suited latent spaces are available. Video VAEs retain accurate information but spend much of their capacity on pixel-level fidelity that control does not require. JEPA representations, in contrast, are developed and evaluated for downstream tasks such as video understanding, depth estimation, and segmentation, which are closer to the needs of embodied agents~ vjepa2,vjepa21 . Previous work aligns VLMs or video-generation models to the JEPA space~ jepawam,leapbot or learns a JEPA-style latent space jointly with the policy~ actjepa ; to our knowledge, no prior work trains a compact world-action policy from scratch in a pretrained JEPA feature space. We introduce Latent Action JEPA (La-JEPA), a world-action model that learns future-feature prediction and action generation directly in the dense spatial and temporal feature space of a pretrained V-JEPA~2.1 video encoder~ vjepa21 . Its World DiT and Action DiT are initialized from scratch, allowing their architecture and capacity to be chosen independently of the visual encoder. Following Fast-WAM and Faster-WAM~ fastwam,fasterwam , actions attend to observed context but not to future tokens, so predictive supervision can shape the policy during training without the cost of generating the future at inference time. Among policies without embodied pretraining, La-JEPA achieves the strongest clean and randomized RoboTwin~2.0 results and the strongest LIBERO-Plus results with corrected instructions (Section~ sec:libero-plus-text ), with about four times fewer deployed parameters than the next-best policies, while running up to 5 faster than Fast-WAM, whose design we follow (Figure~ fig:main-efficiency , Tables~ tab:main-comparison and~ tab:robotwin-comparison ). With the released instructions, it is second only to NowWAM, which is insensitive to the corrupted text (Table~ tab:libero-plus-text ). It also outperforms the closest JEPA-based methods, LeapBot-WA and JEPA-WAM, on LIBERO-Plus and RoboTwin~2.0 (Table~ tab:jepa-comparison ). On real-robot tasks ranging from cube placement to contact-rich pushing and long-horizon manipulation, La-JEPA trained from scratch on the target demonstrations achieves the highest average success among the compared policies, comparable to the embodied-pretrained (Table~ tab:real-robot ). Together, these results demonstrate leading benchmark performance, efficient inference, and competitive physical manipulation without requiring a generative backbone. To understand which design choices enable this performance, we study the impact of the representation space, different targets for predictive supervision, and robustness mechanisms. We adopt a compact first approach, making the architecture viable even for a policy with 0.1B trainable parameters, before increasing policy capacity. Comparisons of JEPA features and VAE latents span both benchmarks and multiple model configurations, showing that JEPA features generally outperform VAE latents, with the clearest gains for out of distribution evaluations (Section~ sec:predictive-design , Appendix~ app:ablations ). Action-only controls separately confirm the benefit of WAM-style future prediction, and studies of temporal encoding, dropout, augmentation, and encoder adaptation complete the recipe. These analyses support the central contribution: a compact, effective world-action policy, together with evidence to guide its design. As a secondary contribution, we show that the released LIBERO-Plus evaluator appends perturbation parameters to most instructions, so that most variants apply two perturbations at once. This corruption affects policies to very different degrees, from no change to 19 points, and obscures the robustness study that the benchmark is designed for; we therefore re-evaluate the openly available baselines with corrected instructions under a single ``clean'' protocol that isolates each perturbation as intended (Section~ sec:libero-plus-text ). Related Work sec:related-work Vision-language-action policies. Vision-language-action (VLA) policies extend pretrained vision-language models with action outputs, predicting discretized action tokens~ openvla or attaching a flow-matching action expert~ pi0 , and broaden their training data to generalize further~ pi05,qwen_robotmanip . All inherit the size and inference cost of a multi-billion-parameter vision-language backbone. World-action models. World-action models (WAMs) instead build on pretrained video or image generators whose representations drive action generation~ cosmos_policy,imagewam,nowwam , reaching the strongest previously reported LIBERO-Plus results among policies without embodied pretraining. Because generating future frames slows inference, recent WAMs predict the future only during training~ fastwam and reduce the action expert to a single layer that reads keys and values cached from all layers of the video backbone~ fasterwam . All retain the generator backbone in the deployed policy. Joint-embedding predictive architectures. Joint-embedding predictive architectures (JEPAs) learn representations by predicting the embeddings of masked inputs rather than reconstructing pixels~ ijepa . V-JEPA extends this objective to video~ vjepa , V-JEPA~2 scales it~ vjepa2 , and V-JEPA~2.1 improves the dense features of V-JEPA~2~ vjepa21 , which makes it especially well suited to robotic policies. JEPA representations have since been used in robot policies: ACT-JEPA learns a JEPA-style latent space jointly with the policy~ actjepa , VLA-JEPA and JEPA-VLA bring V-JEPA targets or features into vision-language-action models~ vlajepa,jepavla , and JEPA-WAM and LeapBot-WA build world-action models on V-JEPA features~ jepawam,leapbot . These two world-action models are the closest to La-JEPA, but both initialize their predictors from pretrained vision-language or video generation models. Compact policies. Policies that are competitive without inheriting either a VLM or video backbone are scarce. While Diffusion Policy~ diffusion_policy , DP3~ dp3 and ACT~ act exist, their performance is rarely close to VLAs and World Models. MINT predicts coarse-to-fine action tokens with a separately trained action tokenizer~ mint and reaches much better success rates, but remains below the strongest WAMs and VLAs. La-JEPA fits in this category as it trains its policy DiTs from scratch while adding WAM-style future prediction in a pretrained JEPA feature space. La-JEPA sec:method La-JEPA learns action generation jointly with future-feature prediction in a pretrained V-JEPA~2.1 ViT-L representation space, following the separation of training-time world modeling from inference-time action generation in Fast-WAM~ fastwam and Faster-WAM~ fasterwam . At decision time , the policy maps multi-camera observations , proprioception , and a language instruction to an action chunk . This section describes the fixed architecture and training procedure (Figure~ fig:architecture ); Section~ sec:design-analysis examines the choices within it. Architecture sec:architecture Visual representations. The pretrained V-JEPA~2.1 ViT-L encoder~ vjepa21 processes each camera independently, producing observation features from the most recent frames, and future targets representing the 32 frames ahead. We normalize and spatially reduce these feature grids before projecting them into the World DiT's embedding space. They are the model's only visual input and prediction target, so the model gets no separate RGB pathway. Future predictions are matched to targets directly in V-JEPA space and require no pixel reconstruction. Language and proprioception. A frozen FLAN-T5-large encoder~ flan_t5 embeds the instruction , and learned projections map proprioception to additional tokens; together they form the conditioning sequence , which both DiTs read through cross-attention. World--action architecture. The model is made of two diffusion transformers (DiTs)~ dit : a World DiT over observation and future-feature tokens and an Action DiT over the action chunk. Both are initialized from scratch with separate attention projections and feed-forward layers, so pretrained knowledge enters only through the visual and language encoders. Rotary visual positional encodings~ rope preserve spatial and temporal information. The two DiTs interact at every layer, where action queries read the World DiT's observation keys and values alongside its own. The attention mask keeps future information out of the action pathway: observation tokens attend only to observations, future tokens to observations and futures, and action tokens to observations and actions. title: RoboARCade: Benchmarking Agentic Robot Control
summary: Improvements in multi-modal capabilities have enabled agents to act directly as robot policies, a setting we refer to as agentic robot control (ARC). We introduce RoboARCade, a benchmark of long-horizon manipulation tasks across three embodiments designed to test in-context adaptation, memory, and reasoning for precise control. The tasks build on existing open-source benchmarks, which we make harder by widening the range of initial conditions. RoboARCade is easy to use and extend: all tasks run on a single simulation backend, MuJoCo, each task is a self-contained data pack, and agents connect through interchangeable interfaces, so new tasks, agents, and interfaces can be added independently. The benchmark separates leading agents: GPT-6 Astra achieves 49.8% compared with 43.6% for Claude Fable 5.1, leaving substantial room for improvement. Comparing two interfaces, we find that a richer visual interface adds only 1.5 to 6.8 points at 1.7 to 2.3 times the cost. Failures stem mostly from choosing a poor manipulation strategy or executing a good one imprecisely, rarely from misunderstanding the scene, and agents incorrectly claim success on 24% to 39% of attempted subtasks. Agents can also improve without human input: one successful demonstration in context raises Astra's score from 53.5% to 73.0% on a five-task subset, and a prompt the agent writes and revises itself reaches 72.0%. Code, videos and full traces are available at roboarcade.org.

Introduction Recently, foundation models (FM) have begun controlling robots through several approaches: training Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models~ brohan2023rt2,kim2024openvla,black2024pi0 , integrating models into hierarchical control systems~ ichter2023saycan,huang2023innermonologue,belkhale2024rth,shi2025hirobot,hu2026hivla , and generating executable perception and control code, as in Code-as-Policies (CaP)~ liang2023code , more recently inside coding-agent harnesses that write programs~ fu2026capx or computation graphs~ chen2026gapgraphaspolicymultiagentselflearning . Frontier multimodal FMs now allow a fourth approach: the agent observes the world directly through pixels and controls robots itself with no learned policy or program in between. We refer to this setting as agentic robot control (ARC). Evaluations of ARC disagree about how well it works. Commanding end-effector motions directly, the models in berman2026clauderobotics completed at most 5.5 of LIBERO tasks, or 32 of a ten-task subset with a cursor tool. Through a 3D visual interface, VIA~ hu2026via reached 96.7 on three LIBERO-Goal tasks. On the 42 tasks of RoboDojo, GPT-6 Astra reached 22.5 zhang2026astrarobodojo . Each study used its own tasks, models, and interface, so these results cannot be compared with one another. RoboARCade provides a common benchmark built for ARC that is not saturated: the VIA interface that nearly saturates LIBERO-Goal reaches 43.6 subtask success here. brings together custom and preexisting tasks and assets in a unified codebase, spanning single-arm and bimanual manipulation, assembly, physical puzzles, and high-precision biolab-inspired procedures. Fig.~ fig:task-lineup shows a subset of the task suite. For tasks adapted from prior work, we increase difficulty by broadening the range of initial conditions and improve visual fidelity through Blender rendering. All tasks run on a single simulation backend, MuJoCo, and each is a self-contained data pack, so new tasks, agents, and interfaces can be added independently. Using this suite, we evaluate two families of frontier agents, Codex and Claude Code, and compare their performance and efficiency across two control interfaces. The first, multi-view RGBD, provides color and depth images from multiple cameras and sends end-effector commands directly to the controller. The second, from Visual Interface Agent (VIA)~ hu2026via , provides an interactive 3D virtual workspace in which agents can adjust a virtual target gripper using visual feedback before commanding the robot to move. The results reveal substantial differences across agents and interfaces: with VIA, GPT-5.6 Sol achieves a success rate of 14.0 , compared with 43.6 for Claude Fable 5.1 and 49.8 for GPT-6 Astra. For Fable, VIA improves success over multi-view RGBD by 6.8 percentage points but increases the average cost per trial by 67 . Even the strongest combination, Astra with VIA, succeeds on fewer than half of trials, leaving substantial room for improvement in both agents and control interfaces. Scene understanding is rarely the obstacle: only 2 to 6 of attempted subtasks end there. Failures come instead from choosing a poor manipulation strategy or executing a good one imprecisely. Retries help with both: Astra’s subtask success rises from 34 on the first try to 50 after five or more. Agents also misjudge their own progress, incorrectly claiming success on 24 (Astra) to 39 (Claude Opus 5) of attempted subtasks. We further evaluate in-context learning from successful rollouts and autonomous text-only prompt optimization on a subset of five tasks. In prompt optimization, agents revise their instructions using rollout feedback. GPT-6 Astra's mean rubric score increases from 53.5 to 73.0 with in-context learning and 72.0 after two rounds of prompt optimization. Despite these gains, precision errors and incorrect claims of success persist. Related Works Foundation Models for Robot Control. There are many ways to leverage the general knowledge of foundation models for robot control. Here, we briefly review the most related ones that turn an LLM or multimodal VLM into robot control policies to help position our benchmark and findings against existing ones. Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models are built by fine-tuning large FMs on large amounts of robot action data to control robots end-to-end~ brohan2023rt2,kim2024openvla,black2024pi0 . Early hierarchical approaches such as SayCan~ ichter2023saycan and Inner Monologue~ huang2023innermonologue use LLMs to select and sequence low-level robot skills. RT-H~ belkhale2024rth predicts language descriptions of low-level motions as an intermediate step between task instructions and robot actions. More recent approaches~ shi2025hirobot,hu2026hivla add a high-level VLM for reasoning and long-term planning that issues language commands to steer a VLA, mimicking the System 1 and System 2 distinction in human cognition~ evans2013dual . Code-as-Policies (CaP)~ liang2023code,fu2026capx,chen2026gapgraphaspolicymultiagentselflearning uses FMs to write code given a task and a rough scene description. In CaP-style approaches, the robot policy is the generated program, and this policy relies on perception primitives like segment and action primitives like grasp powered by neural networks or scripted functions. In CaP-X, the coding FM itself is not involved during execution of each generated program. It generates and revises programs between execution turns using feedback from the updated scene. As FMs improve at multimodal understanding and agents become better at using execution feedback to guide subsequent actions, recent works explore, under different names, a setting where a model or agent acts as the policy itself to control robots directly~ tsui2026demofree,berman2026clauderobotics,hu2026via,zhang2026astrarobodojo . We call this setting agentic robot control (ARC). In its naive form, the agent observes the world directly through pixels and commands the robot by outputting controller targets, such as end-effector poses and the gripper open-close state for an operational-space controller. Visual Interface Agent (VIA)~ hu2026via defines an interactable visual interface that allows agents to probe additional information from the scene by mouse-like operations and visually stage different target poses by operating a virtual target gripper inside a 3D point cloud reconstructed from RGB-D cameras, with raw camera feeds shown alongside. The interface is a virtual workspace analogous to a GUI on a computer. We operate in the ARC setting as it is the most straightforward way to evaluate agents' ability to control robots without relying on extra perception or action primitives. Simulated Robotic Benchmarks. Over the years, many simulated robotic benchmarks have been proposed to measure progress in robotics. These include established suites such as Meta-World~ yu2020metaworld and RLBench~ james2020rlbench , more recent suites such as LIBERO~ liu2023libero and RoboCasa365~ nasiriany2026robocasa365 , and specialized benchmarks such as RoboTwin~2.0~ chen2025robotwin2 for bimanual manipulation and SoftGym~ lin2021softgym for deformable object manipulation. ALFRED~ shridhar2020alfred evaluates household instruction following. EmbodiedBench~ yang2025embodiedbench evaluates multimodal language model agents across household, navigation, and manipulation tasks, but its manipulation tasks supply the 3D position of every object as text and cap each episode at 15 steps, whereas requires the agent to localize targets from its own observations over long horizons. CaP-X~ fu2026capx evaluates FMs using CaP and scaffolds built around vanilla CaP. In , we focus on the simpler ARC setting. We evaluate agents both on their ability to complete robot control tasks and on their ability to perform in-context learning and prompt optimization to improve the task success rate. Benchmarks for FMs and Agents. Benchmarks also play an important role in the development and evaluation of FMs and agents. Visual QA benchmarks such as BLINK~ fu2024blink evaluate FMs' visual perception in images. Video benchmarks evaluate spatial understanding in VSI-Bench~ yang2025vsibench , temporal understanding in MVBench~ li2024mvbench and TempCompass~ liu2024tempcompass , and understanding of longer video sequences in EgoSchema~ mangalam2023egoschema and Video-MME~ fu2025videomme . For 3D scene understanding, ScanQA~ azuma2022scanqa evaluates object-grounded question answering in indoor scans, while SQA3D~ ma2023sqa3d evaluates reasoning about a scene from an agent's specified position and orientation. Computer-use benchmarks evaluate agents' ability to perform closed-loop control through graphical user interfaces (GUIs), including desktop applications in OSWorld~ xie2024osworld , websites in WebArena~ zhou2024webarena and VisualWebArena~ koh2024visualwebarena , and mobile applications in AndroidWorld~ rawles2025androidworld . is a valuable addition to existing agentic benchmarks as its ARC tasks evaluate agents on the combinations of the aforementioned abilities including 2D and 3D visual understanding, active perception, long-term planning with visual feedback, and closed-loop control of robots. In-Context Learning and Prompt Optimization. Agents' abilities to follow instructions open up new ways for them to improve without gradient-based training. In-context learning (ICL) and reflection-based methods allow agents to condition on prior experiences or examples included in their input to improve performance~ brown2020fewshot,shinn2023reflexion,zhang2025ace . Prompt optimization methods improve the instructions and examples supplied to FMs through techniques such as example bootstrapping, textual feedback, and evolutionary search~ khattab2024dspy,yuksekgonul2025textgrad,agrawal2026gepa . In robotics, prior work has explored using FMs to generate reward functions~ ma2024eureka or simulation tasks~ wang2024gensim for policy learning. In , we evaluate how ICL and prompt optimization by the agent itself improve downstream robot control in the ARC setting without fine-tuning model weights. title: Fault-Geometry-Aware Control Allocation for Emergency Quadrotor Landing under Single-Motor Loss of Effectiveness
summary: Partial single-motor loss of effectiveness (LoE) changes the remaining control-authority geometry of a quadrotor and can change which control allocator performs best during emergency landing[cite: 11]. We compare three allocators in Crazyflie software-in-the-loop simulation: bounded weighted least squares (reported as PINV), a finite-candidate residual allocator (QP-lite), and the same residual allocator with scoring parameters tuned offline by the Cross-Entropy Method (CEM)[cite: 11]. For this study, fault geometry is represented by the known failed-motor index[cite: 11]. At $η=0.496$ remaining effectiveness, matched development trials select CEM for M1, M3, and M4 and PINV for M2; the M3 selection is a one-trial margin (29/30 versus 28/30)[cite: 11]. After freezing this routing map, the policy achieves 117/120 safe first-contact touchdowns on fresh seeds and 115/120 in a separate randomized-order integrated-supervisor evaluation[cite: 11]. For the critical M2/PINV branch, Firth regression gives a nominal $η_{50}\approx0.4956$ with a within-model 95% bootstrap interval of approximately [0.4955, 0.4956][cite: 11]. One-factor-at-a-time $\pm10\%$ plant perturbations shift $η_{50}$ by up to 0.05495 for thrust coefficient and 0.04974 for mass; the most frequent violated first-contact criterion also changes from vertical speed in many conditions to angular rate for mass -10% and thrust-coefficient +10%[cite: 11]. At fixed $η=0.496$, PINV has a higher M2 safe count than frozen CEM in 9/11 tested plant states and ties in 2/11; the two ties are both 0/30[cite: 11]. The experiments therefore distinguish motor-conditioned allocator selection from sensitivity to plant-model mismatch[cite: 11].

The experiments therefore distinguish motor-conditioned allocator selection from sensitivity to plant-model mismatch. fault-tolerant control, quadrotor, control allocation, Crazyflie, actuator loss of effectiveness, emergency landing Introduction sec:introduction Quadrotors have little actuator redundancy: degradation of one motor changes the set of control effects available to the vehicle and can compromise landing safety. Rotor faults have therefore motivated fault-tolerant control (FTC), reduced-attitude recovery, control reconfiguration, and constrained control allocation saied2024review,mueller2014loss,lu2015active,merheb2017emergency,nan2022nmpc . Control allocation is attractive because it separates nominal motion control from the redistribution of actuator commands under saturation or failure johansen2013survey,bodson2002allocation,harkegard2002active . This work asks a narrower question than general fault recovery: under the same partial single-motor LoE severity, does the best emergency allocator depend on which motor fails? We compare bounded WLS/PINV, finite-candidate QP-lite residual allocation, and an offline CEM-tuned QP-lite variant in CrazySim llanes2024crazysim . In the implemented supervisor, ``fault geometry'' is represented only by the known failed-motor index; no online geometry estimator or fault detector is evaluated. A second question is whether a controller-selection conclusion remains meaningful when the simulated plant is perturbed. We therefore separate three stages: development-set allocator comparison, frozen-policy validation on new seeds, and an M2-focused plant-sensitivity study. The contributions are: (1) matched evidence that allocator ranking depends on failed-motor location, with a close M3 comparison explicitly retained; (2) frozen motor-conditioned routing evaluated on fresh seeds and in an integrated randomized-order supervisor; and (3) nominal-boundary, OFAT, failure-criterion, and paired-routing analyses that quantify how M2/PINV behavior changes under the tested plant perturbations. Related Work sec:related Fault-Tolerant Quadrotor Control Complete rotor loss has been studied through reduced-attitude or free-yaw recovery mueller2014loss,ke2023uniform , active fault detection/reconfiguration lu2015active , emergency control allocation merheb2017emergency , upset recovery sun2020upset , and nonlinear MPC nan2022nmpc . Partial actuator faults and model uncertainty have also motivated adaptive, sliding-mode, observer-based, and allocation-based FTC baldini2020actuator,zhu2019backstepping,wang2023adaptive . These studies establish that multirotors can retain useful control authority after actuator faults. Our experiments instead hold the fault class fixed and compare multiple allocators under matched failed-motor locations before freezing a location-conditioned routing rule. Control Allocation and Simulation Control-allocation literature includes pseudoinverse methods, constrained weighted least squares, active-set methods, and secondary-objective formulations johansen2013survey,bodson2002allocation,harkegard2002active,harkegard2005redundancy . Experimental and constrained-allocation studies address actuator saturation and bounds kirchengast2018allocation , while multirotor-specific formulations explicitly incorporate rotor constraints santos2022allocation . Gazebo koenig2004gazebo , RotorS furrer2016rotors , AirSim shah2018airsim , and CrazySim llanes2024crazysim provide simulation environments with different levels of vehicle and firmware integration. We use CrazySim because the final experiments execute Crazyflie firmware against Gazebo physics, allowing the same fault injection and bounded allocator implementation to be exercised in SITL. Firth bias-reduced logistic regression is used for boundary data with near-separation firth1993bias,heinze2002separation ; CEM is used only as an offline score-parameter tuner rubinstein2004cem . title: MOMASPLAT: Dynamic Novel-View Demonstration Augmentation for Mobile Manipulation
summary: Visuomotor policies trained through imitation learning are highly sensitive to changes in camera viewpoint. This is particularly problematic for mobile manipulation (MoMa), where robots rarely execute manipulation from the exact same base pose used during demonstration collection due to navigation uncertainty, localization drift, and environmental constraints. Recent approaches use novel-view synthesis (NVS) to augment demonstrations with unseen viewpoints, but they assume static scenes and therefore fail to re-render the manipulated object during the post-contact interaction phase, leaving the most critical parts of the demonstration unaugmented. We present MOMASPLAT, a novel-view demonstration augmentation framework for mobile manipulation that synthesizes full manipulation trajectories from unseen robot base poses, including dynamic object interactions. Our key insight is that standard MoMa data collection naturally provides the multiview observations needed to reconstruct both the static scene and the manipulated object in 3D. MOMASPLAT combines 3D Gaussian Splatting, feed-forward 3D foundation models, and kinematics-based action retargeting to separately reconstruct the scene and manipulated object, render them from novel viewpoints, and generate geometrically consistent synthetic demonstrations paired with transformed actions. We evaluate MOMASPLAT on five real-world mobile manipulation tasks involving both rigid and articulated objects across three scenes, and validate the fidelity of its synthesized demonstrations against ground truth in simulation. MOMASPLAT substantially improves robustness to unseen base poses, more than doubling the average success rate of the strongest baseline and maintaining non-trivial success at large base displacements where all baselines fail, while reducing the need for largescale real-world data collection.
