More information at: INTRODUCTION s:intro Imitation learning has emerged as a powerful paradigm for training visuomotor policies that perform complex manipulation tasks directly from image observations~ chi2023diffusionpolicy, zhao2023learning . However, these policies are notoriously sensitive to changes in camera viewpoint~ yang2025mobi, heo2026anycamvla, fei2025libero . Even small deviations in camera pose can significantly degrade performance, since the policy learns a narrow visual distribution tied to the demonstrations used during training. This sensitivity is particularly problematic for mobile manipulation (MoMa). Unlike tabletop manipulation setups, where demonstrations are often collected from a fixed robot camera pose, mobile manipulators rarely execute tasks from the exact same location at deployment time. Navigation uncertainty, localization drift, obstacle avoidance, and imperfect planning routinely place the robot at different base poses relative to the workspace. As a result, the robot observes the manipulation scene from viewpoints that may differ substantially from those seen during demonstration collection. Robust deployment therefore requires visuomotor policies that generalize across a distribution of robot base poses rather than a single viewpoint. A straightforward solution would be to collect demonstrations from many different robot locations. However, large-scale real-world teleoperation is expensive and difficult to scale~ fu2024mobile, zhao2023learning, mandlekar2023mimicgen . Recent work has therefore explored synthesizing additional demonstrations through novel-view synthesis (NVS), generating virtual observations from unseen viewpoints using real-world captures~ pan2025one, yang2025novel, zhou2023nerf . While promising, existing approaches assume a static scene and therefore fail during the most important part of manipulation: object interaction. Since the manipulated object moves throughout the demonstration, prior NVS methods cannot consistently re-render the object from novel viewpoints during the post-contact interaction phase, restricting augmentation primarily to pre-contact motions or introducing geometrically inconsistent generations. In this work, we present , a demonstration augmentation framework for mobile manipulation that synthesizes complete manipulation trajectories from unseen robot base poses, including dynamic object interactions (Fig. fig:teaser ). Our key insight is that standard mobile-manipulation data collection naturally provides the multi-view observations needed to reconstruct both the static scene and the manipulated object in 3D. During navigation, the robot observes the scene from diverse viewpoints that enable scene reconstruction, while the manipulation demonstrations themselves provide object-centric observations that enable reconstructing the manipulated object and its motion. Building on this observation, separately reconstructs the static scene and manipulated objects using 3D Gaussian Splatting~ kerbl20233d and feed-forward 3D foundation models~ wang2025vggt . Given a novel robot base pose, re-renders the scene, manipulated object, and robot from the new viewpoint and retargets the original actions through kinematics-based transformations to generate geometrically consistent synthetic demonstrations. We evaluate on five real-world mobile manipulation tasks involving both rigid and articulated objects across three scenes, and validate the fidelity of its synthesized demonstrations against ground truth in simulation. Our experiments show that substantially improves robustness to unseen deployment-time base poses, outperforming prior augmentation approaches across unseen base poses ( rollouts per pose) per task as the robot moves farther away from the source demonstration locations. Our contributions are threefold: A novel-view demonstration augmentation framework for mobile manipulation that synthesizes complete trajectories, including dynamic object interactions. A geometry-consistent generation pipeline that separately reconstructs scenes and manipulated objects and retargets actions to unseen base poses. Substantial improvements in robustness to deployment-time viewpoint variation across multiple real-world mobile manipulation tasks. Related Work sec:related Our method proposes a solution to train imitation learning visuomotor policies for mobile manipulators via data augmentation. Here, we review the most relevant related work in those areas. Demonstration Synthesis in Simulation. A prominent line of work synthesizes new demonstrations by replaying source actions in randomized simulated scenes. The X-Gen family~ mandlekar2023mimicgen, jiang2025dexmimicgen, garrett2024skillmimicgen, li2025momagen, lin2025constraint procedurally generates data by transforming and sequencing object-centric trajectory segments, with extensions such as MoMaGen~ li2025momagen addressing mobile-manipulation constraints like base reachability and visibility. However, because the generated plans are purely kinematic, they typically rely on open-loop on-robot rollouts to verify feasibility and capture visual observations, at a cost that rivals manual data collection~ xue2502demogen, pan2025one . A parallel line of work uses simulators to generate data from multiple viewpoints~ sadeghi2018sim2real, hirose2022exaug, seo2023multi , but requires modeling the full environment and task dynamics in simulation, suffering from the visual and physical sim-to-real gap. Our work avoids on-robot rollouts and full-scene simulation by reconstructing the real scene and manipulated object via novel-view synthesis, using simulation only to render the known robot embodiment. Demonstration Augmentation from Real-World Captures. Beyond 2D image augmentation~ laskin2020reinforcement, yarats2021image, hansen2020self , recent methods synthesize observations from real-world captures. Neural simulators~ jang2025dreamgen, bruce2024genie, agarwal2025cosmos use generative video models but can suffer from hallucinations and geometric inconsistencies. Alternatively, novel-view synthesis (NVS) enables viewpoint augmentation~ yang2025novel, zhou2023nerf, xue2502demogen, tian2024view, tagliabue2023tube, chen2024rovi, wang2026efficient, zhang2024diffusion . VISTA~ tian2024view uses ZeroNVS~ sargent2024zeronvs , while Yang et al.~ yang2025novel employ 3D Gaussian Splatting~ kerbl20233d ; however, both focus on third-person tabletop settings requiring multi-camera pre-scans. Closer to our setting, One-Thousand Trajectories~ pan2025one supports moving eye-in-hand cameras, while EgoDemoGen~ xu2025egodemogen generates paired egocentric observations and actions using a generative model. However, these methods do not explicitly reconstruct dynamic objects and restrict augmentation to pre-contact motion. In contrast, jointly models the static scene and manipulated objects, enabling kinematically consistent augmentation across both pre-contact and post-contact interaction phases for mobile robots with egocentric cameras. Mobile Manipulation. Mobile manipulation remains a key challenge in robot learning~ bahety2025safemimic, wu2023tidybot, liu2024okrobot, jiang2025wbvima, yenamandra2024homerobot , particularly in selecting robot base poses. title: SLA: Scaling Spatial-Language-Action Model via Continual Pre-training
summary: Reliable robotic manipulation requires both semantic understanding and precise control in three-dimensional space. However, vision-language-action (VLA) foundations largely inherit visual representations from 2D vision-language pre-training, while spatial supervision is often introduced only during task-specific adaptation. Developing spatial understanding as a transferable foundation-model capability therefore calls for learning from broader robot experience. We present SLA, a Spatial-Language-Action Model that scales implicit spatial alignment to continual pre-training and maintains it during downstream post-training. Initialized from a pretrained pi05 policy, SLA jointly optimizes action prediction and alignment between intermediate visual embeddings and spatial representations from a frozen 3D perception model. We curate and unify heterogeneous robot datasets to support spatial learning across diverse embodiments, tasks, and scenes. To accommodate this diversity, we introduce feature-dependent gates that adaptively aggregate visual embeddings from multiple VLA layers for spatial supervision. The teacher further exploits partially available depth and camera calibration alongside RGB observations, enabling effective use of heterogeneous geometric annotations. Probabilistic state dropout encourages reliance on visual cues and mitigates overfitting to demonstration trajectories. All auxiliary components are used only during training, allowing direct reuse of pretrained VLA weights and preserving the original inference architecture.
full_text: 3 Introduction The development of robotic manipulation hinges on integrating semantic reasoning with accurate physical control in the 3D real world. Recently, vision-language-action (VLA) models~ pi0,pi05,qwenrobotmanip,xiaomi_robotics1,g05,univla,song2026reconvla , capable of instruction following and robotic action execution, have attracted significant attention. By combining the pretrained vision-language model (VLM) with action experts learning on diverse robot demonstrations, these models offer a promising foundation for general-purpose manipulation. However, successful manipulation requires not only recognizing objects and understanding instructions but also executing precise actions in the 3D physical world. Typical 2D VLA foundation models inherit knowledge from VLMs pretrained on 2D image--text pairs and learn robot control without explicitly incorporating 3D physical knowledge during pre-training. This limits their reliability in scenes that demand fine-grained spatial reasoning. A direct approach to improving spatial understanding is to introduce 3D modalities during post-training on top of a pretrained 2D VLA foundation model. Several approaches~ pointvla,geovla,bridgevla use depth maps or point clouds obtained from depth cameras or other 3D sensors, encode their geometric information, and feed it into the VLM backbone or action head. However, some limitations make it difficult to develop a universal and scalable 3D strategy for this paradigm: (1) Reliable 3D sensor data is hard to acquire, as measured depth maps and point clouds can be noisy or incomplete. (2) Robotic sensors vary in types, positions, and calibration status, which introduces substantial heterogeneity into the data. (3) Portions of existing large-scale robot datasets~ oxe,robocoin,molmoact,bridgev2,fractal do not include depth information, which limits the potential of scaling. To address these questions, Spatial Forcing~ li2025spatial has propose a implicit 3D representation alignment strategy to enbow 2D VLA with spatial intelligence without explicit demand of depth information. However, Spatial Forcing still concentrate on post-training, leaving spatial competence as a task-specific add-on and limiting the development of scalable 3D VLA foundation models with transferable spatial understanding. Recently, continual pre-training has been widely adopted as a means of developing specific capabilities at scale while preserving the knowledge acquired during foundation model pre-training~ groundingpi,vpp2 . Motivated by this approach, we propose to build on the strong 2D foundation model and develop spatial understanding through continual pre-training, laying the foundation for subsequent adaptation. We therefore propose , a robotic foundation model with generalized spatial understanding capabilities developed through implicit representation alignment during both continual pre-training and post-training. Intuitively, action generation is conditioned on visual and linguistic representations, making the spatial content of visual tokens directly relevant to action. Higher-quality visual tokens that contain richer spatial information can facilitate generating more precise manipulation actions. Inspired by this, we align the intermediate visual embeddings of the VLA with external spatial representations extracted from a frozen 3D perception foundation model. This spatial alignment objective complements the standard action-learning objective, encouraging the policy to internalize geometric information in the representations used for action prediction. Crucially, this supervision requires no changes to the pretrained VLA architecture or the action-generation head. We can therefore initialize the policy directly from the pretrained foundation~ pi05 and continue training from its learned robotic knowledges. This architectural compatibility allows spatial supervision to shape the foundation model while retaining access to the general knowledge encoded in its pretrained weights. Technically, to support continual pre-training across heterogeneous robot data, we combines a unified training corpus. We curate multiple large-scale public datasets covering diverse embodiments, tasks, scenes, and visual appearances, and unify their state and action annotations through consistent end-effector representations and coordinate conventions. This processing provides a common basis for learning how different robots act in space. The resulting visual diversity also makes a single manually chosen alignment layer restrictive: a certain intermediate visual layer of VLA models suited to one domain data may not be equally suitable for another. We therefore develop adaptive layer selection mechanism, using feature-dependent gates to aggregate visual embeddings from multiple VLA layers for spatial supervision. In addition, we adopt OmniVGGT~ omnivggt as the external 3D perception foundation to exploit partially available camera calibrations and depth annotations alongside RGB images. We further introduce probabilistic state dropout during training to mitigate overfitting to demonstration trajectories and encourage the policy to make better use of visual cues, thereby improving generalization. After continual pre-training, we retain spatial alignment during post-training to adapt the resulting foundation model to specific down-streaming tasks. The teacher, alignment projector, and layer-selection gates are used only during training. At deployment, the policy retains its original inference architecture without requiring the external perception model, alignment projector, or layer-selection gates. Extensive evaluations across three public simulation benchmarks, one public real-world benchmark, and eight real-world deployment conditions are conducted to demonstrate the effectiveness of our . On LIBERO-Plus~ fei2025libero , it achieves an overall success rate of 87.4 under diverse observation, language, and scene perturbations, outperforming the compared baselines. On RoboTwin 2.0~ chen2025robotwin , training on clean demonstrations yields a 72.3 success rate in the Clean2Random setting and a 79.2 average across Clean2Clean and Clean2Random, demonstrating generalization beyond the training conditions. On RoboCasa-Panda~ robocasa , achieves 68.4 success with only 50 downstream demonstrations per task, exceeding compared policies trained with 300--3,000 demonstrations per task. On RoboDojo-Real~ robodojo-leaderboard , a single policy adapted across three embodiments achieves 33.9 overall success, compared with 12.8 for , supporting its applicability to real robot manipulation. Our eight deployment conditions further examine bimanual coordination, spatial and dynamic generalization, few-shot cross-embodiment adaptation, and instruction following. achieves the highest success rate among the compared methods in every condition, averaging 83.8 and improving over by 24.0 percentage points. Controlled data-scaling experiments further show that applying spatial alignment in both training stages outperforms either single-stage alternative at every tested data proportion. Together, these results support developing spatial understanding during continual pre-training and stengthen it during downstream adaptation. Our contributions are summarized as follows: We introduce , a robotic foundation model that implicitly enforces the integration of visual embeddings in VLAs with external spatial representations. We extend to continual pre-training on a carefully curated and unified corpus of public robot datasets, developing a spatially informed foundation model. We apply training principle during downstream post-training and demonstrate strong benchmark performance, together with bimanual coordination, spatial and dynamic generalization, few-shot cross-embodiment adaptation, and instruction following. Related Work sec:relatedwork VLA Foundation Models VLA foundation models learn generalist manipulation policies from large, diverse datasets and adapt them to downstream tasks. Cross-embodiment datasets~ oxe,bridgev2,fractal,robomind,rh20t,abc130k,galaxeaopenworld have accelerated this development. OpenVLA~ openvla , ~ pi0 , RDT-1B~ liu2024rdt , and GR00T N1~ bjorck2025gr00t learn language-conditioned action prediction from robot demonstrations, while GR-2~ gr2 combines large-scale video pre-training with policy learning on robot trajectories. To improve task understanding, RT-H~ Rt-h and ~ pi05 adopt language-conditioned task hierarchies, whereas MolmoAct~ molmoact and MolmoAct2~ molmoact2 incorporate action reasoning into robot control. RT-2~ Rt-2 , , and Xiaomi-Robotics-0~ xiaomi_robotics0 also co-train on robot and vision-language data to support semantic generalization and instruction following. The scarcity of teleoperated robot data has further motivated alternative sources of supervision. HumanScale~ humanscale investigates pre-training on egocentric human videos followed by adaptation with robot data. Separately, the Universal Manipulation Interface (UMI)~ umi enables portable demonstration collection using handheld grippers without requiring robots at collection sites. RDT2~ rdt2 and Xiaomi-Robotics-1~ xiaomi_robotics1 exploit UMI data to expand training scale and coverage of environments and tasks. These advances support generalist action learning, but data scaling alone does not specify how geometric representations should be supervised during pre-training. Our complementary goal is to develop 3D spatial understanding in an existing VLA foundation model through spatially supervised continual pre-training. 3D VLA Models Existing 3D VLA methods introduce geometry through explicit inputs, feature fusion, or representation supervision. PointVLA~ pointvla and GeoVLA~ geovla integrate point cloud features into action prediction. BridgeVLA~ bridgevla projects 3D observations into multi-view images; and FALCON~ zhang2025falcon extracts geometric tokens from spatial foundation models for fusion within the action head. These approaches still require additional geometric input extraction at deployment. Another works use training-time supervision to encode spatial structure in internal policy representations. ROCKET~ rocket explores multilayer spatial alignment, VEGA~ vega supervises visual encoder outputs, and Mind-VLA~ mindvla introduces instruction-aware alignment of target-object representations. Such approaches emphasize adding 3D capabilities during post-training on top of generic 2D VLA pre-training~ pi05,univla,openvla-oft , leaving spatial understanding as a supplementary capability rather than establishing a scalable 3D-aware foundation. Recent studies incorporate geometry into pre-training through egocentric spatial embeddings~ spatialvla , egocentric 3D annotations~ vipa-vla , and object pose estimation~ posevla . However, these 3D-aware pre-training efforts remain relatively limited in scale compared with large-scale 2D VLA pre-training. In contrast, we build on pretrained 2D VLA through continual pre-training to develop generalizable 3D-aware foundation models. Continual Pre-training Continual pre-training extends the domain capabilities of existing foundation models through further large-scale pre-training, providing a basis for downstream adaptation. Early studies~ BioBERT, ClinicalBERT, FinBERT, LEGAL-BERT, Dont-Stop-Pretraining focus on adapting to domain-specific data distributions. Llemma~ llemma strengthens mathematical reasoning through continual pre-training on mathematical text and code. AgentFounder~ agentfounder uses diverse reasoning and action data to establish a foundation for agent capabilities before post-training. Recent efforts extend this paradigm to robotics: ET-VLA~ et-vla uses synthetic data for continual pre-training to transfer existing VLAs to new embodiments, whereas AXIS~ axis investigates how policy performance scales with data. title: PVDepth: Panoramic Video Depth Estimation via Geometry-Aware Spatiotemporal Adaptation
summary: Panoramic video depth estimation is pivotal for applications such as Virtual Reality and World Models. However, advancements in this field are impeded by two primary obstacles: the scarcity of large-scale training data and the unique spatiotemporal challenges of Equirectangular Projection (ERP), which hinder the direct transfer of perspective models. In this paper, we first present PanoCARLA, a large-scale synthetic RGB-D panoramic video dataset, featuring natural motion trajectories and drone-like roaming perspectives. Building on this foundation, we propose PVDepth, an end-to-end framework adapted from perspective video depth models. To tackle ERP-specific geometric distortions and consequent non-linear temporal dynamics, we introduce two core mechanisms: (1) A Progressive Sphere-aware Noise Initialization strategy that anneals the noise distribution from planar to spherical, guiding the model to adapt to non-uniform information density; and (2) A Cube-rectified Temporal Modeling module that incorporates an auxiliary cubemap temporal branch to rectify non-linear temporal dynamics in the ERP domain. Extensive experiments demonstrate that PVDepth achieves superior performance, generating geometrically accurate and temporally consistent depth sequences. Code and data will be released at https:// github.com/ChuanxinSong/PVDepth.

title: RM-VLM: From Natural-Language Task Descriptions to Vision-Grounded Reward Machines
summary: Reward machines (RMs) have been proposed as a reward formulation in reinforcement learning (RL) to capture non-Markovian tasks where credit assignment depends on history. By representing reward functions as automata, RMs expose the task's temporal structure and allow such rewards to be handled within a Markovian framework. However, they assume a labelling function, a proposition-grounding oracle for observations, which must be manually engineered for each environment, limiting their wider applicability. In this work, we address this limitation by proposing RM-VLM, a novel approach in which a large language model (LLM) generates an RM from a natural-language task description, and a vision-language model (VLM) acts as the labelling function, grounding the RM's propositions over image-based observations during RM-guided policy learning. A VLM-based value function estimator is used to assess the agent's progress towards each RM transition and derive a dense reward signal. We evaluate RM-VLM on three domains covering non-Markovian grid-world navigation, robotic manipulation, and 3D object collection. Our experimental results show that RM-VLM consistently achieves higher task success rates than existing VLM-based reward methods across all tested domains.

RM-VLM addresses three challenges: the automated generation of RM automata from natural language task descriptions, with transitions labelled by atomic propositions, the grounding of proposition labels in images, and the induction of a reward mechanism that provides dense feedback and remains robust to imperfect grounding. Specifically, given a set of task descriptions, an LLM is prompted to generate the set of propositions shared across all tasks. Then, for each task an associated is generated over the alphabet . This is done by prompting the LLM to decompose each into a set of independent sub-task RMs, which are then combined together into a single ~ neary2020reward . title: T3R: Training-Free Two-Stage Token Refinement Towards Efficient and Robust VLA Models
summary: Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models enable end-to-end robot control, but inference is increasingly expensive. Each decision processes hundreds of visual tokens, often across multiple cameras, leading to substantial computation while allowing irrelevant background content to distract action prediction under distribution shift. We argue that these issues stem from two complementary forms of redundancy: many visual tokens are spatially irrelevant, while attention over the remaining tokens is often misallocated. Based on this observation, we propose T3R, a Training-Free Two-Stage Token Refinement framework. In the first stage, segmentation-guided token pruning removes irrelevant visual patches to reduce computation and eliminate distracting context. In the second stage, saliency-guided attention biasing reallocates attention toward action-critical visual regions and language instructions within the retained tokens. Together, pruning produces a cleaner candidate set, while attention biasing further emphasizes the most decision-relevant evidence, yielding a better accuracy-efficiency frontier than either stage alone. On LIBERO-Spatial, T3R removes 85% of scene-camera visual tokens while essentially matching the unpruned success rate, and improves success by up to 7 percentage points under out-of-distribution object-placement perturbations. The timing comparison attributes 7.8 ms per inference call to pruning and attention-bias application. As input resolution increases, LLM-forward profiling shows up to a 3.3x speedup over the unpruned baseline. Evaluations across LIBERO, SIMPLER, and RoboTwin with three VLA backbones show the strongest accuracy-efficiency benefits in multi-camera settings. These results demonstrate that training-free token refinement is a practical approach to efficient and robust VLA inference.

At every decision step, the model propagates a long visual sequence through a large language backbone. In a typical OpenVLA-style setup, a image produces visual patches~ siglip , and multi-camera inputs multiply this token load before any action token is predicted. Attending over such long sequences at every control step is expensive and increases latency, which is detrimental to real-time control and can further induce observation--action distribution shift through stale observations and delayed actuation~ sail . Many visual tokens are weakly coupled to the language instruction~ fastv,prumerge . These tokens can diffuse attention and distract action prediction, especially under viewpoint or object-placement shifts. Effective refinement must both remove irrelevant tokens and reinforce instruction-relevant evidence among those retained. Redundancy acts at two coupled stages: token-set construction and attention allocation. Pruning can discard critical cues, while attention steering retains the full token cost and noisy input. We therefore prune first and refine attention only over the retained sequence. Building on this view, we introduce , a training-free two-stage token refinement framework. Stage~1 performs segmentation-guided token pruning with position preservation, so compression happens before the VLA decoder and every transformer layer benefits from a shorter input. Stage~2 compensates for pruning-induced information loss by injecting task relevance into the retained sequence: saliency-guided attention biasing in intermediate layers steers action-token queries toward instruction-salient words and retained task-relevant regions. We evaluate on OpenVLA-OFT~ openvlaoft , CogACT~ cogact , and ~ pi05 across LIBERO~ libero , SIMPLER~ simpler , and RoboTwin~ robotwin . Across these systems, multi-camera settings show greater pruning headroom than the single-camera zero-shot setting. This trend suggests that overlapping visual evidence creates opportunities for token reduction. . RT-1/RT-2~ rt1,rt2 established large-scale vision-language pretraining for manipulation, while OpenVLA and OpenVLA-OFT~ openvla,openvlaoft improved openness and adaptation efficiency. title: Failure Prediction and Classification in Vision-Language-Action Models Via Calibrated Latent Probing
comment: Code, videos, and dataset available at https://vla-tug.github.io
summary: Vision-Language-Action models (VLAs) enable general-purpose embodied intelligence, but their performance is brittle under distribution shift, where unanticipated failures can damage equipment or endanger people. Deploying VLAs in real-world systems therefore requires a runtime monitor that is timely, calibrated, and informative while being efficient enough to run on the edge. Existing methods fail to fulfill these requirements. We present VLA-Tug, a lightweight probe over the latent layers of a VLA backbone that improves early failure detection and bounds the missed-detection and false-alarm rates, with minimal inference overhead. We show that supervising on the pre-failure segment of a trajectory increases early failure detection at matched false-positive rates by up to 30% over the strongest learned baseline. Under shift to unseen tasks, the bounds on missed-detection and false-alarm rates remain valid in up to 86% of runs, versus at most 21% for baselines. Unlike existing methods, VLA-Tug predicts the failure mode to enable corrective actions, raising top-3 accuracy on unseen tasks by up to 44% over a majority baseline. VLA-Tug enables real-time monitoring where the well-timed and informative probe supports lightweight steering that improves task success. We release a dataset of 3,180 annotated manipulation episodes to support future work on latent failure detection in VLAs at https://vla-tug.github.io.

By pairing a VLM backbone pre-trained on internet-scale data with an action expert fine-tuned on demonstration trajectories, they excel at complex dexterous tasks such as tightening screws or assembling cardboard boxes. Yet their performance is brittle and can degrade significantly under distribution shift, such as changes in lighting, novel textures, or rare object combinations wang_libero-x_2026, fei_libero-plus_2025 . A VLA can therefore fail unexpectedly, especially as task and environment novelty increases, and such failures can be costly, damaging materials and robots, or outright dangerous to humans. This brittleness has slowed the adoption of VLAs in factories, homes, and public spaces. Among multiple solutions, one solution that the robotics community is exploring is VLA steering. The idea of steering comes from research on LLMs, where activations are selectively modified to nudge a model towards a desired output turner_steering_2024 . Steering VLAs is particularly interesting because it can unlock behaviors that cannot be reached through prompting alone buurmeijer_observing_2026, swann_sparse_2026 . Various steering methods have recently been proposed li_towards_2026, liu_vls_2026, tan_rl2-vla_2026, swann_sparse_2026, cui_dreamsteer_2026, jeong_learning_2026, liVLAsAreConfined2025 , but they rarely use a calibrated probe to decide when to steer. Some steer continuously li_towards_2026, liu_vls_2026, cui_dreamsteer_2026 , some rely on human-specified offline triggers swann_sparse_2026, liVLAsAreConfined2025 , and others are gated by a one-sided calibrated trigger tan_rl2-vla_2026, jeong_learning_2026 . Overall, they lack an efficient and principled trigger that would make them deployable in real-world systems. Research on failure detection for VLAs is becoming increasingly mainstream gu_safe_2025, agia_unpacking_2024, ma_failurespot_2026, huang_actprobe_2026 . In a nutshell, these methods compute a failure score from signals available in the VLA, often its latent variables gu_safe_2025 or predicted actions agia_unpacking_2024, huang_actprobe_2026, ma_failurespot_2026 , that encode how likely the policy is to fail at the current task. A detection threshold is then calibrated to give probabilistic guarantees on the detector's performance gu_safe_2025 . However, these guarantees often cover only the false-positive rate (FPR), i.e.\ the rate of successes misclassified as failures, and not a target true-positive rate (TPR), i.e.\ the rate of correctly classified failures, which is arguably even more important in safety-critical settings where a single failure could harm a person or damage costly equipment. These methods are also seldom evaluated systematically against ground-truth failure times, which we argue is crucial to assess whether they can prevent failures before they happen and thus enable VLA steering. Finally, they cannot predict failure modes (grasping, pushing, opening), so steering cannot be targeted towards the root cause and would require human interventions. We argue that steering would be best supported by a probe that is (T.) ~timely, detecting failures before they occur; (I.) ~informative, outputting semantic information beyond a numerical score; (C.) ~calibrated, achieving the desired error rates; and (E.) ~efficient to train, calibrate, and deploy. We address this with Like a tugboat beside the vessel it guides, the probe is small next to the policy it monitors and acts only when needed. , a well-behaved probe designed to support VLA steering in the real world. We train on the latent layers of two VLAs intelligence__05_2025, nvidia_gr00t_2025 using 228 distinct tasks in two simulation environments and 8 real-world tasks, and evaluate it against ground-truth failure times. We show that supervision should focus on the pre-failure part of the trajectory to improve early failure detection, and that calibrating the detection threshold to guarantee both TPR and FPR simultaneously yields guarantees that hold far more often, including on unseen tasks. Building on these findings, we propose a real-time architecture that incorporates to autonomously support the detection and prevention of VLA failures. Our contributions are as follows: : A timely, informative, and efficient probe for early failure detection. On unseen tasks, our probe improves the area under the early-detection curve by up to over the strongest learned baseline. also predicts the failure mode, raising the top-3 accuracy on unseen tasks by up to over a majority baseline, at under \,ms per step. Guarantees on false alarms and missed detections. We certify FPR and targets jointly; both held in every certified run, compared to -- of runs for baselines. Under distribution shift to unseen tasks, the false-alarm target still held in -- of certified runs, compared to -- for baselines. A deployable failure-monitoring system. Through real-world experiments, we demonstrate that integrating the timely failure predictions and associated modes with steering strategies can lead to enhanced success rates. An annotated VLA failure dataset. We release a dataset of 289k policy-step VLA backbone embeddings from annotated episodes of diverse tasks. Related Work Existing methods can detect failures, but their alarms are not necessarily timely, informative, or sufficiently calibrated. Our method addresses these limitations through failure-aware representations, onset-based detection, and joint statistical guarantees. Existing works and their limitations. Existing VLA failure detectors leverage different signals to identify potential failures, including external assessments from world models or LLM judges~ liu_checkvla_2026,li_towards_2026 , action consistency across sampled or consecutive action chunks~ agia_unpacking_2024,huang_actprobe_2026 , distributional deviations in policy inputs, outputs, or embeddings~ xu_can_2025,gu_safe_2025 , and internal policy representations~ gu_safe_2025,rajaprakash_safecast_2026,ma_failurespot_2026,chen_aegis_2026,park_hide-and-seek_2026,francis-meretzki_temporal_2026 . These approaches have three key limitations. (1) Detection performance is commonly evaluated at fixed time points using metrics such as AUROC or balanced accuracy~ gu_safe_2025,huang_actprobe_2026 , without explicitly measuring whether alarms precede the actual failure onset. Moreover, supervision ranges from episode-level failure labels assigned to all timesteps~ gu_safe_2025 , to heuristic or human-refined timestep labels~ ma_failurespot_2026 , to failure-free training~ xu_can_2025 , without explicitly accounting for the timing of failures. (2) Most detectors produce scalar risk scores without identifying the underlying failure modes. While semantic supervision and representation interpretability have been explored for embodied policies~ xuVLMADEndtoEndAutonomous2024, swann_sparse_2026, buurmeijer_observing_2026 , they do not directly establish informative failure alarms. (3) Existing calibration methods typically control a single criterion. Conformal methods provide false-positive guarantees for sequential failure detection~ gu_safe_2025,rajaprakash_safecast_2026,park_hide-and-seek_2026 , calibrate anomaly or failure scores~ xu_can_2025,ma_failurespot_2026 , or provide guarantees for one-shot policy compliance and embodied decision making~ yang_repv_2025,chen_reconvla_2026,bhattKnowWhereYoure2025,yangUncertaintyGuidedEnhancementDriving2025 . However, these guarantees do not jointly account for false alarms and timely failure detection. addresses the limitations. We address these limitations by developing a failure detector that is timely, informative, and jointly calibrated. Following the internal-representation probing direction, we reuse the VLA's latent representations and align them with failure-mode semantics, enabling the detector to identify both potential failures and their types. To evaluate timeliness, we measure detection relative to annotated failure onsets and investigate supervision strategies that explicitly account for when failures occur. To provide statistical guarantees, we adopt Learn-then-Test~ angelopoulosLearnThenTest2022 to jointly calibrate multiple detection criteria, including the false-positive rate (FPR) and early true-positive rate ( ). Existing failure detectors primarily raise alarms without steering, while steering methods rely on predefined schedules or calibrated triggers. In contrast, to the best of our knowledge, is the first framework to combine joint FPR and early-TPR calibration, failure-onset-aware evaluation, and failure-mode prediction for calibrated failure-triggered steering. compares against the existing works. Next, we give a mathematical formulation of our problem and then introduce how addresses it. Definitions To facilitate comparisons across methods, we give general definitions for the concepts of failure score, detection threshold, detection time, failure time, and failure mode. Failure score. The score , defined at every timestep , encodes the probe's belief that the VLA is failing. It need not be a probability in the strict sense. Detection threshold. The threshold over separates failures from successes. Detection time. The time is the first time the score crosses the threshold. Failure time. The time , which we also call the failure onset, is when the policy makes an obvious mistake or its progress stalls to the point where an intervention, human or otherwise, is needed. Failure mode. The label is a high-level semantic category assigned to each failure, such as grasping failure, placement failure, or no progress. These definitions are general, and their exact form varies slightly across methods. title: XM4D: 4D Reconstruction through Certifiable Geometric Optimization
summary: Accurate 4D reconstruction remains challenging: jointly estimating camera motion, scene geometry, and non-rigid deformation entails highly nonconvex optimization, making global optimality difficult to guarantee. We present XM4D, a framework for accurate and efficient 4D reconstruction built upon certifiably globally optimal geometric optimization. By separating the estimation of camera motion from non-rigid deformation, we formulate both stages as structured quadratically constrained quadratic programs (QCQP) that admit semidefinite programming (SDP) relaxations and verifiable global optimality certificates. For camera motion estimation, we lift static point tracks into 3D using foundational depth prediction models and formulate a scaled bundle adjustment problem that jointly estimates camera poses, depth scales, and static landmarks. By analytically eliminating translations and landmarks, we reduce the problem to a QCQP over scaled rotations. For non-rigid reconstruction, we represent dynamic motion using an embedded deformation graph (EDG) and show that its tracking, rigidity, and temporal regularization objectives similarly reduce to a rotation-only QCQP. Both problems admit SDP relaxations that we solve efficiently with a GPU-accelerated Burer-Monteiro solver based on Riemannian optimization. The recovered geometry further initializes dynamic Gaussian splatting for photometric refinement. Extensive experiments across seven benchmarks demonstrate accurate camera motion estimation on both static and dynamic scenes, efficient optimization that scales to thousands of frames, and state-of-the-art novel-view rendering quality.

The skeleton in (c) is a subsampled embedded deformation graph (EDG). fig:teaser enhanced, sharp corners, frame hidden, colback=crimson!5!white, borderline west= 2pt 0pt crimson , boxrule=0pt, boxsep=0pt, left=10pt, right=10pt, top=5pt, bottom=5pt, before skip=8pt, after skip=10pt Introduction sec:intro 4D reconstruction aims to recover the time-varying 3D structure of a scene from visual observations. It supports applications including dynamic novel-view rendering~ li21cvpr-neuralsceneflow,lombardi19tog-neuralvolumes , deformable and articulated object reconstruction~ newcombe15cvpr-dynamicfusion,innmann16eccv-volumedeform,yang21cvpr-lasr , digital humans and digital twins~ peng21cvpr-neuralbody,weng22cvpr-humannerf,jiang25iccv-phystwin , and motion retargeting for humanoid control~ allshire25corl-retarget,he24corl-omnih2o,liu26arxiv-grasp . Despite its broad utility, reconstructing a dynamic scene from monocular images or videos remains highly challenging~ gao21iccv-dynamicsynthesis,gao22neurips-dycheck . Camera and object motion are entangled in the visual observations~ chen25iccv-backontrack , while dynamic geometry itself is weakly constrained and may undergo complex non-rigid deformation. Long sequences introduce further difficulties, including fragmented point tracks, noisy and scale-inconsistent monocular depth, and temporally incomplete observations of the dynamic scene~ lei25cvpr-mosca,wang25iccv-shapeofmotion . Recent 4D reconstruction methods commonly rely on coupled nonconvex optimization over camera poses, scene geometry, deformation, and appearance~ lei25cvpr-mosca,wang25iccv-shapeofmotion . Such formulations have achieved impressive results, but their strong coupling makes the optimization difficult: the objective is highly nonconvex and local optimization may therefore be sensitive to initialization and converge to undesired local minima. As illustrated in Fig.~ fig:edg-local-min , local optimization of the motion of an embedded deformation graph (EDG) can converge to an inferior solution whereas the certifiable solver presented in this work achieves an accurate reconstruction. Similar failures of local optimization in static reconstruction were demonstrated in XM~ han25rss-xm (Fig.~10). This raises a natural question: [crgstatement] Can we achieve accurate and efficient 4D reconstruction through globally certifiable geometric optimization? In this work, we present , a framework for accurate and efficient 4D reconstruction based on globally certifiable geometric optimization. Our approach separates camera motion estimation from non-rigid deformation, allowing both stages to be formulated as structured (nonconvex) quadratically constrained quadratic programs (QCQPs) and solved through (convex) semidefinite programming (SDP) relaxations. Fig.~ fig:view-graph (a) illustrates this decomposition as a view graph and Fig.~ fig:view-graph (b) instantiates it on a real scene: static and dynamic point tracks share the same cameras and predicted depth, but static tracks constrain time-invariant landmarks and camera poses, while dynamic tracks constrain the motion of an EDG. In the following, we overview the problem formulation and solution approach for both stages. I: Static stage. As shown in Fig.~ fig:view-graph , let \(t \ 1, ,T\ \) index video frames and \(i \ 1, ,N_s\ \) index static points. The visibility set \( E_s\) contains the tracked point-frame pairs, and \( ^ s _ it R^3\) denotes the corresponding 2D observation lifted to 3D using predicted monocular depth. Because monocular depth predictions are noisy and their scale drifts from frame to frame, we introduce a per-frame scale \(s_t>0\) that corrects this frame-dependent scale error in the predicted depth. Weighting each observation by an optional confidence \( _ it >0\), we jointly estimate camera poses, depth scales, and static landmarks via The objective enforces that observations of the same static point, after correcting the predicted depth scale and transforming them into the world frame, agree on a common 3D landmark. Without a scale constraint, the objective admits a degenerate solution as all variables shrink toward zero. The original XM formulation~ han25rss-xm prevents this collapse by anchoring the first-frame scale to , making the reconstruction overfit onto the first frame. We instead impose a uniform sphere constraint, , which fixes the global scale without privileging any frame. We formulate this problem as a quadratically constrained quadratic program (QCQP), relax it to a semidefinite program (SDP), and solve it efficiently using Burer--Monteiro (BM) factorization together with a Riemannian staircase, following the certifiable optimization framework of XM and SE-Sync~ han25rss-xm,rosen19ijrr-sesync . II: Dynamic stage. After fixing the recovered camera trajectory, we transform dynamic observations into the world frame and model non-rigid motion with an EDG. Each dynamic point is warped by the rigid transformations of its neighboring EDG nodes, where denotes the rest position of node and the skinning weight. Let denote the corresponding depth-lifted observation in the world frame. The tracking loss is We optimize the EDG node transformations with tracking loss, as-rigid-as-possible (ARAP) and temporal smoothness regularization. Unlike MoSca~ lei25cvpr-mosca , which models deformation through relative transformations between frames, we express all node transformations relative to a fixed rest frame. With fixed EDG structure and skinning weights, this choice makes the tracking, ARAP, and temporal smoothness objectives quadratic in the node transformations. Eliminating node translations then yields a rotation-only QCQP that admits the same SDP-based certifiable optimization framework as the static stage. The recovered geometry then initializes dynamic Gaussian splatting for rendering. In summary, makes the following contributions: For static reconstruction, we build on the QCQP--SDP--BM framework of our conference version, XM~ han25rss-xm , retaining its efficient optimization and global optimality certificates. We introduce a uniform sphere constraint that resolves the scale ambiguity without anchoring any individual frame. For dynamic reconstruction, we design an EDG-based non-rigid reconstruction formulation that incorporates tracking, rigidity, and temporal smoothness into a structured QCQP. This formulation admits the same globally certifiable optimization framework. We build , an accurate and efficient 4D reconstruction pipeline that combines certifiable geometric optimization with dynamic Gaussian splatting. Extensive experiments across seven benchmarks demonstrate leading camera accuracy, fast and scalable optimization, and the best average novel-view rendering performance on all three dynamic benchmarks (DyCheck, NVIDIA, and Syn4D). Outline. The remainder of this paper is organized as follows. Section~ sec:related-work reviews related work. Section~ sec:static presents the static stage: the rotation-only QCQP and SDP relaxation, the BM solver with its optimality certificate, and the sphere constraint. Section~ sec:dynamic extends this machinery to the EDG-based dynamic reconstruction and shows that it admits the same certifiable solver. Section~ sec:pipeline describes the complete pipeline. Section~ sec:experiments evaluates camera accuracy, runtime, and novel-view rendering on seven benchmarks. Proofs and implementation details are given in the appendices. Visualizations and code are available on the project page: . Related Work sec:related-work Dynamic Scene Reconstruction Existing dynamic scene reconstruction methods can be grouped by how they constrain the reconstruction. Rendering-based methods fit time-varying scene representations to images, while geometry-driven methods use measurements such as depth and point tracks to estimate structure and motion. Rendering-based methods represent dynamics using time-varying (volumetric) fields~ lombardi19tog-neuralvolumes,li21cvpr-neuralsceneflow , deformable canonical radiance fields and their higher-dimensional extensions~ pumarola20arxiv-dnerf,park21iccv-nerfies,park21arxiv-hypernerf , or moving Gaussians~ luiten243dv-dynamicgaussian,wu24cvpr-4dgs,stearns24sigasia-dynamicmarbles . Many of them incorporate geometric regularization, and some jointly estimate camera motion~ liu23cvpr-rodynrf . However, recovering object or part level motion for downstream scene understanding generally requires additional motion estimation. Moreover, many methods rely on accurate camera poses, carefully designed initialization, and heavy per-scene optimization. Geometry-based methods use geometric measurements and motion priors to constrain dynamic reconstruction. Earlier non-rigid structure-from-motion methods recover 3D shape from monocular point tracks using low-rank or subspace priors~ garg13cvpr-dynreconstruct,zhu14cvpr-dynreconstructsubspace , while RGB-D methods use depth observations with deformation graphs or volumetric models to track motion and reconstruct geometry~ newcombe15cvpr-dynamicfusion,innmann16eccv-volumedeform,bozic21cvpr-neuraldeformgraph . More recently, MoSca~ lei25cvpr-mosca lifts learned depth and point-track priors into a motion scaffold and anchors Gaussians to it for photometric reconstruction. Shape of Motion~ wang25iccv-shapeofmotion represents scene motion using shared motion bases, with per-point weights combining the bases to recover persistent trajectories from monocular depth and long-range 2D tracks. also uses explicit local transformations as an EDG. Unlike them, estimates camera poses and temporally coupled graph transformations from depth and tracks with a certifiable geometric solver, making local rigid motions explicit without involving Gaussians. Learning-Assisted Geometric Reconstruction Learned geometric priors have become important components of reconstruction pipelines. Monocular depth models~ yang24cvpr-depthanything,piccinelli24cvpr-unidepth,hu24tpami-metric3d,bochkovskiy25iclr-depthpro,lin25arxiv-da3 predict dense scene depth, while point trackers~ xiao24cvpr-spatracker,karaev25iccv-cotracker3,doersch24accv-bootstap,zholus25iccv-tapnext,lai26arxiv-cowtracker establish correspondences across frames. Together, depth and correspondence estimates provide complementary constraints for geometric reconstruction: depth informs scene structure, while tracks connect observations over time. Recent feed-forward methods predict richer 3D scene representations directly from images. DUSt3R~ wang24cvpr-dust3r predicts pointmaps for image pairs and aligns them in a shared coordinate frame, and MUSt3R~ cabon25cvpr-must3r extends it to many views, and VGGT~ wang25cvpr-vggt jointly predicts camera parameters, depth maps, pointmaps, and 3D point tracks. In , learned depth and tracks are measurements for an explicit geometric optimization. Certifiable Geometric Optimization Certifiable geometric optimization solves nonconvex estimation problems, such as bundle adjustment, while verifying global optimality~ lasserre06siopt-sparsity,yang23mp-stride,zhao26arxiv-advances . Semidefinite relaxations provide such certificates for pose synchronization~ rosen19ijrr-sesync,yu24ral-simsync , outlier-robust registration~ yang20tro-teaser , and general polynomial formulations of robust estimation~ yang22pami-certifiably . Our prior conference work, ~ han25rss-xm , introduced depth-assisted scaled bundle adjustment with a scalable solver based on BM factorization~ burer03mp-nonlinear and Riemannian optimization~ boumal15arxiv-bm , which extends to dynamic scenes. title: VFlash: Fast, Accurate Visual Planning via Flash Primitive Decoding
summary: Models for physical AI tasks, such as robotics and autonomous driving, need not reason solely in language. They can use visual plans--points, bounding boxes, and trajectories--to represent spatial goals and anticipate motion. However, autoregressive vision-language models generate these plans one coordinate token at a time, making richer predictions increasingly costly. We introduce VFlash, a method for fast, accurate visual planning through Flash Primitive Decoding. VFlash exploits the known structure of visual primitives to predict their coordinates jointly, using a lightweight drafter that generates an entire primitive in one forward pass. The layout adapts to the primitive's type, dimensionality, and length, supporting compact boxes and long, variable-length trajectories. Crucially, spatial accuracy need not require reproducing an autoregressive model's exact token sequence. VFlash therefore trains on annotated primitives and directly accepts structurally valid predictions without target-token agreement. Across the evaluated 2D and 3D robot trajectory tasks, VFlash consistently reduces prediction errors relative to autoregressive decoding. Preliminary single-rollout measurements indicate approximately 25x faster generation for 3D point motion forecasting. A world action model conditioned on VFlash plans achieves 70.2% average success across four MolmoSpaces task suites, compared with 62.6% for the baseline.

Their reasoning need not be expressed solely in language. VLMs can formulate intermediate predictions as visual plans: points and bounding boxes identify relevant locations or objects~ robopoint,rexomni , while trajectories describe intended motion or forecast how a scene will evolve~ rttrajectory,zhang2026molmomotion . Recent work uses spatial traces and visual primitives to guide action generation~ hamster,molmoact,guo2026avp . These plans make spatial goals and anticipated motion explicit before action. Each visual primitive has identifiable boundaries and an organized coordinate layout. Generating such plans efficiently becomes increasingly important as their spatial detail grows. Longer trajectories, additional objects, and joint 2D image and 3D predictions require more coordinate tokens, which autoregressive VLMs decode sequentially~ chen2022pix2seq,bai2023qwenvlversatilevisionlanguagemodel,zhu2025internvl3,qwen3vl . For physical agents that update their plans as new observations arrive, sequential decoding limits spatial detail and update frequency under a fixed latency budget. This motivates decoding methods that can generate complete visual plans with fewer sequential forward passes while preserving their spatial accuracy. Parallel decoding offers a promising route to reducing this sequential cost, particularly for latency-sensitive physical AI systems operating at batch size one. Existing approaches include speculative decoding with parallel verification~ leviathan2023fast,li2025eagle3 and diffusion language models (dLLMs) with parallel denoising~ nie2025llada,arriola2025block . However, dLLMs often exhibit a speed–quality trade-off relative to autoregressive models~ wu2025fast,liu2025sequential . DFlash combines these approaches using a lightweight block diffusion draft model to predict draft tokens in a single forward pass, followed by target verification that preserves the autoregressive model’s output distribution~ chen2026dflash . For visual outputs, LocateAnything exploits spatial structure through parallel box decoding~ wang2026locateanything . In this work, we introduce VFlash, a generalist decoding framework for physical AI (Figure~ fig:teaser ) that accommodates both text (e.g., sub-task plans) and diverse visual primitives, such as bounding boxes, variable-length trajectories, and dense 3D motion predictions. Our study reveals an interesting observation: a lightweight diffusion drafter can even surpass its autoregressive target in spatial accuracy of the visual plans while decoding much faster. The structure of visual primitives helps explain this finding: once a primitive’s type, dimensionality, and length are specified, its boundaries and coordinate layout are known. Aligning draft blocks with these boundaries allows an entire geometric object to be predicted jointly, with tens to hundreds of tokens decoded in a single forward pass. These observations motivate aligning training and decoding with complete primitive boundaries and directly accepting structurally valid drafts without requiring token-level agreement with the target, while retaining verified decoding for text. At the center of VFlash is Flash Primitive Decoding (FPD), which uses the requested output structure to organize both drafter training and inference. A tool call specifies the size of a variable-length prediction, while the primitive type determines its coordinate layout. Conditioned on features from a frozen target VLM, a lightweight diffusion drafter learns to predict complete primitives from annotated spatial data. At inference, the decoder applies layout-specific constraints~ willard2023outlines,geng2023grammar and accepts valid primitives in full. The target VLM supplies context for subsequent predictions, and ordinary text retains speculative decoding with target verification. We evaluate VFlash on 2D and 3D robot trajectories, bounding boxes, and dense 3D point motion forecasting, and study its use in downstream manipulation and driving. VFlash consistently reduces prediction errors relative to its autoregressive target across the evaluated robot trajectory tasks. In the downstream robot manipulation pipeline shown in Figure~ fig:teaser , it reduces inference latency by about 80 on both Jetson Thor and DGX Spark. These visual plans also provide useful conditioning for action models: on MolmoSpaces~ kim2026molmospaces , a world action model~ ye2026dreamzero,nvidia2026worldsimulation conditioned on VFlash plans achieves 70.2 average success across four task suites, compared with 62.6 for the baseline. Beyond acceleration, our work suggests a broader role for parallel decoding in multimodal systems. Lossless speculative decoding preserves the autoregressive target’s output distribution~ leviathan2023fast,chen2023accelerating , whereas structured visual planning instead permits predictions to be judged by their spatial accuracy and usefulness for action, in the spirit of relaxed acceptance criteria~ bachmann2025judge,wang2025specvla . VFlash enables a System-1 mode~ kahneman2011thinking of visual planning in VLMs, producing fast, structured spatial predictions through joint coordinate decoding. This perspective interestingly connects to recent System-1 models such as Jev, which emphasize fast, typed decisions~ almeida2026systemone,yu2026visualjev . VFlash brings this perspective to complete geometric predictions, exploiting structure within each primitive. The resulting gains in both speed and spatial accuracy suggest that autoregressive decoding need not define the quality ceiling for visual outputs. Method sec:method This section presents the generalist decoding framework of VFlash for physical AI, covering both the preliminaries of DFlash and the detailed design of Flash Primitive Decoding (Figure~ fig:pipeline ). Preliminaries sec:preliminaries In speculative decoding, a draft model proposes tokens that the target model verifies in parallel, giving an average per-token latency of where is the expected number of tokens accepted per cycle~ chen2026dflash . DFlash reduces the numerator with a lightweight block diffusion drafter. Features from selected target layers are fused and injected as keys and values into each draft layer. Given a start token , the drafter predicts masked tokens in one bidirectional forward pass, yielding , where is the sequential drafting cost per token. Longer drafts, however, need not increase : greedy verification accepts tokens only up to the first mismatch with the target: often saturates well below . Thus enlarging a block does not necessarily enlarge its final throughput. For text generation, the goal is to preserve the target distribution~ leviathan2023fast via verification. But token-level agreement need not reflect spatial accuracy. VFlash retains the drafting architecture and replaces Eq.~ eq:verified_acceptance with direct acceptance of structurally valid visual primitives. Flash primitive decoding sec:problem_setup Given visual observations and a task instruction, the VLM predicts spatial objects such as boxes, robot trajectories, or future point positions. Each prediction is a visual primitive with a schema specifying its type, coordinate dimensions, and extent. This fixes each coordinate’s role while leaving its value to be inferred from the input. A trajectory’s 2D image coordinates and 3D spatial coordinates can form one primitive and be predicted jointly. For variable-length predictions, a tool call declares the extent, which together with the primitive type determines the layout; for fixed-size predictions such as boxes, the type alone suffices. The structure is thus known before coordinate prediction, and each decoding block covers a complete primitive. The schema defines a block of length : an observed start token followed by masked tokens. An autoregressive target factorizes the blocks as and needs sequential passes. Given the layout and the target context, VFlash instead predicts all positions conditionally independently, in a single forward pass. The complete primitive is thus the unit of parallel prediction, with a speculation budget set by the request rather than by a fixed window. The same principle covers targets that emit coordinates as ordinary text: we align their numeric fields in a fixed-width layout and render the predictions back into the target's text format. Appendix~ app:schemas gives the coordinate conventions and serialization formats of each task. Token representations sec:token_representations Visual plans often require large, variable-length draft blocks. For example, NAVSIM requires eight waypoints over four seconds, while Waymo requires twenty over five seconds. Drafting such blocks introduces challenges in format following and spatial accuracy. We find that two design principles help address these challenges: Boundary alignment decides what is predicted together: each draft block covers one complete primitive, avoiding the splits caused by fixed-length windows. The tool call declares the block length, from which the waypoint count follows, and a shared layout template accommodates different lengths, allowing the whole primitive to be drafted in one pass. Position alignment decides what each position predicts: every slot has a known role---a waypoint, axis, or delimiter---before decoding. This supports parallel prediction with a consistent layout and per-position constraints at inference. Maintaining this layout requires each coordinate to occupy a fixed number of positions. Recent VLMs normalize image coordinates to 0--1,000 and write them as ordinary text~ bai2023qwenvlversatilevisionlanguagemodel,zhu2025internvl3 ; models built around visual primitives often use special tokens~ rexomni,wang2026locateanything . A special coordinate token occupies one position, whereas text tokenization can vary with the value and shift subsequent coordinates. VFlash supports both representations. title: Latent RL Priors for Data-Efficient Dexterous Manipulation
summary: Learning dexterous manipulation from limited visual demonstrations is challenging because policies must acquire both perceptual grounding and precise control, while reinforcement learning (RL) in simulation can acquire rich control behaviors from large-scale interaction with privileged information. We introduce \textbf{Latent RL Prior}, a two-stage framework that reuses this control knowledge for data-efficient visual policy learning. During privileged pretraining, we distill large-scale RL rollouts into a flow-matching action decoder conditioned on proprioception and latent task context. During visual adaptation, we freeze the decoder and learn a visual interface that maps images to its latent context using action supervision alone, without privileged labels or latent targets. The same decoder can further be shared across arms by learning coordinated visual contexts for bimanual manipulation. Across three simulated tasks, our method outperforms full-parameter fine-tuning of $π_{0.5}$ and GR00T N1.7 in the low-data regime; on door lifting and bimanual assembly, it surpasses full-data baselines using $10\times$ and $5\times$ fewer demonstrations, respectively. Further analysis shows that direct visual-to-latent conditioning improves adaptation performance and training stability over routing visual predictions through the pretrained state encoder. Robustness to unseen mass variation and greater linear accessibility of contact-force information in decoder representations further provide evidence of retained RL-acquired control knowledge. Project website: https://yixiaowang7.github.io/latent-rl-prior-page/.

We introduce Latent RL Prior, a two-stage framework that reuses this control knowledge for data-efficient visual policy learning. During privileged pretraining, we distill large-scale RL rollouts into a flow-matching action decoder conditioned on proprioception and latent task context. During visual adaptation, we freeze the decoder and learn a visual interface that maps images to its latent context using action supervision alone, without privileged labels or latent targets. The same decoder can further be shared across arms by learning coordinated visual contexts for bimanual manipulation. Across three simulated tasks, our method outperforms full-parameter fine-tuning of and GR00T N1.7 in the low-data regime; on door lifting and bimanual assembly, it surpasses full-data baselines using and fewer demonstrations, respectively. Further analysis shows that direct visual-to-latent conditioning improves adaptation performance and training stability over routing visual predictions through the pretrained state encoder. Robustness to unseen mass variation and greater linear accessibility of contact-force information in decoder representations further provide evidence of retained RL-acquired control knowledge. Project website: . Training and evaluation code and datasets will be released. Introduction sec:introduction Dexterous manipulation requires coordinated arm and finger motion under changing contacts and object dynamics. Learning these behaviors from limited visual demonstrations is challenging because the policy must acquire both perceptual grounding and precise action generation zhao2023act,chi2023diffusionpolicy . Pretrained vision-language-action (VLA) models offer transferable priors from broad visual, language, and robot datasets zitkovich2023rt2,kim2024openvla,black2024pi0 . We investigate a complementary source of prior knowledge for dexterous control: behaviors acquired through large-scale reinforcement learning (RL) in simulation. Simulated interaction enables RL policies to acquire manipulation strategies across diverse object geometries and physical properties andrychowicz2020dexterous,singla2024sapg,kedia2026simtoolreal . However, these policies often rely on privileged information, such as object and goal states, that is not directly available at deployment. Reusing their control capabilities requires an interface that connects visual observations to the pretrained controller. Our premise is that preserving pretrained proprioceptive processing and action generation can reduce the visual demonstrations needed to adapt these capabilities to downstream tasks. We introduce , a simple yet effective framework for this transfer. We distill rollouts from an RL teacher trained on procedural pose alignment into a flow-matching action decoder lipman2023flowmatching . The decoder receives proprioceptive history through a dedicated pathway and latent context encoding privileged task information. During visual adaptation, we freeze the decoder and learn a visual interface that maps images directly to this context. This latent transfer uses only the action objective on image--proprioception--action demonstrations, without requiring corresponding privileged information, pretrained latent targets, or paired trajectories between the pretraining and adaptation datasets. The same design extends a single-arm RL prior to multiple arms. We share the frozen decoder across arms and learn coordinated visual contexts, each paired with the corresponding arm's proprioceptive history. Bimanual adaptation thus reuses the pretrained control prior while learning inter-arm coordination through the visual interface. We evaluate the shared prior on target pose alignment, door lifting, and bimanual assembly in simulation. With limited visual demonstrations, our method outperforms full-parameter fine-tuning of physicalintelligence2025pi05 and GR00T N1.7 nvidia2026gr00tn17 . On door lifting and bimanual assembly, it surpasses both baselines trained on the full task datasets with and fewer demonstrations, respectively. Comparisons with the same visual policy architecture trained from scratch further support the value of the pretrained action prior. Further investigations examine how to access and adapt this prior. Latent transfer improves performance and training stability over explicit transfer through the pretrained state encoder. Separate adaptation studies favor conservative updates to the image encoder and a frozen action decoder, particularly for precise alignment. We also investigate the control behaviors and physical information accessible after transfer. The adapted policies exhibit robustness to mass variation absent from the visual demonstrations, and their decoder representations make contact-force information more linearly accessible than those learned from scratch. These observations are consistent with retained control knowledge from large-scale RL pretraining. Our contributions are: a framework for adapting a frozen RL action prior through latent visual conditioning with action supervision alone, including reuse of a single-arm decoder for multi-arm manipulation; empirical evidence of improved visual-demonstration efficiency across three dexterous tasks, together with evaluations of the transfer interface and adaptation choices; and behavioral and representational analyses of mass robustness and contact-force accessibility after visual adaptation. Related Work sec:related_work Dexterous control from reinforcement learning. RL with dynamics randomization has enabled dexterous in-hand manipulation andrychowicz2020dexterous . Parallel simulation and scalable policy optimization support learning from large amounts of interaction makoviychuk2021isaacgym,singla2024sapg . SimToolReal trains a single policy to manipulate procedurally generated objects toward goal poses and deploys it using object-pose estimates and goal-pose sequences kedia2026simtoolreal . We build on its released teacher, distill rollouts into an action decoder, and investigate reuse of the resulting control prior through visual conditioning learned from limited downstream demonstrations. Transfer with privileged information. Asymmetric actor--critic training uses privileged information in the critic to learn policies with restricted observations pinto2018asymmetric . Policy distillation transfers behavior between policies rusu2016policydistillation , while Learning by Cheating uses a privileged teacher to train a visual student chen2020learningbycheating . Closer to our interface, Rapid Motor Adaptation (RMA) and its extension to in-hand rotation retain an RL controller while estimating latent representations of physical properties from proprioceptive and action histories kumar2021rma,qi2023hora . Their adaptation modules are trained to match embeddings computed from corresponding privileged information. Our visual adaptation uses action supervision alone: the decoder distilled from RL rollouts remains frozen, while its visual conditioning is learned without privileged information or latent targets in the downstream demonstrations. We reuse this prior across tasks and extend it to bimanual manipulation through a shared single-arm decoder. Visual imitation and generalist robot policies. Action chunking and generative action modeling support learning visual manipulation from demonstrations zhao2023act,chi2023diffusionpolicy . Generalist policies and VLA models transfer knowledge from diverse robot and vision--language datasets zitkovich2023rt2,ghosh2024octo,kim2024openvla . The and GR00T families combine pretrained vision--language representations with flow-matching action models black2024pi0,nvidia2025gr00t . Our approach combines DINOv2 visual features oquab2024dinov2 with a control prior distilled from privileged RL rollouts. We investigate how this source of control experience supports adaptation to dexterous tasks with limited visual demonstrations, comparing against full-parameter fine-tuning of physicalintelligence2025pi05 and GR00T N1.7 nvidia2026gr00tn17 . Latent RL Prior sec:method Large-scale reinforcement learning (RL) in simulation can acquire complex dexterous manipulation behavior through abundant interaction across diverse object geometries, masses, and physical properties. However, these policies often rely on privileged state information, such as object and goal states, that is unavailable at deployment. Therefore, in this section, we investigate how to transfer such dexterous behaviors acquired by privileged RL into a reusable RL prior for downstream visual tasks. Our goal is to preserve dexterous capabilities learned from large-scale simulated experience while adapting a visual interface from limited demonstrations using only deployable observations.
