title: OopsieRecover: Learning Transferable VLA Corrections from Semantic Interventions
summary: Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models can perform a wide range of robotic manipulation tasks, but often fail during deployment. Teaching them to recover from these failures requires substantial corrective data: existing approaches learn to recover from failures by directly associating corrective actions with the observations in which they were demonstrated. For instance, DAgger-like fine-tuning can require tens to hundreds of interactions, yet the resulting policy may still fail to generalize the learned corrections beyond the demonstrated scenarios. We hypothesize that semantics can capture the underlying reasons for failures and their corrections, enabling policies to learn from only a handful of corrective demonstrations and generalize those corrections to novel objects, and scene variations. We propose OopsieRecover, a framework that uses abduction to infer the intent behind a small set of corrective demonstrations and encodes the inferred knowledge as dense spatial representations and conditional costs. These costs capture when a behavior is undesirable and steer the policy toward more desirable action regions. We experiment across 6 tasks and variations in object poses, scenes, and related tasks, and find that only a handful of corrective demonstrations can enable a VLA to overcome failures across a broad range of novel situations, without requiring new corrective data for each variation. Please refer to https://robin-lab.cs.utexas.edu/oopsierecover for videos.
full_text: UT Austin Toyota Research Institute Equal contribution Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models can perform a wide range of robotic manipulation tasks, but often fail during deployment. Teaching them to recover from these failures requires substantial corrective data: existing approaches learn to recover from failures by directly associating corrective actions with the observations in which they were demonstrated. For instance, DAgger-like fine-tuning can require tens to hundreds of interactions, yet the resulting policy may still fail to generalize the learned corrections beyond the demonstrated scenarios. We hypothesize that semantics can capture the underlying reasons for failures and their corrections, enabling policies to learn from only a handful of corrective demonstrations and generalize those corrections to novel objects, and scene variations. We propose , a framework that uses abduction to infer the intent behind a small set of corrective demonstrations and encodes the inferred knowledge as dense spatial representations and conditional costs. These costs capture when a behavior is undesirable and steer the policy toward more desirable action regions. We experiment across 6 tasks and variations in object poses, scenes, and related tasks, and find that only a handful of corrective demonstrations can enable a VLA to overcome failures across a broad range of novel situations, without requiring new corrective data for each variation. Please refer to our Project Page for videos. Introduction Vision-language-action models (VLAs) provide broad manipulation capabilities~ intelligence2025pi_,bjorck2025gr00t,kim2024openvla , but can still exhibit systematic failures during deployment~ oopsieverse , such as collisions, dropping objects, etc. Human interventions offer a natural source of corrective data~ ross2011reduction, kelly2019hg,liu2025robot, murray2026flowdagger , yet existing interactive imitation methods generally treat corrections as additional state-action supervision~ ross2011reduction, kelly2019hg , making generalization depend on collecting enough corrections in similar states. Humans can instead infer a reusable principle from only a few corrections. We ask whether a robot can likewise infer what prompted an intervention, how its behavior should be steered to avoid it, and when the same correction should apply again. An intervention provides only partial evidence about this principle. Before takeover, the robot executes the VLA actions; afterward, the human provides a preferred continuation. Instead, the takeover time localizes the context that prompted the intervention and that generalizes to other similar situations, while the subsequent human-controlled segment provides a preferred continuation from the reached state towards a more optimal situation. A description such as ``keep the mug upright when placing it on the plate'' identifies the semantic property motivating the takeover, which may remain valid despite changes in object(s) poses, robot configuration, background, or even task. Trajectories alone leave ambiguous which property mattered; language alone lacks the sensorimotor grounding needed for visuomotor control. Together, they constrain a reusable correction. This ambiguity motivates , which formulates correction inference as abduction~ kakas1992abductive : finding a simple explanation consistent with the observed interventions despite missing or imperfect information. A vision-language model (VLM) leverages its visual-language priors, together with the scene, robot-controlled initial demonstration, human intervention, and language annotation, to propose candidate explanations. Since several explanations may fit one intervention, evaluates each hypothesis across all available interventions and selects explanations that capture the underlying corrective behavior without being overly narrow or permissive. In this formal-methods inspired procedure, the VLM proposes plausible semantic hypotheses, and the corrective evidence determines whether they are retained or refined. We represent the selected explanation as one or more gated costs. Each combines a logical predicate specifying when the correction applies with a continuous cost specifying how the behavior should optimize/change. E.g., a gate may activate during placement, while its cost penalizes tilting the mug away from upright. This separation keeps corrections local rather globally biasing the policy. To execute these costs, grounds task-relevant robot parts, object parts, and spatial locations and regions as semantic point sets. At test time, the VLA samples candidate action chunks, and predicts how each candidate would move these point sets, how they evaluate on the gated costs, and which candidate would lead to the lowest cost overall. The frozen VLA supplies plausible behaviors, while the inferred correction steers its choices whenever the same semantic situation reappears. We evaluate on 3 tasks in both sim and real using pi0 in RoboCasa and DROID, with only 5-8 corrections per task. improves real-world task-progress from 35.1 to 61.0 , a 74 relative improvement over the next-best baseline, and transfers corrections to unseen poses, objects and scenes. We show that our gated costs generalize to novel variations in object poses and scenes zero-shot, and successfully steer the base policy. Our contributions are: i) a semantic, abductive formulation of few-shot VLA correction from human-in-the-loop interventions; ii) a generate-and-test procedure that synthesizes and verifies gated costs; and iii) a test-time steering mechanism that applies and generalizes them without retraining the VLA. Related Works Interactive Imitation Learning. Having a human intervene when a robot is about to fail and retraining on the resulting corrective segments is a common approach for improving control policies. DAgger ross2011reduction aggregates on-policy states labeled by an expert, while HG-DAgger kelly2019hg and IWR iwr improve sample efficiency by intervening only when the policy is likely to fail and up-weighting the resulting corrective segments during retraining. SIRIUS liu2025robot extends this paradigm to continual learning. Expert Intervention Learning~ spencer2020learning additionally treats pre-intervention behavior as implicit negative evidence. YAY Robot shi2024yell incorporates semantics by training a high-level policy that produces language embeddings for a low-level policy, while OLAF liu2023interactive relabels intervened states with actions generated by a VLM conditioned on semantics to improve the base policy, requiring several dozen human corrections~ sun2025dynamic . However, these approaches primarily use interventions to relabel the actions and update the policy, limiting the ability of the corrections to generalize beyond the specific situations in which they were collected. In contrast, we focus on extracting a structured representation from the intervention and its associated semantics, allowing the correction to be applied to novel situations in a zero-shot manner. Failure Detection for VLAs. Detecting failures is a key first step toward recovery. To this end, SAFE~ gu2026safe trains a multitask failure detector on VLA latent representations to flag anomalous or unsafe executions. FailSafe~ lin2025failsafe similarly focuses on failure reasoning and recovery signals, identifying failure modes that can trigger intervention. Failure detection is also a central component of , however, like most existing methods for failure detection zhang2026foresight, ren2023robots, sinha2024real, liu2024model, liu2024multi, gu2026safe these approaches require additional training or fine-tuning, whereas we target the extreme data-scarce regime of learning from only a handful of corrections. We instead leverage point-sets as structured representations and guarded costs to detect when the policy is failing and steer it without requiring any additional training. Inferring objectives/constraints from semantics. Another line of work is that of inverse reinforcement learning (IRL), where given a (correction induced) demonstration, the goal is to infer the reward function that defines it. One-at-a-time bajcsy2018learning extracts the reward by weighting predefined features, and use Bayesian IRL ramachandran2007bayesian, hadfield2017inverse to maintain posterior over rewards. Physical-correction methods~ bajcsy2017learning, bobu2020quantifying similarly infer underlying objectives rather than directly imitating corrected actions. Other work uses VLMs to infer rewards~ ma2024eureka,ma2406dreureka,baumli2023vision,pmlr-v235-wang24bn or constraints from observations~ kumar2026open or demonstrations~ gumbsch2026demonstrations . ReKep~ huang2024rekep and VoxPoser~ huang2023voxposer further synthesize grounded spatial objectives from VLMs. Programmatic imitation learning (PRL) tremblay2018synthetically, xin2024programmatic is another data-efficient approach for representing policies as programs from few demonstrations patton2024programming . Code as policies liang2023code relaxes the demonstration assumption and entirely generates the policy code using an LLM. While these works represent policies as explicit, human-interpretable programs learned from demonstrations, they typically synthesize a new policy or program de novo for each task rather than preserving a base policy. In contrast, extracts a local, guarded correction that supplements a frozen, general-purpose VLA only when the relevant semantic context arises, preserving the base policy’s broader capabilities. Steering-based methods. One line of research focuses on steering generative policies using RL, either by autonomously steering the latent space wagenmaker2025steering, hong2026tmrl or through human-in-the-loop interventions tang2026improving, murray2026flowdagger . These methods remain relatively sample-inefficient, often requiring several successful trajectories to learn an accurate -function for effectively steering the base policy. Works like RecoveryChaining~ vats2025recoverychaining show direct sim2real transfer of recovery behaviors, however, they require re-training of recovery skills for every new scenario. In contrast, we focus on steering policies with as few corrections as possible, on the order of only a handful of interventions, while being able to transfer to new task instances zero-shot. An alternative to RL-based steering is to steer the base policy with a verifier in the loop. FOREWARN~ wu2025foresight steers the policy by training a latent dynamics model and fine-tuning a VLM to align with it, enabling the VLM to predict the outcomes of imagined trajectories in language and select the most promising one. Do What You Say~ wu2025you generates multiple candidate trajectories using a simulator and employs a VLM as a verifier to rank them against the VLA's task-level intermediate plan. Most closely related to our work is VLS~ liu2026vls , which uses a VLM to extract reward functions for each task sub-stage, then generates diverse trajectories through gradient-based guidance and ranks them according to the extracted reward functions before executing the best action sequence. V-GPS~ nakamoto2024steering , Inference-Time Policy Steering~ wang2025inference , and DynaGuide~ du2026dynaguide similarly steer pretrained policies at inference time. Unlike these approaches, synthesizes, calibrates, and verifies reusable, context-gated costs from very few human interventions to steer frozen VLAs across tasks and scenes. learns reusable correction objectives from human interventions and uses them to steer a pretrained VLA. summarizes our method. title: WAM-Sim0.1: World Anchored Memory Meets Online RL for Consistent and Realistic Driving Simulation
summary: Autoregressive driving world models systematically suffer from structural drift, identity drift, and quality decay over long rollout horizons due to transient conditioning signals that lack persistent state. We present WAM-Sim, a driving world model anchored by a persistent hierarchical memory and optimized via online flow-matching RL. WAM-Sim structures persistent context across three temporal and semantic scales: pose-aligned structural tokens encoding persistent road topology, read-only scene tokens supplying geolocated background appearance, and write-once instance tokens preserving individual traffic participant identities across occlusions and chunk boundaries. To restore visual sharpness and physical plausibility degraded by multi-scale conditioning, we introduce an online post-training framework that optimizes self-generated rollouts via flow-matching RL guided by hierarchy-aligned visual rewards and a vision-language model physical judge. The invariant memory empirically confines policy optimization within the anchored context, helping suppress semantic collapse and reward hacking, while online RL systematically enforces physical commonsense and fine-grained visual fidelity. On the nuScenes benchmark, WAM-Sim achieves a superior generation fidelity (FID=3.47, FVD=25.72) and strong downstream perception performance (24.16 mAP, 71.23 road mIoU). On minute-scale rollouts of self-collected data, WAM-Sim substantially mitigates structural and identity drift, preserving high scene similarity and subject identity coherence across extended horizons. Project page: https://fudan-generative-vision.github.io/WAM-Sim.
full_text: Autoregressive driving world models systematically suffer from structural drift, identity drift, and quality decay over long rollout horizons due to transient conditioning signals that lack persistent state. We present WAM-Sim, a driving world model anchored by a persistent hierarchical memory and optimized via online flow-matching RL. WAM-Sim structures persistent context across three temporal and semantic scales: pose-aligned structural tokens encoding persistent road topology, read-only scene tokens supplying geolocated background appearance, and write-once instance tokens preserving individual traffic participant identities across occlusions and chunk boundaries. To restore visual sharpness and physical plausibility degraded by multi-scale conditioning, we introduce an online post-training framework that optimizes self-generated rollouts via flow-matching RL guided by hierarchy-aligned visual rewards and a vision-language model physical judge. The invariant memory empirically confines policy optimization within the anchored context, helping suppress semantic collapse and reward hacking, while online RL systematically enforces physical commonsense and fine-grained visual fidelity. On the nuScenes benchmark, WAM-Sim achieves a superior generation fidelity (FID=3.47, FVD=25.72) and strong downstream perception performance (24.16 mAP, 71.23 road mIoU). On minute-scale rollouts of self-collected data, WAM-Sim substantially mitigates structural and identity drift, preserving high scene similarity and subject identity coherence across extended horizons. Introduction sec:intro Video world models offer a scalable paradigm for controllable closed-loop simulation in autonomous driving, synthesizing driving observations conditioned on ego trajectories and agent controls~ hu2023gaia,gao2024vista,wen2024panacea,russell2025gaia . Despite recent progress, standard training and evaluation regimes remain predominantly constrained to short temporal clips and instantaneous point-estimate metrics. As rollouts extend toward minute-scale horizons, generation systematically degrades through three recurring failure modes: 1) structural drift, where road geometry and background appearance detach from geographic reality; 2) identity drift, where traffic participants undergo unconstrained appearance, category, or tracking mutations; and 3) quality decay, where accumulated autoregressive errors recursively compound over time. Although recent architectures incorporate extended context windows, temporal filtering, or instance masking~ guo2024infinitydrive,huang2025selfforcing,liu2026rollingforcing,cheng2026m4world,basant2026omnidreams , these capabilities operate in isolation without a persistent and addressable state. We argue that long-horizon generation failure is not merely a function of limited context window length, but fundamentally demands persistent, multi-scale memory semantics to anchor identity, appearance and geometry. In conventional driving world models, conditioning signals such as high-definition (HD) maps, 3D bounding boxes, and reference frames are provided as transient per-frame or per-chunk inputs. While transient conditioning constrains immediate frame synthesis, it fails to establish a persistent memory state across extended rollouts. Recent retrieval-augmented models and object-centric attention mechanisms demonstrate the value of persistent scene context and isolated participant conditioning~ wu2025longtermspatialmemory,xiao2025worldmem,li2025vmem,jia2026spatialretrieval,seo2026seoulworldmodel,yang2026consisdrive . However, existing methods deploy these mechanisms in isolation, failing to jointly preserve global route geometry, geolocated scene appearance, and individual object identities under dynamic mid-rollout interventions. Consequently, once generation extends beyond the initial context window, persistent states must be reconstructed from noisy self-generated histories, causing errors to compound over time. Overcoming this bottleneck requires a unified memory architecture that represents road structure, environmental appearance, and participant identity as distinct visual tokens, maintains each according to its temporal persistence, and retrieves each through mechanisms matched to its spatio-temporal validity domain. To address this challenge, we present a driving world model anchored by a persistent world anchored memory. The memory organizes the driving world across three temporal and semantic scales: static structural tokens encoded from HD lane maps serve as persistent geometric anchors; read-only scene tokens retrieved from geolocated databases supply background appearance via temporally routed cross-attention; and instance tokens registered in a write-once appearance bank preserve individual object identities across chunk boundaries and occlusions through instance-masked cross-attention. Although this explicit memory substrate substantially mitigates structural and identity drift, injecting such dense, multi-scale conditioning signals inevitably shifts the generator off its pretrained distribution, compromising native visual sharpness and multi-agent physical plausibility. To overcome this trade-off, we introduce Drive DiffusionNFT, an online post-training framework that optimizes self-generated rollouts via flow-matching reinforcement learning guided by hierarchy-aligned visual rewards and a physical judge. Beyond their individual roles, we empirically observe a practical synergy between explicit memory persistence and online policy optimization: the invariant memory state appears to confine the effective policy optimization space, coinciding with reduced semantic drift and reward hacking during recursive rollouts, while online RL systematically restores fine-grained visual fidelity and enforces physical commonsense without compromising global stability. Extensive evaluations on the standard nuScenes benchmark and a self-collected challenging long-horizon dataset demonstrate the effectiveness of WAM-Sim. On nuScenes, WAM-Sim achieves superior generation fidelity ( , ) alongside strong downstream perception performance ( mAP, road mIoU). On minute-scale rollouts of self-collected data, it effectively mitigates quality–horizon decay, preserving high scene similarity ( ) and instance identity coherence ( ) across extended temporal gaps. Furthermore, human preference studies and physical evaluations confirm that tightly coupling persistent hierarchical memory with online flow-matching post-training substantially mitigates structural and identity drift, synthesizing realistic and physically sound driving simulations. Related Work sec:related Driving World Models. Driving video generation has evolved from action- and trajectory-conditioned models~ hu2023gaia,russell2025gaia,gao2024vista to layout- and map-conditioned video synthesis~ wang2024drivedreamer,wen2024panacea,gao2024magicdrive,gao2024magicdrivedit,zhao2024drivedreamer2,wang2024drivewm,li2023drivingdiffusion,mei2024dreamforge , autoregressive long-horizon generation~ jia2023adriver,hu2024drivingworld,zhang2025epona,guo2024infinitydrive , geometry-aware 4D modeling~ yang2025xscene,dive2025,dist4d2025,unimlvg2025 , and driving-specialized foundation models~ nvidia2025cosmos,ren2025cosmosdrive,ni2025opendwm,basant2026omnidreams . InstaDrive~ yang2026instadrive propagates instance features to preserve identity, yet treats such evidence as transient per-chunk conditioning; HorizonDrive~ zhang2026horizondrive extends rollouts toward minute-scale horizons via streaming context. Across these methods, maps, boxes, and retrieved context remain transient, with no persistent, addressable state binding geographic location and instance identities; we replace transient conditioning with a world anchored memory. Memory and Long-Horizon Consistency. Persistence in interactive world models is achieved by attention caches~ valevski2024gamengen,decart2024oasis,parkerholder2024genie2,deepmind2025genie3 , retrieval over past observations~ xiao2025worldmem,yu2025contextasmemory,li2025vmem,zhao2026spatia,wu2025longtermspatialmemory , or geographic grounding~ deng2024streetscapes,wang2025terasimworld,jia2026spatialretrieval . Orthogonal efforts extend or compress context~ qiu2024freenoise,kim2024fifo,henschel2024streamingt2v,zhang2025framepack,huang2025memoryforcing,furuta2025worldpack and mitigate exposure bias~ chen2024diffusionforcing,yin2025causvid,huang2025selfforcing,liu2026rollingforcing . Closest to ours, ConsisDrive~ yang2026consisdrive encodes instance identity and trajectory through instance-masked attention and losses; we adopt its mask to specify where identity applies, while our write-once appearance bank determines what persists across occlusions and chunk boundaries. Spatial Retrieval~ jia2026spatialretrieval grounds generation geographically, but retains no persistent scene or instance state. Each mechanism addresses persistence in isolation; we unify geometric anchoring, scene appearance, and instance identity within a single memory substrate. Reinforcement Learning for Visual Generation. Reward alignment of visual diffusion models has advanced from policy gradients and preference optimization~ black2023ddpo,fan2023dpok,wallace2023diffusiondpo,xu2023imagereward to online group-relative flow-matching post-training~ liu2025flowgrpo,xue2025dancegrpo,zheng2025diffusionnft . Recently, RL post-training has been applied to video world models: RLVR-World~ wu2025rlvrworld leverages verifiable rewards for video generation, while Reward Forcing~ lu2025rewardforcing distills reward signals into streaming autoregressive diffusion rollouts. Orthogonal to these approaches, which optimize generic video rewards, WAM-Sim is, to the best of our knowledge, the first to combine forward-process DiffusionNFT optimization with memory-aligned hierarchical driving rewards---unifying multi-scale visual fidelity with VLM-guided physical plausibility---to constrain policy search and mitigate structural and quality decay on self-generated multi-chunk rollouts. Method sec:method As shown in Figure~ fig:framework , we present a long-horizon driving world model (Section~ sec:method:formulation ) built on two mutually reinforcing components: a persistent world anchored memory that anchors generation to a real geographic location and to per-instance identities (Section~ sec:method:memory ), and Drive DiffusionNFT, an online post-training stage that optimizes visual and physical realism on self-generated rollouts (Section~ sec:method:rl ). The two components are synergistic by design: the memory state delimits the manifold within which reward optimization operates, while the rewards are aligned with the memory hierarchy, so that the policy improves precisely the properties that memory persists. Problem Formulation sec:method:formulation Given a local HD-map , 3D bounding-box agent controls , a global ego pose trajectory , and a persistent memory state , the model autoregressively synthesizes driving video chunks of frames across camera views: Here, encodes 3D bounding-box layout sequences for surrounding agents, and provides the global ego trajectory used for geolocated reference retrieval. denotes the number of camera views. Specifically, is an append-only operation: it registers newly emerging traffic instances into the appearance bank upon initial observation and advances temporal segment indices, guaranteeing that existing memory entries are never overwritten or corrupted by self-generated video content. Long-horizon generation satisfies three requirements: 1) no structural drift---the video remains anchored to the road geometry and background appearance; 2) no identity drift---each tracked participant preserves its appearance across chunks, occlusion, and re-emergence; 3) no quality decay---visual and physical fidelity do not degrade with horizon. title: When Does Test-Time Search Help World Action Models? An Empirical Audit of Candidate Selection and Simulator Integrity
summary: World-action models increasingly apply test-time scaling, spending extra inference computation on candidate selection and adaptive allocation to improve control. Such gains are credible only when candidates carry exploitable signal, nominal compute savings become real speedup, and evaluation stays reliable. We audit all three on Cosmos Policy and RoboCasa with a premise-first, pre-registered methodology. On clean data, a learned value selector is 1.66 pp worse than random; a hindsight oracle gains only 1.40 pp, with an episode-level interval spanning zero; and 82% of states show identical candidate outcomes, leaving little selection headroom. Token pruning cuts per-forward FLOPs by up to 47% but yields at most a measured 1.15$\times$ end-to-end speedup on the deployed path (1.25$\times$ on a decode-excluded path), short of a 1.5$\times$ target, and our adaptive-allocation experiment is inconclusive under a power gate. We further identify and fix a silent rendering corruption whose rate rises sharply along compute-heavy planning paths while leaving the official direct-policy result unaffected, and release a detector, fix, and scripts. These findings show why test-time scaling should be audited as a chain of premises (decision signal, realized efficiency, evaluationintegrity) rather than by success rate alone. Conclusions are scoped to the tested configuration.

Introduction sec:intro World-action models (WAMs) such as Cosmos Policy~ kim2026cosmos adapt large pretrained video models into robot policies that jointly generate actions, future states, and values within a shared latent diffusion process. A central promise of this design is test-time scaling: by generating candidate actions, predicting their future consequences, and evaluating them with a value function, WAMs can allocate additional inference-time computation to identify promising actions. Related peer-reviewed work has explored complementary aspects of this problem, including model-based planning with action-conditioned video world models~ zhu2025irasim and efficient diffusion-based robot policies through one-step distillation~ 3780338.3782852 , training-free adaptive caching~ ji2026bac , and rollout-adaptive pruning and activation reuse~ ji2026sag . Yet whether extra inference-time computation improves control remains insufficiently examined. More computation helps only if it exposes decision-relevant candidate differences, produces practical end-to-end effects, and is evaluated reliably; success rates alone cannot distinguish a weak selection signal, unrealized compute savings, and simulator artifacts ~ li2024evaluating . We therefore audit test-time scaling as a chain of premises rather than a single performance number: is useful signal present, do nominal savings translate into end-to-end gains, and does the evaluation path remain reliable under added computation? We instantiate this audit on Cosmos Policy and RoboCasa~ robocasa365 . Rather than proposing a planner, we combine paired candidate comparisons and a deployment-conditioned hindsight oracle, pre-registered decision criteria and a power gate, complete-query latency measurements, and a framebuffer-sentinel integrity check. The audit yields three findings. (1) Candidate selection is limited by the available signal, not just by the selector. On render-verified clean data, the deployable value selector performs \,pp worse than random, and even a hindsight oracle (an upper bound) gains only \,pp with an interval including zero, because in of query states all candidates share an outcome. This does not show selection is generally ineffective; it shows selector quality must be read alongside the separability of the candidates it receives. (2) Nominal compute reduction is not a reliable proxy for practical acceleration. Directly timing the complete query, token pruning yields at most a measured end-to-end speedup on the deployed path ( with future-image decode excluded), below the pre-specified target, because the gain is bounded by the irreducible autoencoder encode and decode. A separate joint-allocation diagnostic falls below the measurement's noise resolution and did not clear its power gate, so it is inconclusive rather than evidence of no effect. (3) Evaluation integrity can depend on the inference path being evaluated. We identify and fix a silent rendering corruption in the RoboCasa/robosuite stack whose frequency is small under the official direct-policy protocol but rises sharply in the compute-intensive planning path. It is more than a generic simulator bug: changing inference-time computation changes exposure to a measurement failure, so the compute-intensive paths that realize test-time scaling are the most exposed. Together, these findings make the contribution a testable audit methodology and a configuration-specific case study, not a claim that test-time scaling fails for all WAMs. Related Work sec:related models for control. World models that predict action-conditioned futures have advanced rapidly, spanning diffusion-based video prediction alonso2024diffusion, guo2024prediction,chun2026sparse , 3D and persistent representations zhou2026learning, lu2025gwm , and manipulation-specific models kim2026dexterous . The backbone we study, Cosmos Policy~ kim2026cosmos , follows the joint action-video line in which actions, futures, and values are produced within a single denoising process guo2024prediction . We do not propose a new world model; we audit whether the inference-time computation layered on top of such a model improves control. world-model inference. Because prediction and planning in these models are costly, a growing body of work reduces their inference cost, through sparse imagination of rollouts chun2026sparse , disentangled dynamics prediction yin2026ddpwm , efficient on-policy rollout in diffusion world models cohen2026horizon , and warm-started prediction that reuses spatiotemporal consistency li2026step . These methods report nominal compute reductions. We audit whether such reductions convert to end-to-end latency on a representative stack, and find that token-level savings are capped by an irreducible encoding fraction rather than realized as speedup, and that the joint allocation effect lies below the measurement noise floor. X-WAM~ guo2026xwam audit underscores why architectural avenues can be more fruitful than token pruning alone for practical speedups. -time scaling and candidate selection. A parallel line scales inference by sampling and selecting candidate actions, through verifier-free scoring jang2026verifier , relative action critics li2026vlaattc , and reward-ranked world-model rollouts zhang2026worldinworld ; analogous strategies in text and digital-agent settings use self-verification, process reward models, and execution-free critics zhao2025sample, bilal2026what, hua2026learning, shum2026swe,jang2026verifier . These works propose selectors and report positive scaling. We instead audit whether the selection signal exists, and find a learned value selector worse than random on a strong base policy where candidate outcomes rarely differ. of policy evaluation. Recent work asks whether simulator- and world-model-based evaluation is trustworthy, training learned evaluators to match real rollouts li2026scaling , testing robustness under real-to-sim translation jangir2026robotarena , and reducing evaluation cost while preserving rankings chen2026manipevalagent . These address the fidelity of a learned evaluator or a synthesized scene. Our reliability finding is at the level of the evaluation stack itself: a silent rendering corruption in the standard RoboCasa and robosuite pipeline whose rate rises with per-query inference compute, for which we release a detector and a fix. A Diagnostic Methodology for Test-Time Compute sec:methodology Because extra inference compute can change outputs without improving control, success-rate movements alone are not evidence of scaling gains. Our pre-registered, falsification-first audit tests for usable candidate signal and reliable evaluation before interpreting success (Section~ sec:reliability ). Verify the Premise Before Measuring the Gain subsec:premise-first Before evaluating an inference-time mechanism, we test whether its required signal exists. For best-of- planning, candidate outcomes must differ in ways a selector can recover; we test this directly in Section~ sec:planning-audit , rather than infer it from downstream success. Supplement Figure~ fig:methodology summarizes the audit gates. Causal Ablation and an Oracle Headroom Estimate subsec:oracle For each query state, we replay all candidates under a fixed continuation policy and let a hindsight oracle select a successful one. This estimates outcome-level selection headroom in the current candidate pool; because it uses unavailable outcome information, it is not deployable. We also probe input importance by leave-one-out patch masking, trusting the probe only if irrelevant background ranks below relevant end-effector and contact regions in a pre-registered sanity check. Pre-Registration and Statistical Power Control subsec:prereg For the selection audit, we fix decision thresholds and the replicate-consistency gate before inspecting the corresponding data and report the gate's verdict even when it fails. A power gate avoids launching experiments unlikely to yield a verdict: from a smoke sample, we estimate the paired-residual standard deviation and project the two-sided confidence-interval half-width at the planned sample size, launching the full run only if , the separation between the pre-registered outcomes; otherwise the run is not launched. Every reported comparison states its bootstrap resampling unit and interval, so that an effect whose significance depends on that choice is presented as such rather than as a settled result. Closed-loop success is measured by snapshot replay, in which we restore a state, execute a candidate action chunk, and continue under a fixed dense base policy, rather than inferred from a single-step action deviation. Scope subsec:scope Our empirical findings are limited to Cosmos Policy on RoboCasa. The audit components—premise checks, oracle headroom, a power gate, and render-integrity verification—can also inform audits of other diffusion control policies. We release a framebuffer-sentinel detector, a fix for the identified OpenGL-context bug, and reproduction scripts; the detector principle may transfer across backends, but this fix is stack-specific. Auditing Best-of- N Planning Selection sec:planning-audit We apply the audit to best-of- planning, comparing the model's value-based ordering with random selection and estimating outcome-level headroom using a hindsight oracle. Setup subsec:planning-setup On render-verified clean data, we compare the value selector, random selection, and the deployment-conditioned hindsight oracle on paired sets of candidates with common continuation seeds. Differences from random are reported with state-within-task and episode-within-task bootstrap intervals. protocol. title: Reviving the Discarded High-Resolution Feature for Transformer-Based Tiny Object Detection
summary: Tiny object detection remains challenging because tiny instances occupy only a few pixels, and their fine-grained details are easily lost during feature downsampling. Although the highest-resolution feature preserves rich local details for tiny objects, DETR-like detectors often discard it due to its large computational cost, while directly reintroducing this feature also brings dense background noise. To address this problem, we propose ReDHF, a novel framework that Revives the Discarded High-resolution Feature for tiny object detection. ReDHF has three cooperative components. Cross-Scale Deformable Fusion (CSDF) first constructs a semantically enhanced highest-resolution feature and injects its fine-grained details into the shallow feature under a moderate cost. Ellipse-Guided Shallow Supervision (EGSS) then guides the enhanced feature to learn more reliable classification and localization priors by applying geometry-adaptive auxiliary supervision. Full-Scale Query Interaction (FSQI) further enables decoder queries to access both low-level details and high-level semantic information, allowing them to aggregate richer cues for tiny objects. Extensive experiments show that ReDHF consistently improves multiple baselines across different DETR variants and achieves state-of-the-art performance on the evaluated benchmarks. The best ReDHF variants surpass their baselines by +1.4 AP on AI-TOD-v2, +1.6 AP on VisDrone, and +1.5 AP on SODA-D, with especially notable gains on tiny and small objects.

Although the highest-resolution feature preserves rich local details for tiny objects, DETR-like detectors often discard it due to its large computational cost, while directly reintroducing this feature also brings dense background noise. To address this problem, we propose ReDHF, a novel framework that Revives the Discarded High-resolution Feature for tiny object detection. ReDHF has three cooperative components. Ellipse-Guided Shallow Supervision (EGSS) then guides the enhanced feature to learn more reliable classification and localization priors by applying geometry-adaptive auxiliary supervision. Full-Scale Query Interaction (FSQI) further enables decoder queries to access both low-level details and high-level semantic information, allowing them to aggregate richer cues for tiny objects. Extensive experiments show that ReDHF consistently improves multiple baselines across different DETR variants and achieves state-of-the-art performance on the evaluated benchmarks. The best ReDHF variants surpass their baselines by +1.4 AP on AI-TOD-v2, +1.6 AP on VisDrone, and +1.5 AP on SODA-D, with especially notable gains on tiny and small objects. Introduction Object detection has advanced rapidly, with both CNN-based detectors~ dai2016r-fcn, girshick2015fast, he2017mask, FPN, liu2016ssd, peng2024scene, redmon2016yolo, ren2015faster, tang2024hic, wang2023gold and Transformer-based detectors~ carion2020end, chen2024lw, huang2024deim, liu2022dabdetr, meng2021conditional, peng2024dfine, zhang2022dino, zhao2024detrs, zhu2020deformable achieving strong performance. However, detecting tiny objects remains difficult, especially in aerial, remote sensing, and traffic scenarios. Tiny objects occupy only a few pixels, leaving their edges, textures, and geometric cues weak in the image and further weakened by feature downsampling. As a result, high-level features often fail to preserve sufficient discriminative details for tiny objects, as illustrated in Fig.~ fig:introduction (b). To address the issues of tiny object detection, a natural idea is to preserve these weak cues by using higher-resolution inputs or features. Prior works have shown that high-resolution information is important for tiny objects. For example, Deformable DETR~ zhu2020deformable points out that small objects rely on high-resolution feature maps, and DM-EFS~ sharma2025dm shows that shallower high-resolution features can improve tiny-object representation. However, many detectors~ liu2018path, zhang2022dino, zhu2020deformable, liu2022dabdetr still discard the highest-resolution backbone feature to control computation. This design saves overhead but sacrifices the local details that are critical for tiny objects. As shown in Fig.~ fig:introduction (a)(c), discarding this feature becomes especially detrimental on AI-TOD-v2~ Aitod-v2 , VisDrone~ zhu2021visdrone , and SODA-D~ SODA , where ultra-tiny objects with a short side no larger than 4 pixels appear frequently and may be compressed to nearly a single point even on a stride-4 feature map. Meanwhile, directly reintroducing the highest-resolution backbone feature is also impractical, since it has a much larger spatial size that may lead to unacceptable extra cost, and its shallow responses contain dense background activations that may overwhelm weak tiny-object signals. These issues highlight the pressing need for detection frameworks that can balance fine-grained information preservation with computational efficiency. In this work, we propose ReDHF, a novel and efficient plug-and-play high-resolution detail reintroduction framework for Deformable-DETR-like detectors, which revives the discarded highest-resolution backbone feature while controlling computation and background disturbance through three cooperative components. First, to address the contradiction between the limited representation of small objects and the high cost of utilizing high-resolution features, we design a lightweight Cross-Scale Deformable Fusion (CSDF) module that semantically enhances the highest-resolution feature to provide more useful fine-grained cues with moderate cost. Second, considering that high-resolution features mainly include low-level edges and textures and are more likely to introduce background noise, we apply Ellipse-Guided Shallow Supervision (EGSS) to guide the shallow feature to learn more stable classification and localization priors. Moreover, since final predictions in DETR-like detectors are query-driven, we further propose Full-Scale Query Interaction (FSQI), which integrates the semantically enhanced highest-resolution feature together with higher-level features into the encoder memory, so that decoder queries can directly access pixel-level details and improve their ability of detecting tiny objects. Overall, ReDHF makes more effective use of the highest-resolution backbone feature with only a modest extra cost and significantly improves tiny object detection. Extensive experiments show that ReDHF consistently improves multiple DETR-like~ zhang2022dino, zhu2020deformable, dome-detr baselines and achieves state-of-the-art performance. Specifically, the best ReDHF model achieves 35.7 AP on AI-TOD-v2~ Aitod-v2 , improving AP to 20.8 (+1.2 ) over its corresponding baseline. In addition, the ReDHF variant built upon DINO-4scale~ zhang2022dino reduces GFLOPs by 86.7 compared with directly integrating the highest-resolution feature, as detailed in Appendix~ app:efficiency_analysis . On VisDrone~ zhu2021visdrone and SODA-D~ SODA , ReDHF again brings consistent gains. The best ReDHF model achieves 40.6 AP and 38.7 AP, and also improves AP to 33.1 (+1.6 ) and AP to 21.4 (+1.7 ), respectively. These results support our claim that the highest-resolution feature, though often discarded for efficiency, can be effectively revived through semantic enhancement. In summary, our main contributions are: [itemsep=2pt] We revisit the commonly discarded highest-resolution backbone feature in DETR-like detectors and show that its effective reuse requires addressing not only computational cost, but also weak semantics and noisy shallow responses. We propose ReDHF, which revives the discarded feature through semantically enhanced highest-resolution feature construction (CSDF), training-time shallow auxiliary supervision (EGSS), and decoder full-scale query interaction (FSQI), thereby enabling efficient high-resolution detail reintroduction for tiny-object detection. We validate ReDHF on multiple DETR-like baselines across AI-TOD-v2, VisDrone, and SODA-D. It achieves state-of-the-art performance and consistently improves the baselines with average gains of +1.5 AP , +1.7 AP , and +1.8 AP on the three datasets, respectively. Related work Tiny object detection Identifying tiny objects is inherently difficult because tiny instances provide limited visual evidence and are vulnerable to complex background noise. Early CNN-based detectors, such as Faster R-CNN~ girshick2015fast, ren2015faster , often struggle with such objects due to inadequate feature representation and limited context modeling. Some works improve tiny-object learning by enriching training samples, such as copy-pasting augmentation~ kisantal2019augmentation and instance-level transformations~ zoph2020learning . Recently, transformer-based models~ carion2020end, li2022dn, liu2022dabdetr, peng2024dfine, huang2024deim, zhang2022dino, zhao2024detrs, zhu2020deformable have shown strong potential by bypassing hand-crafted post-processing like NMS and leveraging self-attention mechanisms. Cross-DINO~ cao2025cross combines deep MLP representations with transformer encoder features through a Cross Coding Twice Module to enhance small-object details. DQ-DETR~ huang2024dq introduces density maps to adjust query numbers and positions based on instance density, while Dome-DETR~ dome-detr further improves tiny object detection by generating density-oriented features. However, these methods often rely heavily on specific density modeling or carefully designed query mechanisms, which may complicate the optimization process and limit their flexibility across different datasets. Multi-scale and high-resolution features Feature pyramids~ FPN are widely used to handle object scale variation. Advanced architectures like BiFPN~ bifpn and DetectoRS~ detectors , improve cross-level information flow through bidirectional fusion or recursive feedback. For tiny objects, fusion factors~ fusion further regulate adjacent pyramid levels to reduce the learning burden. Recent works also explore high-resolution information more explicitly. QueryDet~ querydet refines sparse locations from low to high resolutions. ESOD~ liu2024esod uses patch slicing and sparse prediction to reduce redundant computation on high-resolution features. DM-EFS~ sharma2025dm expands feature sets to enrich small-object representations. These works show the value of high-resolution cues for tiny objects. However, many detection pipelines still discard the highest-resolution backbone feature to keep computation affordable, leaving the finest local details underused. In contrast, our method revives this discarded feature through semantic enhancement, making its fine-grained details more compatible and usable for tiny object detection. Auxiliary supervision and label assignment Auxiliary supervision has been widely used to strengthen intermediate representations in object detection. In CNN-based detectors, DSFPN~ yang2019dually , LAF-YOLOv10~ farooqui2026laf and Jin et al.~ jin2022you attach auxiliary prediction heads to early backbone stages or bottom-up pathways to improve feature learning. A similar idea is adopted in DETR-like models~ zhang2022dino, huang2024dq, dome-detr, peng2024dfine, huang2024deim , where auxiliary losses on intermediate decoder layers are commonly used to stabilize training and facilitate optimization. Beyond intermediate decoder supervision, MLP-DINO~ cao2024mlp introduces query-independent category supervision to mitigate the sensitivity of category predictions to bounding box prediction. Label assignment is another key factor affecting detection performance. ATSS~ zhang2020bridging shows that positive and negative sample definitions are critical. For generic object detection, AutoAssign~ zhu2020autoassign and IQDet~ ma2021iqdet select high-quality regions according to predicted quality scores, while FCOS~ tian2019fcos formulates detection as dense per-pixel prediction. For transformer-based detectors, DS-Det~ cao2025dsdet introduces a unified Single-Query paradigm and disentangles cross-attention-based box localization with one-to-many assignment from self-attention-based deduplication with one-to-one assignment. However, tiny objects make assignment more difficult because small localization shifts can strongly affect matching quality. Recent methods therefore redesign assignment for tiny objects. UGS~ sun2025uncertainty shows that IoU-based assignment can be unstable for tiny objects and proposes a classification-based objective. DCNet~ zhang2025tiny uses dynamic scale-aware assignment, while RFLA~ rfla matches Gaussian receptive fields with ground truth to alleviate positive-sample scarcity. Unlike these methods that mainly design assignment for final prediction, our work focuses on strengthening intermediate representations. Specifically, we propose a geometry-adaptive assignment strategy and auxiliary supervision to build coarse classification and localization priors for tiny objects, while the auxiliary head is removed during inference. title: MCUFlowNet: Hardware-Aware Neural Architecture Search for Optical Flow on Microcontrollers
comment: Submitted to IEEE ISCAS 2027 (under review). 5 pages
summary: Dense optical flow allows small drones to avoid obstacles. However, few dense optical flow networks are designed for microcontrollers (MCUs) with neural accelerators, whose on-chip SRAM limits the input resolution. We present PACE-NAS, a macro-to-micro neural architecture search framework that decouples memory from latency: a macro design fixes the backbone and its peak SRAM, and a micro design searches operators and depths to trade accuracy against compiler-estimated latency. We apply it to EdgeFlowNet on a Grove Vision AI V2 board (Ethos-U55), where profiling locates the peak SRAM at the full-resolution output head. Replacing transposed convolutions with bilinear upsampling and convolutions lowers the peak SRAM by 18%, and two lightweight context modules lower the endpoint error (EPE) without raising the peak. All searched subnets share this peak, so the search needs no memory constraint. We name the Pareto-optimal models MCUFlowNet; the fastest variant, MCUFlowNet-S, runs 1.76x faster than a retrained EdgeFlowNet at a 1.6% higher EPE and, in simulated forest flights at 2 m/s, reaches the goal without collision in 51.5% of trials, against 41.8%. PACE-NAS also applies to semantic segmentation, where a searched PIDNet-S variant runs 1.17x faster at similar accuracy. Code is available at https://gitlab.kuleuven.be/emedia-research-lab/esat-stadius/mcuflownet/mcuflownet.
full_text: Dense optical flow allows small drones to avoid obstacles. However, few dense optical flow networks are designed for microcontrollers (MCUs) with neural accelerators, whose on-chip SRAM limits the input resolution. We present PACE-NAS, a macro-to-micro neural architecture search framework that decouples memory from latency: a macro design fixes the backbone and its peak SRAM, and a micro design searches operators and depths to trade accuracy against compiler-estimated latency. We apply it to EdgeFlowNet on a Grove Vision AI V2 board (Ethos-U55), where profiling locates the peak SRAM at the full-resolution output head. Replacing transposed convolutions with bilinear upsampling and convolutions lowers the peak SRAM by 18 , and two lightweight context modules lower the endpoint error (EPE) without raising the peak. All searched subnets share this peak, so the search needs no memory constraint. We name the Pareto-optimal models MCUFlowNet; the fastest variant, MCUFlowNet-S, runs 1.76 faster than a retrained EdgeFlowNet at a 1.6 higher EPE and, in simulated forest flights at 2~m/s, reaches the goal without collision in 51.5 of trials, against 41.8 . PACE-NAS also applies to semantic segmentation, where a searched PIDNet-S variant runs 1.17 faster at similar accuracy. Code is available at . Introduction sec:introduction Small aerial robots rely on timely dense optical flow, the per-pixel displacement between consecutive frames, for collision avoidance~ Bouwmeester2023NanoFlowNet , and on optical flow for autonomous landing and self-motion estimation~ ParedesValles2024Neuromorphic . Perception delay shortens the time available to avoid obstacles~ Falanga2019Latency , which motivates onboard processing~ Palossi2022Frontnet , and strict weight and power budgets favor microcontrollers (MCUs)~ vanDijk2024RouteFollowing . EdgeFlowNet, a compact multi-scale network of standard convolutions, brings dense optical flow to the Coral Edge TPU~ Raju2025EdgeFlowNet , but on MCUs its full-resolution output head sets the peak SRAM and thus bounds the input resolution. Hardware-aware neural architecture search (NAS) adapts networks to a target device~ Tan2019MnasNet ; on MCUs, it treats peak SRAM as a constraint and can be co-designed with the memory scheduling of the inference engine~ Lin2020MCUNet,Lin2021MCUNetV2 . For optical flow, however, NAS has typically targeted GPU-scale models~ Lin2024FlowNAS , and few dense flow networks are designed for MCUs with neural accelerators. This paper proposes PACE-NAS, a macro-to-micro framework for hardware-aware NAS that adapts existing dense flow networks to MCUs by decoupling memory from latency (Fig.~ fig:pace-overview ). Its macro design profiles the target platform, restructures the layers that set the peak SRAM, and adds two lightweight context modules for image-wide context where SRAM is spare; these steps fix the backbone and its peak SRAM. Its micro design trains a weight-sharing supernet over operators and depths that leave this peak unchanged, then runs an evolutionary Pareto search over endpoint error (EPE) and the latency estimated by Arm's Vela compiler~ Arm2025Vela450 . To the best of our knowledge, this is the first work to use hardware-aware NAS to design dense optical flow networks for MCUs. On Grove Vision AI V2, a board with an Arm Cortex-M55 MCU and an Ethos-U55 accelerator, we apply PACE-NAS to EdgeFlowNet and retrain two Pareto-optimal subnets, which we call MCUFlowNet-S and MCUFlowNet-L. Both our models need less peak SRAM than a retrained EdgeFlowNet; MCUFlowNet-S is 1.76 faster at a 1.6 higher EPE, while MCUFlowNet-L matches EdgeFlowNet's latency at a similar EPE. Mainly because of its lower latency, MCUFlowNet-S also raises the success rate in simulated obstacle avoidance from 41.8 to 51.5 . On semantic segmentation, PACE-NAS finds a faster PIDNet-S at similar accuracy. Related Work sec:related-work Accurate optical flow networks typically run on GPUs: RAFT refines flow recurrently from all-pairs correlations~ Teed2020RAFT , and NeuFlow~v2 reaches real-time operation on embedded GPUs with coarse global matching and lightweight recurrent updates~ Zhang2025NeuFlowV2 . Lighter pyramid networks estimate flow from coarse to fine: SPyNet warps one frame toward the other at each level and predicts a residual flow~ Ranjan2017SPyNet , and FastFlowNet adds a compact cost volume, which stores matching costs between features of the two frames~ Kong2021FastFlowNet . On MCUs, classical block matching has been accelerated with multicore parallelism~ Kuehne2022ParallelFlow , and NanoFlowNet runs on GAP8 with depthwise separable convolutions~ Bouwmeester2023NanoFlowNet . EdgeFlowNet instead uses an encoder--decoder of standard convolutions, without cost volumes or warping, and accumulates flow increments predicted at three scales~ Raju2025EdgeFlowNet ; all its operators run on the Ethos-U55, so we build on EdgeFlowNet. NAS has not yet been applied to dense optical flow on MCUs: FlowNAS searches optical flow encoders for GPU-scale models under a parameter budget~ Lin2024FlowNAS , and multi-objective zero-shot NAS returns a Pareto set for image classification~ Narduzzi2025SteerableNAS . NAS on MCUs has targeted classification and detection, where peak SRAM also depends on how the inference engine schedules layers in memory. MCUNet first fits its search space to the memory budget, then searches within it and co-designs the inference engine~ Lin2020MCUNet ; MCUNetV2 jointly searches networks and patch schedules to lower peak SRAM, at the cost of recomputing overlapping features~ Lin2021MCUNetV2 . Like MCUNet, PACE-NAS designs before it searches, but it first lowers peak SRAM by restructuring the backbone and then searches only choices that leave this peak unchanged, so the search needs no memory constraint. PACE-NAS: A Macro-to-Micro Design Framework sec:method Fig.~ fig:pace-overview outlines the four steps of PACE-NAS: platform profiling (P) and architectural restructuring (A) form the macro design, which fixes the backbone and its peak SRAM; supernet training over a configuration space (C) and evolutionary Pareto search (E) form the micro design. Fig.~ fig:backbone-space shows the resulting backbone for optical flow; the search changes only its 11 searchable boxes. Platform Profiling and Bottleneck Diagnostics (P) On Grove Vision AI V2, firmware and frame buffers leave 1434~KiB of SRAM available for the tensor arena holding intermediate tensors. Fig.~ fig:resource-profile presents per-stage Vela profiles of EdgeFlowNet in 8-bit integer (INT8) precision at , before and after restructuring: before, the peak SRAM reaches 1430~KiB at the full-resolution output head (top), only 4~KiB below the available budget. This peak arises because the head must hold its upsampled input and its output simultaneously. Together, this head and the transposed convolution feeding it also account for about 40 of the estimated cycles, so we target the transposed convolutions for restructuring. Architectural Restructuring (A) Vela~4.5.0 can cascade compatible layers (e.g., convolutions), computing them stripe by stripe so that the feature maps between them are never stored whole, but it does not cascade transposed convolutions~ Arm2025Vela450 . We therefore replace all 11 transposed convolutions with standard convolutions of the same kernel size and insert a bilinear resize before each of the four former stride-2 layers ( 2 in Fig.~ fig:backbone-space ), but keep EdgeFlowNet's coarse-to-fine accumulation of flow increments. The peak then moves to final flow upsampling (Flow accum.\ in Fig.~ fig:resource-profile ), and the restructured backbone fits a input, at which EdgeFlowNet exceeds the tensor arena. Because each convolution sees only a local window~ Hu2018SENet , we use the spare SRAM in the early stages (Fig.~ fig:resource-profile ) to add image-wide context before flow prediction. Efficient channel attention (ECA)~ Wang2020ECANet reweights the channels of the lowest-resolution feature, at of the input resolution (DB0 in Fig.~ fig:backbone-space ), where features carry broad spatial context and the tensor is small. A global broadcast gate adapted from squeeze-and-excitation~ Hu2018SENet then uses this context to modulate the decoder feature, which feeds all three flow heads (Fig.~ fig:backbone-space ). Configuration Space and Supernet Training (C) The configuration space of PACE-NAS (Fig.~ fig:backbone-space ) covers convolutional operators and residual-block depths and fixes connections, channel counts, upsamplers, ECA, and the gate. It contains no depthwise convolutions: on the Ethos-U55, depthwise convolutions reach at most about 10 of peak throughput, whereas standard convolutions exceed 90 once channel counts reach 32~ Zhao2025H4H . Unlike channel counts, its choices leave tensor sizes unchanged and change only layers that need less SRAM than final flow upsampling, where the peak lies; no subnet can raise the peak, so the search needs no memory constraint (Section~ sec:analysis ). E0 and E1 each choose among three convolutional operators, which set the spatial context passed downstream; EB0, EB1, DB0, and DB1 each hold one to three residual blocks, which set capacity across scales; and each of the five costly high-resolution head convolutions uses a or kernel for local context (Fig.~ fig:backbone-space ). Together, these choices give subnets. We train a weight-sharing supernet on FlyingChairs2 (FC2)~ Ilg2018Occlusions by sampling single paths, as in Single Path One-Shot (SPOS)~ Guo2020SPOS . Because subnets are scored with these shared weights instead of being retrained, we use FairNAS-inspired balanced sampling~ Chu2021FairNAS to give competing operators comparable training exposure. Because the paths share weights, each sampled path pulls the shared layers toward its own features during supernet training~ Lin2024FlowNAS . We therefore add FlowNAS's feature alignment distillation to the multi-scale flow and uncertainty losses~ Raju2025EdgeFlowNet : at corresponding layers, every path learns to match a frozen EdgeFlowNet teacher, so all paths move toward the same features. Evolutionary Pareto Search and Model Selection (E) As in SPOS, we score each subnet by its FC2 validation EPE with inherited supernet weights (supernet EPE) and by the latency that Vela estimates from its exported INT8 graph. NSGA-II~ Deb2002NSGAII then searches for the EPE--latency Pareto front. From this front, we retrain two subnets from scratch and deploy them in INT8 (Section~ sec:evaluation ): MCUFlowNet-S, the fastest, and MCUFlowNet-L, the closest to EdgeFlowNet in Vela-estimated latency at , for an equal-latency comparison. Experimental Evaluation sec:evaluation Experimental Setup The supernet is trained on FC2 at for 200 epochs, after which NSGA-II evaluates 800 of the 23 , 328 subnets; together, these take an estimated 17 H200 GPU-hours, about half of one full EdgeFlowNet training run (Fig.~ fig:pace-overview ). For Table~ tab:deployment , we train MCUFlowNet-S, MCUFlowNet-L, and EdgeFlowNet from scratch at , the largest input at which EdgeFlowNet fits the tensor arena, with the same recipe: 400 epochs on FC2, then 10k steps on random FC2 crops resized to the input and 80k steps on a 3:1 mix of FC2 crops and FlyingThings3D (FT3D) frames~ Mayer2016FlyingThings . For every model trained on FT3D, we keep the checkpoint with the lowest FT3D validation EPE. Test EPE is computed on all pairs of the Final pass of the MPI-Sintel training set~ Butler2012Sintel at its central crop, without clipping large ground-truth displacements; deployed models see resized inputs, and their outputs are rescaled to the crop. The deployed models are quantized post-training to INT8 with 64 FC2 calibration pairs and compiled with Vela 4.5.0 for an Ethos-U55 with 64 multiply--accumulate (MAC) units at 400~MHz. Latencies in Tables~ tab:deployment and~ tab:segmentation are measured on the board with TensorFlo

title: Hierarchical Incremental Beta Splatting for Online Reconstruction
comment: accepted to WACV 2027, project page: https://linus-franke.com/hibs/
summary: Online 3D Gaussian Splatting reconstructs a scene during capture: each keyframe spawns primitives once and refines them for only a few dozen iterations, leaving little chance to fix poor initialization or missing detail. Gaussians are also inherently soft, needing many overlaps for solid surfaces. We present Hierarchical Incremental Beta Splatting (HIBS), which brings beta kernels to incremental reconstruction. Their shape parameter interpolates between a soft, Gaussian-like profile and a flat-topped, near-opaque surfel, acting as a confidence dial for geometry. Our confidence-aware spawning uses geometric observability and multi-view depth agreement to initialize both opacity and shape, producing solid primitives where geometry is verifiable and soft, correctable primitives where it is not. As online densification, error-driven relocation recycles stale primitives into photometric-error hotspots. Bounded beta kernel support enables exact tile culling and faster rasterization, and a closed-form, shape-preserving merging formulation provides a level-of-detail (LOD) hierarchy for fast optimization and real-time rendering. On Mip-NeRF 360 in the on-the-fly protocol, HIBS improves PSNR by up to 0.8 dB while reducing optimization time by up to 40%. Project page: https://linus-franke.com/hibs/
full_text: We present an online method for incremental reconstruction of primitive-based radiance fields from an unordered image stream. Building on beta kernels, we use kernel shape as a confidence dial: each keyframe spawns primitives with opacity and shape initialized from measured multi-view confidence. Short optimization bursts, fused rasterization, error-driven relocation, and closed-form LoD merging enable efficient reconstruction. Compared to i3DGS~ meuleman2026immediate , we achieve higher quality with about faster optimization. fig:teaser Online 3D Gaussian Splatting reconstructs a scene during capture: each keyframe spawns primitives once and refines them for only a few dozen iterations, leaving little chance to fix poor initialization or missing detail. Gaussians are also inherently soft, needing many overlaps for solid surfaces. We present Hierarchical Incremental Beta Splatting (HIBS), which brings beta kernels to incremental reconstruction. Their shape parameter interpolates between a soft, Gaussian-like profile and a flat-topped, near-opaque surfel, acting as a confidence dial for geometry. Our confidence-aware spawning uses geometric observability and multi-view depth agreement to initialize both opacity and shape, producing solid primitives where geometry is verifiable and soft, correctable primitives where it is not. As online densification, error-driven relocation recycles stale primitives into photometric-error hotspots. Bounded beta kernel support enables exact tile culling and faster rasterization, and a closed-form, shape-preserving merging formulation provides a level-of-detail (LOD) hierarchy for fast optimization and real-time rendering. On Mip-NeRF 360 in the on-the-fly protocol, HIBS improves PSNR by up to 0.8 dB while reducing optimization time by up to 40 . \ firstname.lastname\ @uni-wuerzburg.de Introduction sec:intro 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS)~ kerbl3dgs has made high-quality radiance-field capture practical, but the standard pipeline is offline: images are collected, poses are recovered by structure-from-motion~ schoenberger2016sfm , and the scene is optimized for tens of thousands of iterations. Recent work instead reconstructs during capture~ meuleman2025onthefly,matsuki2024monogs,keetha2024splatam , providing immediate feedback and reducing the delay from capture to observable reconstruction to seconds. We target this online regime by reconsidering the primitive itself. Online reconstruction inverts the assumptions of offline 3DGS. Each incoming image is registered as a keyframe, spawns new primitives once, and is optimized only for a short burst before the next keyframe arrives. This leaves little room for gradient-driven clone/split densification, opacity resets, or long optimization schedules to repair poorly initialized primitives. In practice, what spawning produces is largely what the model keeps. The critical decisions---what to place and how much to trust it---must therefore be made at initialization from measurable evidence. We argue that under these constraints the primitive itself can be improved, and that the Gaussian is suboptimal. A Gaussian is fully opaque only at its center and translucent elsewhere; representing a solid surface therefore requires overlapping many Gaussians, together with the densification and long optimization that offline 3DGS can afford. Without this machinery, online reconstruction must spawn translucent Gaussians and hope a short optimization burst can arrange them correctly. We instead use the beta kernel~ liu2025dbs , whose bounded profile has a learnable shape parameter that continuously interpolates between a Gaussian-like volume and a flat-topped, near-opaque surfel. A single beta primitive can thus be a flat-topped surface patch while retaining a soft representation for uncertain geometry, thin structures, or volume. While Deformable Beta Splatting~ liu2025dbs uses this parameter offline as a compactness degree of freedom learned over long optimization schedules, we use it from geometric evidence as a confidence axis. The key question is therefore not only how to optimize the shape, but whether the available evidence justifies treating a primitive as a solid surface. That evidence must be geometric, not merely photometric. Naively spawning solid kernels is harmful: a compact, near-opaque primitive at the wrong depth blocks transmittance and suppresses gradients behind it. Conversely, a low photometric error does not guarantee correct geometry. When the triangulation baseline is small relative to depth, many depths explain the observed views similarly well, yet only a narrow range remains consistent under parallax. We therefore use the beta shape parameter as a confidence dial. Confidence-aware spawning combines two independent geometric cues, Multi-view stereo (MVS) agreement with an aligned monocular prior and depth observability, to initialize each primitive along this soft-to-solid axis: well-constrained candidates are spawned solid, while ambiguous ones remain soft and correctable. As additional views arrive, a lifetime controller updates the same parameter from accumulated multi-view evidence, progressively turning confirmed geometric confidence into solidity. To compensate for the absence of offline densification, we introduce error-driven relocation. Near-dead primitives are recycled into photometric-error hotspots, where render-preserving copies provide additional capacity precisely where the current model is deficient. The beta representation is also performant. Its bounded support yields an exact tile-culling bound and faster rasterization, while its closed-form moments enable a shape-aware level-of-detail hierarchy for large captures. Together, these components yield an online reconstruction system in which the primitive is adapted to the short optimization horizon rather than relying on offline densification to compensate for it. Our experiments show improved reconstruction quality and efficiency across online, benchmark, and large-scale captures. In summary, our contributions are: We identify the Gaussian primitive as suboptimal in the spawn-once, optimize-briefly regime and adopt the beta kernel as a confidence-adaptive online primitive whose shape ranges from soft to solid. We introduce confidence-aware spawning, which initializes opacity and shape from independent depth agreement and geometric observability. We introduce error-driven relocation, a render-preserving online alternative to clone/split densification that recycles near-dead primitives into photometric-error hotspots. We derive a closed-form merge for beta primitives, preserving their shape statistics and enabling a level-of-detail hierarchy for large-scale reconstruction. We develop a fast beta rasterizer with a shape-correct culling bound that exploits the kernel's compact support. The project page and source code can be found at: . Related Work sec:related Novel View Synthesis. Neural Radiance Fields~ mildenhall2020nerf,barron2022mipnerf360 synthesize photorealistic novel views from posed images, but volumetric rendering remains computationally expensive. 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS)~ kerbl3dgs instead enables efficient rasterization and fast optimization. Subsequent work improves compositing and rendering fidelity~ yu2024mip,radl2024stopthepop,hahlbohm2025htgs and scales to large scenes with hierarchical representations such as Hierarchical 3DGS~ kerbl2024hierarchical and Octree-GS~ ren2024octree . These methods are predominantly offline, relying on precomputed poses and long optimization schedules, whereas we target reconstruction during capture. A range of systems reconstruct 3DGS maps incrementally from video, including SLAM-based methods~ matsuki2024monogs,keetha2024splatam,huang2024photoslam,peng2024rtgslam,zhu2025loopsplat,homeyer2024droid,cheng2025s3pogs and joint pose-and-reconstruction approaches~ Fu_2024_CVPR,lin2025longsplat . SLAM methods spend far more per keyframe, e.g., hundreds of mapping iterations, densification, and long final refinement~ matsuki2024monogs,zhu2025loopsplat . Feed-forward and hybrid methods~ jiang2025anysplat,lin2025depthanything3,li2025streamgs,li2026artdeco trade scene-specific optimization for speed, typically at reduced fidelity. Closest to our setting, On-the-Fly NVS~ meuleman2025onthefly and i3DGS~ meuleman2026immediate reconstruct image streams with short optimization bursts and no densification, using learned matching and hierarchical structures. However, these methods retain the Gaussian and spawn it once per view. Our work instead revisits the primitive itself, introducing a controllable notion of solidity specifically for this short-burst regime. Primitive Kernels and Densification. Alternative splatting primitives have been proposed to improve compactness, surface accuracy, or geometric fidelity, including generalized and radial kernels~ hamdi2024ges, huang2025deformable , planar Gaussians~ huang20242dgs , point sprites~ ruckert2022adop,aliev2020neural, harrer2023inovis , linear and convex primitives~ vonluetzow2025linprim,held2025convex , volumetric ellipsoids~ mai2025ever , and trilinear splats~ franke2024trips . Deformable radial kernels~ huang2025deformable are flexible, but planar and without closed-form moments, which our spawning and merge rely on. Most closely related, Deformable Beta Splatting (DBS)~ liu2025dbs,liu2026universal introduces a bounded beta kernel with a learnable shape parameter spanning Gaussian-like and surfel-like profiles. DBS learns this shape offline together with densification; we instead initialize it from geometric evidence and update it online throughout. 3DGS densification has been refined through error- and gradient-based splitting, budget-aware pruning, and MCMC-based relocation~ rotabulo2024revising,yu2024gaussian,fang2024minisplatting,kheradmand2024mcmc . In particular, 3DGS-MCMC~ kheradmand2024mcmc reuses low-opacity primitives by relocating them onto live ones with render-preserving corrections. These techniques assume long offline optimization and periodic densification, whereas our online setting has neither. We adapt relocation to this regime by recycling near-dead primitives and targeting them using attributed photometric error. Efficient Rasterization. Recent work accelerates 3DGS through improved backward passes, gradient reduction, tighter tile bounds, and fused optimization~ mallick2024taming,durvasula2024distwar,radl2024stopthepop,hanson2025speedy,hahlbohm2026fastergs . We build on these ideas for the online burst, but derive the rasterization bounds for the bounded beta kernel. In particular, the Gaussian cutoff is not valid for low-opacity solid kernels, making the beta-specific bound a correctness requirement in addition to an efficiency improvement. Depth Priors and Uncertainty. Monocular and multi-view depth predictors are commonly used to initialize or regularize radiance-field reconstruction~ yang2024depthanythingv2,lin2025depthanything3,wang2025vggt ; for example, Meuleman .~ meuleman2025onthefly combine aligned monocular depth with guided MVS. Uncertainty is often estimated post-hoc or used for view selection~ goli2024bayesrays,jiang2024fisherrf . We instead incorporate uncertainty directly into the online primitive lifecycle: agreement between independent depth estimates and geometric observability determine the primitive's opacity and shape, while the evolving shape field provides a live confidence representation. In i3DGS~ meuleman2026immediate , registration matches each frame against previously registered keyframes using place recognition and learned feature matching~ alibey2023mixvpr,potje2024xfeat,lindenberger2023lightglue , initializes the pose

title: InstantHand: Feed-Forward 3D Gaussian Splatting for Animatable Hand Avatar Reconstruction from a Single Image
summary: Hand avatar reconstruction typically relies on multi-view capture or per-subject optimization, limiting its scalability. We introduce InstantHand, a feed-forward framework that constructs an animatable 3D Gaussian hand avatar from a single image using off-the-shelf MANO, camera, and mask estimates, without test-time optimization. Image-averaged losses provide insufficient supervision for alpha leakage, which thickens thin finger contours. To address this issue, we propose a Soft Alpha Band regularizer that concentrates supervision on silhouette boundaries. Furthermore, colors regressed from image features can drift toward a learned prior even in observed regions. Our Reliability-gated Appearance Transfer preserves observed appearance by transferring source colors according to each Gaussian's rendering contribution, while completing unobserved regions using the learned prior conditioned on global source identity. InstantHand constructs an avatar in 2.84 seconds and renders at 161 FPS, matching per-subject-optimized baselines on InterHand2.6M and remaining competitive in zero-shot evaluation on HanCo.
full_text: Single-image Feed-forward Gaussian Hand Avatar Reconstruction. InstantHand constructs an animatable 3D Gaussian hand avatar from a single image without per-subject optimization. fig:hook Hand avatar reconstruction typically relies on multi-view capture or per-subject optimization, limiting its scalability.
